paragraphs.text: You ask me, most reverend of priests, how we should answer the Arians, who try with blasphemous mouth to assert: "It cannot be," they say, "but that the begotten is younger than the unbegotten." In reply, as though ordered to break my whole silence, I will venture to speak, not so much to give instruction on the matter as to confess the faith. I will take care above all not to wrap things already obscure in themselves in the effort of polished speech, but to set out some indications from a poor understanding, which may seem to serve comprehension rather than ornament. I answer, then, as disciples are accustomed to answer masters who question them. So I speak at the bidding of your Beatitude, so that you may examine my lack of skill; I implore you to teach me. For if I kept silent before so learned a man, I could hardly know what I do not know. In speaking of the unbegotten, we must know that the substances of things are one thing and the names of things another. For example, when you have said "gold" and "silver," you have not at once produced the metal itself, but the words for the metal. For gold is one thing in the property of its kind and another in the naming of speech; it is one thing when we name it and another when we hold it.

Begotten and unbegotten are a signification of the deity, not the deity itself; they are a name for the nature, not the nature. The designation of unbegotten and begotten serves to let you understand who subsists from whom, and to recognize that the Father is not from the Son, but the Son from the Father. Principle from principle is both one and without beginning, just as when you say "God from God," yet not two gods but one is meant. So begotten, unbegotten, and proceeding from both point to persons, not natures. For the majesty, which in the Father is undivided from the Son and the Holy Spirit, can be distinguished by names but cannot be ranked by degrees.

At this point you must be forewarned and apply the attention of your mind. Perhaps you say: "Because he is from him, he is later than him." Come, let us nourish our understanding on this with some comparisons. Let us see whether anything exists from another and yet is not later in age than that from which it exists. For example, this very name "son" is believed to be derived from the name "father," and yet it is not found to be later, because unless the one were born, the other would not be called father. Here is a name absolutely coeval with that from which it comes; and though the son is from the father, the son gives the father his name: the person of the one born acquires for the begetter the title of fatherly love. Though the one is from the other, the one is not proved later nor the other older. Again, since the Son is called by the name "arm" from the mighty powers of his works, see: the arm proceeds from the body, and yet the arm is no later in age than the body. A word is uttered from the voice, and yet, though it is born from the mouth, it is not proved to be later than the voice. Fire and heat form an undivided partnership; but though heat is understood beyond doubt to come from fire, fire is by no means recognized as prior to its heat. See, here is a thing that seems to exist from another, and yet it is joined to that from which it exists without any interval of time.

But when we come to God, "begotten" is like just and justice, wise and wisdom, merciful and mercy. We understand, according to the Apostle, that justice and wisdom arise absolutely from God, who is just and wise; and just as he was never just without justice or wise without wisdom, so the Son is from the Father, but the Father could never be without the Son.

No doubt the Arians do not dare deny our Savior, but in calling him lesser they cannot assert that he is God. For God by nature subsists in the dignity of fullness, and their impiety testifies in its first confession that it worships one God. But because it makes him younger, it makes two through the one thought to be older, and cuts through the solidity of the unity. For the very name "lesser" points to another who is greater than he. Who is older than he who declares of himself, "I am the Alpha and the Omega, the first and the last"; who, when the Jews asked him who he was, answered, "The beginning, who also speak to you"; who confirms with truthful voice through the prophet, "Before me there was no God, and after me there will be none"? If the Father says this, he confirms that no inferior began after him; if the Son, he declares that there was no one at all before him. Of him the prophetic word clearly intimates: "This is our God, and no other shall be reckoned beside him," and after this: "He was seen among men and lived among men." According to these texts, then, between begotten and unbegotten there is no order, because he is one; no time intervenes, because he is first; he is not to be placed after, because he is alone; he is not to be called lesser, because he is full. Therefore he is called perfect and of simple nature, beyond reckoning and impassible, even though we truly and for our salvation confess that he suffered for us according to the flesh.

After this, in the next place, you ask me how, with respect to the substance of God, it could be written in a certain letter: "He felt nothing with the feeling of one who suffers, but he felt with the affection of one who suffers with another."

First, it is very easy to know something that did not escape even the philosophers: that in man the various affections, that is, justice, mercy, holiness, benevolence, and devotion, are things that come to him from outside, and for that reason they are called affections. But God is not affected by them in a passible way, because they are known to be in him continually and by nature. So what in man is affection and grace is in God power and nature. As for the saying, "He felt nothing with the feeling of one who suffers, but felt with the affection of one who suffers with another," why should anyone not venture to say it in that sense, since the prophetic word also records: "Lord, do not rebuke me in your anger, nor chasten me in your wrath"; and, "The Lord has sworn, and he will not repent"; and again, "The Lord was angry with his people and abhorred his inheritance"? Likewise, with differing affection, he is described as having loved Jacob and hated Esau. He is said to be grieved by our sins and to rejoice in his works; and, as one subject to affections, he says of himself, "I repent that I made man"; and from the highest seat of heaven he declares, "Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?" He even seems to show the affection of one who suffers with another when he says, "I was hungry and you gave me food, I was thirsty and you gave me drink," and other things of this kind, which come to mind in abundance.

Suppose some priest, endowed with a manifold knowledge of languages and placed among various nations, sets out to instruct a Hebrew in Hebrew, a Greek in Greek, and a Roman in Latin. He would shape his words to the understanding of each, fit the speech of his mouth to the mind of each one, and distribute the differing voices of one heart and [sinner's] breast to various hearers. In the same way God, when about to speak with man, deigns to take up man's language; and, being about to take on human form as well, he expresses the affections of our condition through the sounds our understanding knows. For when he describes the functions of the five human senses, saying, "The eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous, and his ears are open to their prayers"; and again, "The mouth of the Lord has spoken"; likewise, "And he smelled the sweet savor"; and, "My hand made all these things. Heaven is my throne, and the earth is the footstool for my feet"—he conveys to our hearts the workings of things under the figure of bodily members. Hence, by his ineffable condescension toward the human race, which does not disdain to name and address servants as friends and sons, man converses with him in turn in human speech and manner.

Moreover, God's anger is justice; God's fury is the vigor of severity; God's having sworn is his having decreed; God's having repented is a sentence that has nonetheless often been changed; and when he says that he is harmed by someone persecuting him, he shows the guilt of the one who does harm. If these exchanges of human speech are taken away, the ministry of prayer, and every means by which God is either understood or preached, is entirely shut off to us. Why, then, among such sayings, may it not be said: "but he felt with the affection of one who suffers with another"?

If, then, a simple and plain answer has satisfied the master who examines me, let us pass on to the third question, which you bid me answer: what among created things is to be considered corporeal, and what incorporeal. On this I will set out some points, not from presumption in my own judgment but according to the opinion of the holy elders, especially since these matters cannot harm the mind, can nourish it toward faith, and, to the extent that they show the Son to be equal to the Father, can arm and guide us against the perversities of the Arians. So, since the discussion concerns a loftier subject, our sense and mind must be prepared for a subtler understanding. Some of the most learned of the fathers assert that some things are invisible, others incorporeal. Whatever has been created, they define as matter, comprehensible to its maker and corporeal. For they assert that the nature both of souls and of angels is corporeal, because these are circumscribed by a beginning and by space. As we read in a certain treatise of St. Jerome: "They think," he says, "that the globes of the stars are embodied spirits"; and again: "If angels," he says, "and even the heavenly bodies are said to be unclean in comparison with God, what do you think man should be reckoned?" Yet amid all this you deny that the soul is corporeal, on the ground that, according to the opinion of some, it is not local and does not subsist in quality or quantity—which, it is clear, must be believed of the majesty of God alone. For we read in a certain treatise of the fathers that is most widely accepted: "To enter and fill all things," he says, "is possible for the Trinity alone, which so penetrates the whole intellectual nature that it can not only embrace and surround it, but also glide into it and, being incorporeal, be poured into a body. For although we declare that there are some spiritual natures, such as angels, archangels, and the other powers, and our own soul too, or certainly this subtle air, yet they are by no means to be thought incorporeal. For they have, in their own way, a body by which they subsist, though one much finer, beyond comparison, than our bodies, according to the statement of the Apostle, who says, 'There are both heavenly bodies and earthly bodies.' From this it is plainly gathered that nothing is incorporeal except God alone, and that therefore all spiritual and intellectual substances can be penetrated by him alone." Since this is so, you object to me that the soul is not corporeal because, as was said, it is not local and does not subsist in quality or quantity. How dangerous it is to believe this will be shown in what follows. For now, at this stage of our treatise, the discussion will turn on this point: if the soul is neither local nor subject to quantity, let us concede that it is beyond doubt incorporeal; but if we show that it is bounded by quantity or enclosed in a place, then you yourself will no longer doubt that it also consists in a body. How is it not local, when, set within the limbs and bound to the inward parts, it is held enclosed by the condition of its substance, free to wander only in its motions? But if you think it must be asserted that the soul is not local because it roams over various things through its senses and is spread abroad in its thoughts, it must first be understood that the state of the soul is one thing and the movement of thought that is born from the soul is another. Therefore we should rather suppose this: whenever it imagines something to itself, it is rather occupied with its own motions within itself; and whatever else it seems to behold is rather pictured for it in the mirror of memory. For when it thinks of a dear one who is absent, has it thereby satisfied its longing as though it had seen him? Or when, for example, it paints the likeness of Peter or Paul in the hidden places of the mind, has it at once entered the innermost dwellings of paradise, where we know them to be? Or when, after a reading, it sets before itself in its heart the flames of that rich man, has it already gone down to the places of his torments and the depths of hell, inaccessible to the living? Beyond doubt it either fashions all these things within the hidden places of the breast through various likenesses, or, if unsteady thought, driven by a slippery motion, runs about outside the soul's seat, it does this very thing in a local way: whether it thinks of a city or of any region, it is fixed only where its attention lingers, wherever the mind's intent snatches it. It can imagine some things to itself; it cannot embrace all things at once. So when the soul has thought of Alexandria or Jerusalem, if it was truly there with its whole presence, as you suppose, let it describe to us the layout of the places, the faces of the people, the movements and doings of the crowds. Take this very thing: we are now exchanging words with one another through the action of the spirit. I feel that I am speaking with you, but within my own consciousness; I do not feel that I have come to you. For if the soul is truly believed to be carried along with its senses, then it is itself present through its thoughts to those whom it remembers. See, in these present moments I think of you and see you with a remembering mind, but I am wholly ignorant of what you are doing, and whether you are at rest or occupied with reading or prayer. This happens because I reach you by the affection of the heart, not by the very reality of my substance. For the nature of our soul does not consist in its motions, which we feel to be now very good, now very bad. If it is to be believed to consist of its thoughts, why, when these sometimes vanish and perish, does it itself endure in its vigor and liveliness? How many frequent thoughts and cares die in us, even to our benefit, and rather serve the freedom of the inner life! If the soul consisted of them, without doubt it could not survive their perishing. Hence reason itself tells our consciences rather this: that each soul either brings forth many thoughts conceived within itself from the causes of things, or sends out its senses, like certain officers or servants, to be occupied with various needs, while it itself rests in the chamber of its body, from which it will depart once. Therefore, to bring forward once more a sufficient example that the soul is local: was not the soul of Lazarus within his body while life remained? When life withdrew, was it not exiled from the dwelling of the body? And when it was poured back into the lifeless body, did it not return, called back to the place from which it had been absent? You see it, as it were, driven out of its lodging and restored again to the lodging from which it had been absent—and do you contend that it is not local? But why do I speak of corruptible man, when he whose flesh did not see corruption possessed a spotless soul, yes, but a local one, which he certainly had within himself when he was fastened to the cross, and which beyond doubt he sent out of himself when he lay in the tomb? How is that not local which the flesh contains, life joins, and death separates? But if, as you say, the nature of souls does not admit the constraint of place, are those souls that are shut in the prison of hell not then absent from the region of paradise? Tell me, I beg you, if they are not local, how does that vast chasm, by its grim interposition, separate sinners from the company and fellowship of the righteous, so that they can neither go from here to there nor cross from there to here? Now it is perfectly plain that things contained in spaces are circumscribed by quantity. If you have acknowledged that the soul is local, grant that it is corporeal. Tell me, did not the very soul of our glorious Redeemer leave the world when he rose to heaven?

For my part, I would not doubt that even the angels are local. It is certain that they are now contained in the heavens, now borne through the empty spaces of the air, now sent down to earthly things; the divine word describes them ascending and descending in the patriarch's vision. Surely, if they were not local and were everywhere, they could not come and go by ascending and descending. The most blessed Gabriel himself, who testifies that he stands before God, when he announced that the Lord of the heavens was to be poured into Mary's womb, and stood before the eyes of the mother under [the ordinance of the Lord's command], was beyond doubt absent from heaven; he did not occupy the seas, he did not fill the empty and wide expanses of the vast air, but occupied only the place in which he was. Since this is so, whatever occupies a place is a body. And I do not know how one can escape the law of place who is sent from place to place, and like a body is carried along by motion and approach, comes down by weight, runs about by mobility, goes, returns, is absent, and ascends. Or that other one, I suppose, is local, who has not been in heaven since he was cast out of heaven; and he showed that he was not the only local being when, hurled down from on high, he dragged with him a third part of the stars. Tell me, if he has no body, what fell in that casting down? Why do you deny a corporeal nature to one whose fall you dare not deny? And if, as you say, he has no body, he will not burn; but where, except in a body, will he feel that fire which is prepared for the devil and his angels? I think it superfluous even to mention the claim that he drew a certain density from a concretion of elements through his dwelling in this air. Tell me, if he had no body, where in the air was there any concretion, where could this density, whatever it is, gather itself, if he did not bring down with him something corporeal from that heavenly citadel? He will carry, as I see it, someone else's body to torment! So recognize, even from your own assertion, that it is a body. That is a body which is tainted, which is stained, which is altered by any addition that comes to it. This one, then, once the firstborn of the angels, has now become the prince of darkness, and, as though corporeal, was once beautiful and is now degenerate; once conspicuous with heavenly splendor, now defiled by the foul horror of hellish sin. That, I say, is a body which has a place, is driven out by action, is circumscribed by quantity, is changed by quality, and is wasted by pain. Since this is the case, see into what a deep crime those plunge themselves who call the soul incorporeal. First, since God, the author of the universe, is recorded to have made all things in number and weight, then the soul is believed to be exempt from the matter of the whole creation. Since it is not corporeal, it is not local either; if it is not contained by place, then it is diffused everywhere, and is said to enter, to fill all things, and to be present everywhere—as though the creature were joined to its creator and frailty to its author, so as to be reckoned no longer a thing of God but a part of God. See where the fall into deep error leads those who assert it. Indeed, the things that are above us are invisible to us; but to him all things are both comprehensible and corporeal, for he made all things from nothing, and as he established them by his work, so he embodied them in matter; and to all things, among which the soul too is counted, just as he assigned weight, number <and measure>, so he also set quantity. Amid all this, if someone perhaps thinks it should be asserted, as was said, that the subtle angelic nature, through a certain contagion gathered by mixing with this air, is found liable to the flames, then the punishment will rage in the air alone (if, as he says, it is the airy part that will burn)—not in the angel himself, but outside him. Yet beyond doubt it is nothing other than the substance of a body where the force of pain can hold sway. See where this rash and ignorant notion tends: whoever speaks of the soul as incorporeal also confesses it incomprehensible, and so ascribes to the thing made what belongs to the Maker alone, shares the privileges of majesty with created things, and stretches an unmerited power in the creature to the point of wronging the Creator. If we inquire carefully into the outcome to which you are carrying your thought: it was this very belief, above all, that rolled the devil down from his station in that blessed seat, and for this he lost the dignity of an angel, presuming that he had the nature of God.

There is, therefore, one incorporeal God, because he is both incomprehensible and diffused everywhere; for he took no material beginning from the matter of any corporeal thing that was made. And therefore the Son is coeternal with the Father, because, founded by no work and circumscribed by no beginning, he is diffused in incorporeal majesty over all the things that he wrought within the body of the world, things comprehensible and corporeal to their potter. Begotten from the unbegotten, that is, from the Father, yet always with the Father, in the undivided fellowship of the Holy Spirit, he rules over the things he called forth from nothing.
PREFACE.
To the most learned and excellent Sollius Sidonius, former prefect [?] and patrician, from Claudianus.

You, who judge carefully when to keep silent and weigh well when to speak, have ordered me to publish the books I composed on the state of the soul. It was right for me either to yield to the expertise or to trust the friendship of so learned and so loving a man. But as you know very well, many others, and very great men, gave me this same task along with you. I would not have taken it on lightly had I not judged that refusing it was more dangerous than doing it was laborious. Yet even unprompted it would have been my duty too, for my own part and as far as I am able, to assert the truth. So I have written these few things as seeds of reasoning, as it were. Any diligent person who takes them up in earnest will, I think, be able to draw much from them, and though these flow from narrow little veins, over a longer course they will swell into great rivers. For my part, short of time and preoccupied in mind, I was content, given the importance of the matter, to point out as briefly as possible, as if with a finger, what is to be avoided and what is to be followed. As for that little work published without an author and broadcast everywhere, it has been led out into battle with its whole column and has fought us hand to hand. Whether it has won or given way, you, most eloquent of the eloquent, must give the verdict. But so that every reader may learn from this preface the order of my writing: at its very beginning the first book briefly establishes that the impassible Godhead is subject to no passion whatever. After that it carries on a varied struggle with the adversary about the state of the soul. Then, likewise, to instruct the reader in the more obscure matters, it gives, modestly, with restraint and as sparingly as it could, a foretaste of some points from geometry and arithmetic, and also from dialectic and from certain rules of the philosophers, as they proved useful, while engaging again and again with the opposing side. And so, with some of my own points added and without inserting the words of others, the book comes to its end.

After its opening, the second book discusses measure, number and weight, not idly and, I believe, not without profit. There, if the student is attentive, he will be helped by piety to climb through the ranks of different creatures. He may not yet reach the happiness of contemplating the Trinity, Creator of all things, but he will surely reach a firmer confidence in believing in it. From there to its end the whole book makes use of witnesses.
The third argues a little at its beginning. Then it pursues the wounded as they scatter from the enemy line. Finally it neither spurns peace nor fears battle with the unknown adversary.

There, most learned of men, you have read what you are about to read. Only be sure to remember that what you order to be made public must not be put out without care for your own name. My doubt is not about the weight of the subject but about the slightness of my treatment. So stand by your advice and defend it, because if anything here is amiss, I shall be at risk for having written it, but you for having published it. Farewell, and flourish in good strength, restorer of the ancient eloquence.
THE FIRST BOOK OF CLAUDIANUS MAMERTUS ON THE STATE OF THE SOUL.
I. ON THE OPINIONS OF THE IGNORANT AND THOSE WHO STUBBORNLY DEFEND THEIR PRIDE.

A great fault in the human race, Sollius Sidonius, dearest brother, and the fault of many, is arrogant ignorance together with a stubborn persistence in defending opinions wrongly assumed. Most mortals are either deceived in their mind's eye by images of bodily things drawn in through the bodily senses, like shadows of things, or else in old age they become children again, clinging to the tender convictions they once held in infancy. If they have any skill in speaking, they neglect the causes of things, scorn the soul of reason, and love the body of words. There are two roads to the truth: either we submit in faith to an authority already established, or we press on to knowledge by reasoning. These people say nothing that is chiefly commanded by authority or urged by reason. Scorning the few who are learned, they deceive the ignorant, who are the great crowd. But they in turn are deceived by those same people they deceive. For they are praised, praised falsely, and they believe it, and this above all endangers the health of the mind. Add to this the constant striving of an ever-souring envy, which is both the crime and the punishment of a jealous mind. For if those whom they assail with unjust hatred put forward anything true for the common good, they at once maintain the opposite, even when they think the same. And so, keeping their hatred unspent and firm toward those they have resolved to hate, they have no fear of having thrown away the truth. They hate their neighbour, then, and they hate God as well. And since they have scorned these two commandments, in which all the precepts and the whole law are fulfilled, it is no wonder that they do not think rightly about either God or man, when they drive both far from themselves by hatred. Yet this vice of theirs, though it deserves punishment, troubles me less, because even when they forge the weapons of ill will against others, they themselves are pierced more by their own blows and receive the wounds they try to inflict. The authors of hatred are the first to be punished by its goads. By far the greatest and far more dangerous crime is this: they foolishly conceive opinions hostile to catholic soundness, put them forward emptily, assert them proudly, write them rashly and defend them vehemently. And since they have slipped through imprudence, as humans do, they choose to defend the guilt of their boldness with stubborn obstinacy, so as not to seem capable of having sinned. They assert their opinions openly, yet no less do they mutter in secret, earnestly begging the ignorant with seductive flatteries to accept their opinion above all and to agree with them. They even swear that what they teach is full of truth and brings salvation. If you ask for authority, they reply that the secrets of such matters can by no means be approached except by reason, that most subtle searcher of things. If you demand that same reason at the decisive point, they add that one ought rather to yield to authority, and not, as I said before [?], to enter the sea of disputation because of certain hidden reefs in the arguments. So they evade reason by appealing to authority, and authority by objecting with reason, and they use both in such a way as to use neither. And if disputation shuts them in a little more tightly, they say there are certain saints for whom it is very easy to solve questions of this kind, that they themselves depend rather on another's authority, and that they will follow above all whatever someone else has laid down. Who could bear this, or think it could be borne in any way, that someone should both deny knowledge and lay claim to teaching, asserting his own ideas when there is no examiner and covering them up when there is one? 'But,' you say, 'where is this speech going?' I have indeed spoken at greater length than I wished, out of vexation and weariness with present affairs. For recently I came upon some people who were reading a certain document with great eagerness. As is the way of mortals, they were drawn by finding a new work and had set their minds intently on understanding it. When they pressed it on me unasked, as though it were something I needed to know, I did not refuse to look at it.
II. WHERE HE RECALLS THAT HE CAME UPON A BOOK WITHOUT AN AUTHOR.

The first part of the little work concerned God begotten and unbegotten. It barely wandered about the doors of that most sublime question, and it put forward an opinion not wholly uncatholic, though argued far below its subject. So in my judgement the gravity of the subject made up for the weakness of the reasoning. When I read on and came to the rest, I noticed that the author of the little work was striving hard, with certain circumlocutions, to make the Godhead be believed capable of suffering. I asked his name, but it was revealed neither by any reply nor in the writing. I confess I began to regard the pen behind such a page with great suspicion. And as we usually do in places that give way because constant water undermines them, or are slippery with a smooth slope, or overhang a hollow, or are rough with stakes, I tested the unknown path with cautious step rather than running along it, until I entered the third part of the question, as it is there divided. From that point there appeared an opinion that called not for examination but for rejection, expressed in thoughtless language and earnestly eager to make it seem, if it could somehow, that the soul is a body. So with no force of argument, with no law commanding it and no reason persuading, the third discourse ends in this plainly futile undertaking.

And first I would like to ask what reason there could have been for him to avoid being known when about to take up such great questions and speak of such lofty things. If you argue with a good conscience, why do you hide your name? If you are afraid of being recognized, why do you publish the work, not to say why do you write such things at all? Or are you perhaps following the example of our forebears in this? But I see that the prophets, the evangelists, the apostles, and afterwards many of the authentic commentators set their names at the head of their volumes. Others even began their works with their own names, as in 'Peter, an apostle of Christ', and 'Paul', and so too other founders and teachers of the Church. Clearly they knew that the empty or harmful things of the apocrypha had to be guarded against. Yet even so they could not escape the fabrications of reckless deceivers. That is why our catholic soundness does not accept many writings headed with the names of Paul and of many saints: it does not judge the merit of a work by the allure of a name, but [judges] its author by the truth of what is written [?]. Indeed, the fact that this page is put about while its author is hidden gives clear evidence that it was condemned even by the man who composed it. For no one seeks to be hidden unless he fears being recognized. I cannot wonder enough, however, why the man who could show such judgement in suppressing his name showed no concern to avoid doing harm.
III. THAT THE IMPASSIBLE GODHEAD IS SUBJECT TO NO PASSION WHATEVER.

But to return to our purpose, let us look at the actual words of the work mentioned above. Addressing the man to whom he sends these things, a man he took care to keep hidden just as he hid himself, he says: "You ask me in what sense it was said in a certain letter, with regard to the substance of God…" Here he chose not to indicate what letter it was, whose it was, to whom it was written, or whom it was about. He goes on to say of God: "He felt nothing with the feeling of one who suffers, but he felt with the affection of one who suffers with another." He adds that even the philosophers were aware of this: "For," he says, "in man the various affections, that is, justice, mercy and holiness, are accidental things, and for that reason they are called affections. But God is not affected by them passibly." O "not passibly"! O "is affected"! How is he affected if he does not suffer? Why is your memory so quick to forget even what you yourself have put forward? You said that justice and mercy are affections because in man they are accidents. Therefore, if they are affections in man because there they are accidents, then in God, where they are not accidents, they are not affections. So he did not feel with the affection of a fellow-sufferer, for in him there was no accident, and so there could be no affection. But you add: "So what in man is affection and grace is in God power and nature." Yet is what is power in God not power once it has been given to man? God is without doubt power, and if he is immutable, then even when he has given himself to man he is power in man. So what is power in God is power in man as well. The only difference is that there it is present substantially, and here as something added. Hence the Lord says to the apostles: "Stay in the city until you are clothed with power from on high," and the prophet says: "I will love you, O Lord, my power." But you say that God is power in himself and is not power in man. The reason for this view is clearer than daylight: it follows, of course, that the one you say is affected you are claiming is changed.

First I must examine closely the proper meaning of this word. "Affection" is surely so called because something affects, and whatever is affected suffers, that is, is acted upon. But to suffer belongs only to a passible and created substance. Such a substance was called out of nothing by the supreme essence, which is God, so that it might exist, and so it stands midway between that from which it was made and that by which it was made. It can therefore be affected by higher things [?] so as to advance, just as by lower things so as to decline. I am speaking, of course, of the human soul. So nothingness cannot be affected in any way, because it has no substance. Nor can God, because he suffers no losses and receives no increase. It is the things in the middle that are affected, as was said above, either by advancing or by declining. Indeed, whatever is affected suffers, and no sane person will deny that whatever suffers is not God. The two terms are reciprocal: nothing can be mutable unless it is passible, and nothing can be passible unless it is mutable. He says, on the testimony of the philosophers, that mercy, justice and goods of that kind are affections of the passible creature, and that the same qualities exist in God essentially rather than as additions. He does not notice that he is contradicting himself. An affection is something added, but nothing is added to God, and therefore he is not subject to affection. For whatever is affected is open alike to contrary and to agreeable influences, and so is subject to passion in both directions. Therefore, if the supreme Godhead felt with the affection of a fellow-sufferer, it is also subject to the goad of evil passion. "He felt," you say. But to feel is surely an accident in one who did not feel before. Eternity, however, knew the passion of Christ everlastingly, since it ordained that passion itself. So at the time of the passion nothing new came to it that it might know, still less that it might feel.

But why should I now discourse about affection and argue that he is impassible, when the very man we are contradicting [?] has plainly admitted that God suffered with the crucified man? What, I ask, does this mean: "He did not feel with the feeling of one who suffers, but he felt with the affection of one who suffers with another"? What is "he felt," and what is "he did not feel"? Or how did he suffer if he did not feel? If someone says, "That man is walking, and this one is walking with him," or "That man is speaking, and this one is talking with him," does he not mean that the one who talks with him speaks and the one who walks with him walks? Or if someone says, "That man has died, and this one has died with him," does he not affirm that both have died? For he who dies with another certainly dies. So too he who suffers with another certainly suffers. If the Godhead suffered with him, then it suffered, and so perhaps it also died. Or, if even to think that is impious, then God did not suffer, and therefore he was not affected either. Where now is the affection of the fellow-sufferer?

Next he cites what the saints of old, by the prophetic Spirit, spoke figuratively in order to frighten and restrain those who think in a carnal and human way. He quotes the texts: "O Lord, do not rebuke me in your anger," and "The Lord has sworn and will not repent." Earlier, appealing to the philosophers, he did not ascribe accidents to God; here, appealing to the prophets, he even imposes on him the constraints of vices. Things that are meant figuratively must be examined skilfully from within; otherwise one does not reach the life-giving spirit but remains in the letter that kills. That is to say, if we consider the oracles of the prophets, which are animated by hidden allegorical meanings, only in the body of the letter, we will believe that the undefiled essence of the most exalted Godhead is passible. When the prophetic oracles say that he is angry or repents, it is the effects of these passions that we must consider, not affections. Furthermore, a modern writer who holds that his little reflections should be weighed after the pattern of prophetic speech is presenting himself not as a commentator but as a prophet. Yet the virgin's childbirth sealed the mouths of the prophets so as to unseal their prophecies. It goes against what reason demands, then, to weave oratorical periods in the mystical style of the prophets, for the result is that the man who promises to explain other people's words cannot be explained himself. So either do not use the prophets' words, or prophesy. Prophecy is by no means fitting for the present time, nor prophetic speech for a commentator. So whatever you have borrowed from prophetic language in your own defence works against you rather than helping you. For either a defence that has to be hunted for confesses weakness, or an unsuitable advocacy fails to clear away the error.

The inviolable Godhead, then, is in no way rightly said to be affected. The effect comes from the maker; the affection is in the thing made. When God punishes someone in time by his eternal counsel, it is surely the one who is punished who suffers. God too would suffer something if he learned of someone's sins in time, or if he were moved by anger to exercise justice against him. Everything that is temporal, movable and mutable is encompassed by the immutable and abiding everlastingness. It affects some things for their salvation and allows others to be affected in judgement, while it remains wholly foreign to every affection and to all motion of time and place. It has only that motion which is called stable. From it, through it and in it exists everything that it moves in time alone, and everything that it moves through both time and place rather than in time only. But more of this elsewhere. For now let us set these things aside, for their merit and strength are such that it is right to reject them but unnecessary to attack them. Let us come to the testimonies he has borrowed from the apostle in his own defence. He asks why it cannot be said, "He felt with the affection of a fellow-sufferer," when the apostle thought it right to say, "They would never have crucified the Lord of glory"; for, he says, just as light can feel no blow from a wound, so the author of light felt no pain in the passion. "So it can be said: but he felt with the affection of a fellow-sufferer." It can indeed be said, since all things are lawful; but it ought not to be said, since not all things edify.

Even so, I can hardly keep from laughing at comparisons and pronouncements of this kind. A little earlier you had asserted that God ceases to be power and is therefore changed. Now, with an equally limp argument, you declaim that just as light can feel no blow from a wound, so the author of light felt no pain in the passion. Is light, then, the only thing that feels [no?] blow [?]? Do earth or water or air feel the blow of a wound? Or is light perhaps alive? Can any lifeless body feel? Or is there any body which cannot be wounded, even if it does not feel the wound? Light, then, can be wounded even though it cannot feel. Just as night is broken when light breaks in, so light is wounded by darkness. That is why a very famous poet wrote playfully in charming Asclepiads: "And rival light drives on the absent day, from which night flees defeated, its mantle torn." What are you saying? That just as light does not feel a blow, so the Godhead did not feel the wound in the passion? If so, then it could be wounded even if it could not feel, and insensibility was one thing and corruptibility another. If it could be wounded, then it was not because of incorruptibility that it felt no pain, since light is both insensible and vulnerable. Consider whether this is not the slide into deep error that you think we ought to approve. You bring in bodily light, which man and beast share alike, to the point of using it to explain God's not feeling the wound inflicted on him. A body, however beautiful, is still a body, and you do not merely liken it to the supreme incorporeal being but make it equal to him. Holding so punishable an opinion, you claim for yourself the privilege not only of innocence but of praise, and you declare that we are outside the faith because we say that the likeness of God is incorporeal, so that it may be a likeness of him as he really is. But more of that later; for now let us discuss affection. Suppose, then, that Christ was crucified in such a way that the whole world must believe the inviolable incorruptibility of the supreme Godhead was crucified. Tell me, please, if the question is not offensive: who may rightly be believed to have been exalted by the supreme God, that is, by the Trinity itself, after the humiliation of death, and to have had conferred on him the name that is above every name? Surely, I think, it is the one who became obedient even unto death and who, because of the obedience of his ineffable humility, was ineffably raised up into the glory of God the Father. Dare, if you will, to deny that the one you confess to be the Son of Man is also the Lord of glory! But you will want to use the text "they would never have crucified the Lord of glory" to make it believed beyond doubt that the Godhead itself can be affected, if it could be crucified. So you have revealed your opinion openly. You think you were blameless in saying that God is affected, because the apostle says that the Lord of glory was crucified. Truth, however, urges that "the crucified Lord of glory" be understood in such a way that the Godhead is not believed to have been crucified. Yet you argue all the more stubbornly that the Godhead is affected. In your eagerness to defend your error you fail to notice that you are saying the punishment which the persecutors' crime carried out on the man Christ was inflicted on the inviolable Godhead itself. If that is so, God could have suffered for men even without assuming a man, for if he was passible in the man, he could have been passible outside the man as well. But perhaps you will contend that he was changed by contact with human substance and therefore became passible after he assumed the man. Then God is not incorruptible, since whatever can be made worse can certainly be corrupted. But the Godhead cannot be corrupted or changed, and therefore it cannot suffer either.

It remains, then, to say this. Christ, true man and true God, is one person of a twofold substance, both God-man and man-God. So the same Lord of glory both was not crucified, by reason of his inviolable Godhead, and was crucified in the man, by reason of the unity of the person. Thus, in a wonderful and inconceivable way, [the man] God suffered, and yet the Godhead did not suffer. See now, then, that you have claimed the apostle's testimony only with this result: not that your opinion might gain strength from it, but that the perversity of your crooked opinion might not stay hidden. You say that the Godhead is affected, as though truth were guaranteeing it to you through the apostle. But the apostle compels us to understand the crucified Lord of glory in that part of himself in which he could be crucified. So this opinion is left to you, and to you entirely alone: that the inviolable and inestimable Godhead was beaten with scourges, pierced with nails, run through with a lance, afflicted with pains and consumed by death. For you refuse to believe that in one and the same Christ one thing was subject to death and another [not subject?] to suffering [?]. But under pressure from the truth you change your words, saying that the things by which created substance is affected exist in God substantially, not as additions. Keep speaking that way, so that presumptuous ignorance may not scatter falsehood into the purity of the truth. To err is human; to repent of error is human. No one sins more dangerously than the one who defends his sins. As you yourself declare, you do not refuse to hold with the philosophers that the essence of the supreme Godhead is impassible and subject to no affection. So drive this civil war out of your mind. Be sure that truth can no more be mixed with falsehood than essence with nothingness. Yet you say that he is affected, while you deny that he suffers. If he is not free of affection, then to profess that he is impassible is false, and the one claim flatly contradicts the other. Whoever says, "He felt with the affection of a fellow-sufferer," is not saying that he felt nothing in the passion. Again, you say that God is not affected passibly; therefore he is affected non-passibly. That is just as if someone said, "He is standing while running," or "He is asleep while awake"; the clash of contraries certainly does not allow it. What, then, is gained by adding "passibly," when it could be said most truly and fully that God is not affected? This two-headed expression is not free of the stain of suspicion. You say that God, whom you say is affected, does not suffer. Affection and passion mean one and the same thing: either you remove both, or you keep both in either one. So we must not say, "God is not affected passibly," but, "God is not affected." If he is not affected, he did not feel with the affection of a fellow-sufferer. If he felt with the affection of a fellow-sufferer, it follows that he is affected.

I say: the divine substance is affected by nothing. You say: God is not affected. Let us be reconciled. Away with whatever has spattered you with disgrace, though perhaps you did not know it; that you were careless is certainly plain. But you go further and declare that the apostle said of Christ, already enthroned in heaven: "We have such a high priest, who is able to suffer with our weaknesses." And, as if there were nothing here to examine and discuss, you boast that you have achieved your purpose and prepare to pass on to the third question. To reply as briefly as possible: that high priest, I believe, is the one who above all offers the oblations of the human race before the Godhead of the supreme Trinity, expiates sins and commends prayers. He, therefore, is the true priest. The Son of God, insofar as he is equal to the Father, does not so much pour out prayers as hear those who pray. So it is rather the man who must be understood here. The apostle calls him high priest and declares that he suffers with our weaknesses, and he also says of him: "Christ Jesus, who died, yes, who also rose again, who is at the right hand of God, who also intercedes for us." So the high priest who suffers with us is the one who also intercedes for us. But the one who grants the request of the one interceding, the Trinity itself, would certainly have no one who needed to intercede with it if it could suffer or be affected in any way. Do you see now that a testimony of truth that is really against you is being taken up in defence of falsehood? As we said above, if anything of this kind is found in the divine books, it must be referred to the unity of the person. Just as soul and body, though of different substance, are one man, so God and man, though of different substance, are one Christ. And so, since he is one person of different substance, in a certain sense he petitions himself, and in a certain sense he himself hears himself on our behalf. Countless things could very readily be said on this subject. But what collapses of its own accord need not be demolished with great effort, so for the present let this suffice on these matters.
4. FROM HERE ON HE DISCUSSES THE NATURE OF THE SOUL.

Now the nature of the human soul, that is, of the divine image, is called into question. This is the third question I spoke of. On entering upon the reasons for distinguishing natures, this friend of mine declares that the spirit of life is a body. He claims that on this point he is putting forward the decrees of the fathers as an authority already settled. Yet he himself records that they did not so much define something they had grasped with the mind as hold certain opinions. And since he himself, to judge by what he says, has deferred not to proven reasoning or inviolable authority but rather to human opinion, he labours hard to make us scorn divine authority, set aside clear reason, and agree with him with our eyes shut, as the saying goes. Whoever thinks truly and piously about God understands as a consequence that nothing which ought to have been created was left uncreated by him. The cause of the creation of things is the goodness of the Creator. He is able to create whatever he wills. If he had created nothing, he would have exercised no goodness, and if he had made something only half complete, he would have shown only half his kindness. It would seem strange to say that something would be lacking to the fullness of things if the little rose blossom did not exist, but that nothing would be lacking if incorporeal substance had not been created. So that what was lacking to the fullness of creation should not be the most important thing, rather than some trifle, incorporeal substance too had to be created. But perhaps it may be thought an insult to the Creator to say that he made something incorporeal and like himself, since nothing like God is found in a body. Yet the human soul is called the likeness of God by God himself, and there can be no divine likeness in a body. So whatever is like God will be incorporeal. The human mind was made in the likeness of God. Therefore the human mind is incorporeal.
5. THAT THE INCORPOREAL IS SUPERIOR IN DIGNITY TO THE CORPOREAL, AND THE NON-SPATIAL TO THE SPATIAL.

Everything incorporeal ranks above the corporeal in the dignity of its nature, as the non-spatial ranks above the spatial, the indivisible above the divisible, and the living above the non-living. Indeed, it has already been established that a substance better than every body and like the Creator ought to have been created. If the Creator, who is supremely almighty and also supremely kind, did not create it, then either he did not will to or he certainly could not. If he neither willed nor was able, he lacked omnipotence. If he was able and did not will it, which is impious even to think, he begrudged it. But omnipotence cannot be unable, and goodness cannot begrudge. So he was both able and willing to create the incorporeal, and therefore he created it. Unless perhaps you say that what he could will ought not to have been made, though he could will nothing but what he ought to do. Why would you now argue that what you do not doubt ought to have been created was not created? It certainly ought to have been created. The incorporeal Creator is the greatest good. A created incorporeal being is a great good. A created body, which exists only by being created, is a good of some sort. So, just as the supreme God, the greatest good, created a body as a good of some sort, so he ought to have created the great good of the incorporeal. It would not befit the almighty Good, who made all things very good, to leave the perfection of the fullness of things incomplete even in the least things, let alone to leave the most important things uncreated. But perhaps someone will claim that the incorporeal creature is not a good, or that a good ought not to have been created, or that what ought to have been made could not be made. But the incorporeal Creator is the supreme good, and the incorporeal creature is a great good. So a great good ought to have been made by the supreme good, and the Almighty was able to do what, being good, he ought to will. He therefore created incorporeal substance, since he could not fail to do what ought to be done. Unless perhaps someone says that something ought to have been made which he did not make; but then it would follow that he made something he ought not to have made.

But you will say to me: "If something incorporeal was created, then it is equal to the Creator." Our inquiry concerns the true man, that is, the soul of man. The soul is not equal to God but like him. It is like him insofar as one incorporeal being is like another, but inferior insofar as the created is inferior to the Creator. It is like him as intellectual light is like intelligible light, but unlike him as a mutable creature is unlike the immutable Creator. Truth is one thing, and the image of truth is another. But just as there can be no image of a bodily thing except a body, so the image of the incorporeal is never found in a body. Where Moses speaks of the creation of man, he says: "And God said, 'Let us make man in our image and likeness.' And he made man in his image and likeness. In the image of God he created him, male and female." This oracle of divine authority cannot be evaded by eloquence, deceived by argument, overcome by force or corrupted by skill. If the human soul is the image of God, it is the image of something incorporeal. If it is the image of something incorporeal, it is certainly incorporeal itself. If it is not incorporeal, it is not the image of the incorporeal at all. But it is the image of the incorporeal, and therefore it is incorporeal. Because it was created, it is not God; because it is the image of God, it is not a body.
6. THAT WHILE EVERYTHING INCORPOREAL IS INVISIBLE, NOT EVERYTHING CORPOREAL IS VISIBLE.

But you add that you are taught by certain people, though you keep their names from us, that some things are incorporeal and others invisible. Expositors of fearsome expertise, no doubt, who have penetrated even to this secret: if some things are incorporeal and others invisible, then incorporeal things are not invisible. So the incorporeal must be ranked below everything corporeal, since Truth says through the apostle: "The things that are seen are temporal, but the things that are not seen are eternal." Yet you distinguish the creating substance from the created in such a way that some things are incorporeal and others invisible. Then every corporeal thing is invisible, and every incorporeal thing visible. At this point I dare to ask: is God invisible or visible? If you deny that he is corporeal, you do not refuse to call him visible. If you call him invisible, you confess that he is corporeal. On this view, then (may it be far from you and from us), the eternal, invisible, incorporeal God will either not be incorporeal, or he will be visible and so not eternal. Still, this teacher, ignorant of causes that are plain to see, wanted to think something but could not express it. I believe he meant to say that there are certain corporeal things which cannot be seen, since it is proper to everything incorporeal not to be seen. On this account some corporeal things can be invisible, while incorporeal things cannot be anything but invisible. For while everything incorporeal is invisible, not everything invisible is incorporeal. A voice, for instance, is not seen, and yet it is a body. We do, it is true, speak of "seeing" things that belong to the other senses because sight is preeminent. We often say, "See what it sounds like," though sound belongs to hearing and not to sight. But we do not say, "Hear what is shining," because sight, which ranks above the other senses, loosely claims for itself what belongs to the lower ones, though it does not mix its own power with their faculties. So if we refer everything to sight, all things that can be perceived by any bodily sense are visible. But if we give back to each sense what is specific to it, not all things are visible. Hence all the primary bodies, which are called elements, are without doubt visible, since we find by experience that they are perceived. A living body is made from them when they are combined in measured proportion, with their dimensions fixed in due ratio and a soul giving it life. There are indeed many things that are not animated and yet cannot be denied to live. But we are speaking of those that not only live but also perceive, such as animals that lack reason. Putting off the discussion of these for a little, we speak of ourselves.

Since we consist of soul and body, the body cannot be the mind, and in the same way the mind cannot be a body. So the mind that perceives in the body perceives invisibly, even though it perceives through something visible. For sight is one thing and the eye another; the ears are one thing and hearing another; the nostrils are one thing and smell another; the mouth is one thing and taste another. Nor are the hand and touch the same. By touch we distinguish hot things from cold, but we do not touch the sense of touch itself, for there is neither cold nor heat in it. By taste we perceive sweet and bitter things, but we cannot taste taste, for there is nothing bitter or sweet in it. With the nostrils we take in odors, yet we do not catch smell by smelling, because smell smells of nothing. With the ears we drink in sounds, but since hearing makes no sound, we do not hear hearing itself. With the eyes we look at colored shapes, and we discern them with the eyes because they are colored and shaped. But we do not see sight, because it is neither colored nor shaped. If sight shone, we would see continually; if hearing sounded, we would always be hearing; if smell were fragrant, we would be smelling perpetually; if taste had flavor, we would taste without tiring; and if touch touched itself, we would be touching forever. To say nothing of the rest: if taste could be tasted, no one could ever go hungry. And if a sense perceived itself, there would be no need to supply things from outside for the senses to work upon. So the member through which we perceive is one thing, and the sense by which we perceive is another. Between the invisible incorporeal and the visible body there is an invisible corporeal, and in us this is sight, hearing, smell, taste and touch. These exist only in an animated body. They come from the joining of two different things, and so they are both corporeal and invisible. They are corporeal because of the visible body and invisible because of the incorporeal mind. So it will not be true, as your view holds, that what is invisible is what is not incorporeal, as if it were proper to the incorporeal to be visible and to the corporeal to be invisible. Nothing in the body would be invisible unless the invisibility of the incorporeal made it so. As we said above, in the same human being there is both the invisible incorporeal, which is the soul, and the invisible corporeal, which the soul works invisibly out of the visible body.
7. That the five senses of the body consist of the four elements.

Now each of the things we perceive with the bodily senses belongs specifically to one particular sense, and each sense admits no other to share in what is properly its own. Among all corporeal things, the light of the sun is without doubt the most excellent. It belongs to the highest element in the corporeal universe, which is called fire. This is why sight has received the chief place among all the senses in the human body as well. From the inner heat of the heart and liver, certain little fires, sparkling without pause, fly up into the vault of the head as into the heaven of our body. Rays from these pour out through the middle of the eyes and mingle with the light outside. Then they rebound from the bodies they strike, turn back, and draw in the colors and shapes of those bodies. You observe, then, that fire is supreme among the elements, light the most beautiful of colors, and sight the foremost of the senses. Hearing comes next to sight in merit and power, and it shares in the element the Greeks call ether. Ether is of the nature of air. But it sends certain dregs, as it were, down from its upper regions toward the bottom, and so it is purer and finer, and it surpasses in both place and dignity this stormy air of ours, which by nature breeds clouds. This is why the purest air makes hearing easier and lets it reach farther. For just as the eyes cannot see without the shapes of bodies and light from outside, so the ears perceive nothing unless the air is either struck or blown. So too with the sense of the nostrils. Just as the air is tinged with sounds so as to produce hearing in the ears, so likewise the same air is tinged with odors so as to produce smell in the nostrils, and odors are not perceived to be present in the nostrils naturally unless air is drawn in. As for the sense of taste, a clear sign shows that it cannot act at all without the help of moisture: nothing that has flavor is perceived if it is placed on a dry tongue. As for touch, I do not think anyone can doubt that it is most like the lowest of the elements, that is, earth.

Come now, let us return to the point for which we have discussed these things. Look: sight beholds and perceives light, and other bodies by means of light. Does hearing claim any of this for itself? Again, the passages of the ears receive sounds and articulate voices. Does sight claim any of this for itself? Through the caverns of the nostrils we take in odors of countless kinds, but hearing certainly cannot perceive any of them. Does taste perhaps share with smell in exploring flavors? Or does touch allow taste any part in perceiving what is rough or smooth? You see, a voice is not seen by sight, the more eminent sense; light likewise is not heard; a voice is certainly not caught by the nostrils; fragrance is not received by taste; flavor is perceived only in the mouth.
8. That no soul whatever was made from any element or from any body at all.

Here you have a body of every kind, blended from all the elements into the structure of the human body by the scarcely conceivable measures and harmonic proportions of that eternal music. Choose now which kind of body the soul comes from, if the soul is a body. For if the soul does not come from one of these bodies, or from some of them, or from all of them, it is not a body. But what am I to do now? Where am I to turn, when the talent and skill of a most acute and learned debater have forestalled me? He understood, of course, that no body can exist unless it was either created originally from nothing, as the elements of bodies were, or formed from these elements in due proportion. So while deciding that the soul is a body, he preferred to have it fashioned from one of the primary bodies rather than composed from all of them. Cunning and cautious, he evidently did not want to assemble the substance of the soul from a mixture of many bodies. If the soul were drawn from the same principles as the external body, and it were said that it could be formed in the same way, it might seem that it could be dissolved in the same way too. For this reason he chose air, and he decides that the soul is either made from air or like it. He adds the testimony of some authority of his or other, whose words are these: "There are some spiritual natures," he says, "such as angels, archangels and the other powers; our own soul too, or certainly this fine air; yet they are by no means to be thought incorporeal." Are such words really written down on parchment? Is this the business we are engaged in? Setting everything else aside, the whole matter will hang on this one scale. If reason, once it has examined the question, shows that the soul is either made of air or like air, I shall go over, as they say, to the opinion first of my opponent and then of his teacher, and beg pardon for my error. But I myself claim, by right of established truth, that not only the human soul but every soul whatever is made not only not of air but of no body at all. If reasoning proves this, it will be only right for you either to agree with us or to forgive us.
9. Argument that the soul was created from no body at all.

It has already been shown above that the element of fire surpasses the element of air in power as well as in place. This is plainly shown by our earthly fire, which moves with scarcely comprehensible speed and is carried upward by its natural weight, as if to its own region. Even if this did not let us recognize it, it could be clearly understood from the fact that all air grows bright when the sun is present and dark when it is absent. There is also this very weighty argument: air is acted on by fire so that it grows hot, but fire is not acted on by air so that it grows cold. Air can be shut up and held in any kind of vessel, but this never happens to fire. Clear reasoning shows, then, that fire is more excellent than air. Now our sight comes from fire, and this sense is common to man and beast, though some irrational animals surpass human beings in keenness of sight. If, then, it cannot be denied that sight comes from fire, and if the soul comes from air, as you reason, then the eye of a beast is more eminent in dignity of substance than the soul of a man, because the one comes from fire and the other from air.

Anyone who judges the soul to be made of air is quite consistent in thinking it local and in asserting that it is shut up in the prison of the body. So now you must choose one or the other: either the soul is inferior to the sight of a beast, if it is airy, or it is not airy, if it is superior. You see how easily this fiction of ignorant presumption has vanished, quite apart from the countless arguments that could readily be brought on this point. Surely, if the soul is airy, its darkness is the departure of this corporeal sun, and its light is likewise the coming of this same sun. Then what the evangelist declares will be false: "He was the true light, which enlightens every man coming into this world." So will what the prophet says in the person of sinners: "So the light of righteousness did not shine on us, and the sun did not rise on us." Had these men, living in this world, not seen this corporeal sun? Or were their incorporeal eyes seeking an incorporeal sun? It would seem very strange if this light had eyes to enlighten but that true light had none. Or if it has them, as it truly does, eyes by which the incorporeal can be seen, then I think they are not only not airy but not corporeal at all.
10. That a substance already formed cannot be called matter.

Now what are we to make of this? At the very beginning of your discussion you thought the reader should be told to prepare his mind for thinking about those subtler matters. Yet you are trying to lead our reason away from the highest things to the lowest, from incorporeal things to corporeal ones. And as though teaching us to prepare the eye of the mind for subtle matters, a little later you add that whatever is created appears to be matter, and you decide that matter is corporeal. If the creature is still matter, then man has not yet been formed, for it is said to God: "You who created man from formless matter." The world is full of forms, more or less beautiful according to their quality or kind. But matter is formless, while the world is formed. Therefore the creature is not matter.
11. That everything that exists, whether incorporeal or corporeal, is created.

After this you argue that nothing incorporeal is created, because whatever is comprehensible to its maker cannot be incorporeal. On this reasoning, then, God is unknown to himself. Suppose he created nothing incorporeal so that nothing created might exceed the creator's knowledge. Nothing, corporeal or incorporeal, has come into existence except through the prior knowledge of the one who created it, for he made nothing in ignorance. Then he is ignorant of himself above all, since he incorporeally surpasses every substance he created. And so he is greater than himself, being unable to grasp himself. Reason does not allow us to say this. It follows that it is not true that he created nothing incorporeal in order that nothing created might be incomprehensible to him, since he himself, the supreme incorporeal being, cannot be unknown to himself. See how little effort it takes for the warmth of truth to melt the frost of chilly words! You cannot distinguish matter from what is created, the formed from the formless, or spirit from air. Yet you pronounce on the image of God as if you were an expert in the greatest matters, when you are shown to be ignorant of the smallest. Then, driven above all by a lack of testimonies, you append a passage from a work of Saint Jerome, which it is clear you did not understand. In it he says: "They suppose that the globes of the stars are embodied spirits." There is no doubt that anyone who supposes is in doubt. You say that blessed Jerome is reporting what certain people suppose. Perhaps he follows the opinion of those who suppose, that is, of those who doubt, and you follow his opinion in turn. Doubt in someone who supposes comes only from ignorance. So you must recognize that to us who are seeking the truth you have brought, instead of the one knowledge you promise, the ignorance of many. You use as your most approved testimony a man who is in doubt about those whose testimony he uses, and who brings forward as witnesses men who are themselves in doubt. What, then, are we to think you can declare, when you come third after the doubtful source of your doubting authority and are now in doubt yourself?
12. That, not understanding the philosophers, he supposed the globes of the stars to be embodied spirits, and decides that angels are bodies.

I do find the philosophers saying this, however. In a number of their discussions they maintain that the very globes of the moon and sun are given life by incorporeal spirits, under the governance of a certain divine mind. But you must recognize that this same testimony not only does nothing for your opinion against us, but does a great deal for us against your opinion. This happened to you because you did not understand the philosophers' view. You put forward as supporting your side what, when properly understood, can support only ours. If they had said that the spirits were corporeal, the whole hinge of your argument would still have wobbled, resting on the authority of men who were not defining but only supposing. But they said, not doubtfully but knowingly, that the spirits were not corporeal but embodied. Is it not obvious, then, that whatever is embodied is not corporeal? Otherwise they would have said that the spirits were corporeal, not embodied. For the corporeal is that which an incorporeal spirit animates, and the incorporeal is that by which the body is animated. They clearly distinguished the body that receives life from the incorporeal that gives it life. So it seems to me that this advocate of the body either did not understand the philosophers' view on incorporeal substance or should never have raised it in his own favor under the name of Saint Jerome.

He goes on to add: "If angels," he says, "and even the heavenly bodies are said to be unclean in comparison with God, what do you think man is to be reckoned?" As far as I can see, this most violent debater does not understand this either. For he believes that angels are of one and the same substance, and so he thinks more highly of the stars, which he judges to be embodied spirits. What else will the learned Jerome be judged to have said here, except that the bodies of angels far surpass human bodies in agility and power? Again, when he said "if angels" and added "even the heavenly bodies," he wanted two things to be understood, angels and heavenly bodies. For while angels are embodied spirits, there are certain things in heaven that are bodies only. So he clearly shows that no body, however high its place and however powerful its motion, can be ranked above incorporeal beings. Then, moving a step further in the comparison, he says that man is so far from being comparable to divine things that not even an angel can be compared to them. He also distinguishes between body and flesh, because while all flesh is also body, not every body is flesh. Hence the apostle says: "There is one flesh of birds, another flesh of fish, and another of men. And there are heavenly bodies and earthly bodies." He clearly shows that an earthly body is also flesh, but a heavenly body is not also flesh. Unless perhaps it is fitting to apply here what he recalls this same Jerome saying: "They suppose that the globes of the stars are embodied spirits." Then the stars themselves, or the bodies of angels, would certainly be heavenly bodies, while the spirits embodied in them would not be corporeal. In the same way we say that God became incarnate, and the human soul itself certainly becomes incarnate when it takes on flesh to govern it. Scripture testifies that "the body that is corrupted weighs down the soul," and this may happen to the soul. Still, we must not believe that it is turned into body, however much the weight of the flesh burdens it. Nor will the body ever be changed into the nature of the soul, however much the soul's life moves it; otherwise it would not be a body. So the apostle said: "and heavenly bodies and earthly bodies." Did he mean this to be understood of angels, or of stars, or of any earthly bodies whatever, about which there is no question? What follows will make it clear. For he immediately goes on to say: "The glory of the heavenly is one thing, and that of the earthly another." And to show plainly what these heavenly bodies were, he says: "There is one brightness of the sun, another brightness of the moon, and another brightness of the stars; for star differs from star in glory. So it is with the resurrection of the dead." He is teaching, that is, that the risen bodies will differ according to the diversity of their merits, just as the stars differ in quality. Here, beyond any doubt, the teacher of the Gentiles used comparisons of this kind while discussing only the resurrection of human bodies. For this is how he begins the subject of this passage: "Someone will say, How will the dead rise? And with what kind of body will they come?" From this point up to the comparison with the stars he pursues this same subject without inserting any other topic, and he makes no mention of the soul. He did this so that no one, judging perversely, would think that what he said about the differences of sun, moon and stars, which are certainly heavenly bodies, was said about souls.
13. On the resurrection.

Now then: suppose the human body, which is earthly and mortal, will be transformed into such glory that from fleshly it becomes spiritual, as the Apostle says: "It is sown a natural body, it will rise a spiritual body." Suppose also that the human soul is spiritual now in such a way that it is still a body. Then human flesh will be raised to the dignity of the soul once it has become a spiritual body. And the soul, which rightly ruled the body, served the Lord with piety and justice, and faithfully believed God, or perhaps even knew him, will gain nothing at all in the quality of its own substance, while its flesh is made equal to it. Where, then, is that saying that it is not the one who has cleansed the eye of the flesh but the one who has cleansed the eye of the heart who will see God? For "Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God." Perhaps, then, the body will be blessed in its own way and the soul likewise in its own way. The body will be changed so that it serves the spirit in everything at its nod, though it often stubbornly resisted it. The soul will be changed so that it sees God, for whom it longed with the ardour of chaste love. The Apostle distinguished spirit, soul and body when he said, "that your spirit and soul and body may be kept whole." After the resurrection we are not to live a natural, animal life, where there is eating or drinking, sleeping or intercourse. So the whole natural body will pass into a spiritual body, because the whole soul too will pass into spirit, and the whole will be a spiritual body because of the spirit dwelling within it. Surely, if that spirit in this life lusted against the flesh and did not yield to the flesh lusting against it, it will rightly feel no difficulty for all eternity from the flesh whose difficulties it overcame by the power of heavenly help. Nor would it be fair for what yielded to its master unwillingly to be made equal to that master, while what conquered willingly remained in the condition of a servant. From this we are given to understand that in this life the substance of the human soul, being incorporeal, surpasses the natural body in dignity, and after the resurrection and the reward it will likewise surpass the spiritual body. But whatever is superior to a spiritual body is not, I think, a body. So, according to the treatise of this close friend of mine, who decrees that angels are nothing but bodies, the angelic nature will be inferior to human substance. For we hold it as certain on divine authority that the bodies of the saints, which will be found worthy to be changed into glory, are to be made equal to the bodies of angels, since the Lord says: "And they will be like the angels in heaven." If, then, angels are only spiritual bodies and of a single substance, and the human body is raised to the dignity of the angelic body, man will be equal to the angel in the quality of his body and will surpass him in the dignity of his spirit. But if that seems absurd, as it certainly is, then angelic substance is twofold, just as human substance is.
