It has a body of complete agility and the greatest beauty, so that it can appear to men when it is commanded to, and it has an incorporeal part by which it always sees God, according to the Gospel saying: "for their angels always see the face of my Father."
14. That spiritual things can in no way be seen with bodily eyes.

I am greatly astonished that any Christian, especially one in the position of a teacher, can declare that God will be visible to some body, however beautiful and lofty, but still a body, and that the universal God can be seen locally, when to see God is to understand. Even by understanding we know that understanding is not local, because if understanding is local, what is understood will also be local. For nothing is local that is not itself also a place. But if understanding is local, and God is in it because what is understood in it is God, then God is local. Since this is unacceptable, we must understand that man consists of the corporeal and the incorporeal, each of which is to be reshaped for the better, and that the angel consists of both body and spirit, formed with a dignity preeminent among creatures. Its spirit is more powerful than every created spirit, and its body is loftier, since it is made from the most powerful of all the elements. This agrees with the prophetic saying in which angelic substance is declared beyond doubt to be twofold: "Who makes his angels spirits and his ministers a burning fire." It is clear that fire is not spirit, and equally that spirit is not fire, because nothing here is to be taken allegorically, as in the place where the Lord says, "I came to cast fire on the earth," when he was speaking of the Holy Spirit. For we may not believe that human souls are kindled to divine love by sharing in the angelic spirit, because man is good by the same gift by which an angel is good, and both are blessed by the same gift. Both desire the very same thing with the same will, that is, by the same Spirit. Both grasp this same thing with an incorporeal capacity, and man, angel and God become one spirit, as the Apostle says: "He who cleaves to the Lord is one spirit." But I do not see how a body could be blended with the incorporeal so that it may rightly be called one spirit. For if the soul is a body, the corporeal will then have to be changed so that it can be one with the incorporeal. And so we are necessarily brought back to the argument by which it is said that something incorporeal could have been created. For if something incorporeal can come from the corporeal, it could also have been created from nothing. The only alternative would be to say that the unchangeable God somehow becomes corporeal so that he can be one with a body. But let that be the faith of certain lost souls. For if it is good for an angel or a man to cleave to God, the unchangeable Creator will not be degraded to the level of the creature; rather, the changeable creature will advance toward the Creator. This is why the Lord says in the Gospel: "Father, may these be one in us, just as we also are one."
15. That all corporeal things become greater by being joined together, and many are greater than few, but all incorporeal things are neither increased when many nor diminished when single.

Nor may we believe that a joining of any bodies imitates the unity of the Trinity or can be united with it without confusion. For it is perfectly clear that any one body is doubled by adding an equal body. In a body there is up and down, right and left, front and back, and, according to its size, length, breadth and height. But we do not say that in the very Trinity of God there are parts and extents of this kind, divisible and located in place. Yet the one who made us says that, in its likeness, we are one and can be united with it, as we read in the Acts of the Apostles that those who believed and willed had one mind and one heart. Still, I do not think that many souls were so joined to one another that some larger soul came into being from many souls. For the Trinity, through which and with which all good souls become one, is not less in any one person of that Trinity than in the three, nor greater in the three than in each one. So too the substance of the human soul, in imitation of him whose image it is, is neither greater in bulk when many nor less in bulk when single, since these are powers, not bodies. And the creating Power rightly surpasses created powers, above all by the very fact that it created them. For we often both experience and have learned that one soul is superior to another, yet we do not believe that the soul we know to be superior in power is greater in bulk, of which it has none. Nor, I think, will you deny this either: any number of perfectly wise souls know no more than one perfectly wise soul; many souls do not will more strongly, by wholly not-willing [?] it, what one soul wills wholly; and many do not remember better, by tenacity of memory, what any single soul remembers perfectly. A large body, on the other hand, has more weight than a small one, a multitude of bodies is stronger than a few, and many hands hold, support or push a thing more strongly than single hands. Now let us examine what follows.
16. That souls are incorporeal.

Souls, you say, have in themselves a body by which they subsist, though it is much finer than our bodies, incomparably so. Let it be granted, if it is so. But I would like you to answer this: who is it that says, "The soul has a body incomparably finer than our bodies"? If these are the soul's words, which does it call its own body: the body it itself is, or this fleshly one to which it gives sensation and life? For the soul itself says: "The soul's body is finer than my body." What body could the soul call its own except the one it itself is, if the soul is a body? So either the soul is a body and is wrong to call this fleshly body its own, since what is properly its own is what it itself is; or, if this body is the soul's body, then the soul itself, we are given to understand, is not a body. After this he again speaks to the one who consulted him, as follows: "You object to me that the soul is not corporeal because it is not local and does not subsist in quality or quantity. How dangerous it is to believe this we shall show in what follows. For now, at this stage of our treatise, the discussion will turn on this: if it is neither local nor subject to quantity, you may believe without doubt that it is incorporeal; but if we show that it is bounded by quantity or enclosed in a place, then you too should no longer doubt that it is consequently held within a body." You have indeed made your whole treatise depend on this point: if the soul could be proved to be local and subject to quantity, it would follow that it should also be believed corporeal. And yet a little later you declare that it shapes its various thoughts and stirs up its movements within the workshop of the breast.
17. On life: that the soul gives life to the body without being in a place.

First, please answer me: in what place in the body is the soul itself? Is it in the whole or in a part? If it is in a part, how does it move the whole body everywhere and give it sensation? If it is in the whole, how does it shape its thoughts and carry out its movements within the workshop of the breast alone? Or perhaps it is not only in the breast but also in the head, and not only in the head but in the sole of the foot and in the bones? Wherever you believe the soul is located, there you will also have to admit that it is wise and thinks in a located way. And if it is corporeal, it is in the body in such a way that, like water in a wineskin, it fills smaller parts with a smaller part of itself and larger parts with a larger one. It necessarily follows that it has more thought in the breast and less in the finger. And so, whatever portion of a living body someone cuts off, he also cuts off the whole corresponding portion of the soul that gives it life. Because of this, the power of thinking or of remembering will not be as great in a soul so weakened. For no one doubts that air, from which or like which you declare the soul to be, is divisible and can be cut. When we breathe in and out, we draw in and give back particles of it, which those vessels the Greeks call arteries take up to nourish the whole body, and by them this same air is also spread, through the tireless motion of the lungs, to temper the three elements. But if, as you hold, the air we breathe in serves to nourish the soul, since of course an airy thing is fittingly fed on air, then, as was said above, the soul is cut along with the body it gives life to. The power of memory surely belongs, without question, to the whole soul. Moreover, every body, however large or small, can certainly be cut, and this happens to it because it is made up of parts. Whatever has a part can of course be divided, since one part can be torn from another. Therefore, if the soul is a body, it can certainly be cut; if it can be cut, it can be diminished; if it can be diminished, then anyone who loses a part of his living body also loses a part of his soul. And with part of the soul, part of the memory perishes, so a soul whose substance has been diminished must certainly remember less. Thus, if the soul is in a place, it can be broken up by repeated cutting and destroyed by the frequency of that breaking. But a sound mind, not to say a learned one, does not accept this. So, to make the soul's freedom from place clearer, as far as we can set it out with God's help, let us discuss motions. For there will be no doubt that, just as what moves from place to place is a body, so what does not move from place to place is not a body.
18. That there are three kinds of motion.

It is already known that there are three kinds of motion: stable, non-local and local. Stable motion belongs to God, non-local motion to the soul, local motion to the body. Stable motion is this: God did not always make creation, yet he did not will to create it by a new act of will at the moment he created it, because he always willed to create it at the moment he made it. "At the moment" signifies time; "always" has nothing to do with time. This "at the moment", then, belongs to the beginning of time, not to time, because the stability of the eternal will contains temporal motion within itself. Therefore always willing "at the moment" is stable motion. Here you must accept that nothing can be moved except by something unmoved. To show this by example: we certainly cannot move a finger unless the hand stays still, and the movement of the arm depends on the shoulder holding steady. And not to dwell on it longer: in walking, one foot must be planted so that the other can move forward. Keep this in mind while we briefly distinguish the motion of the mind from the motion of the body. For just as God, as was said above, moves stably, so the soul moves in time. It is in time that the soul was proud a little while ago and is now humble, was glad before and is now sad, loved before and now hates, earlier forgot something and now remembers it. The body has no share in such motions of the soul; the soul is moved by them while the body remains unmoved. From this we are given to understand that the soul moves through time but not from place to place, and that the body is moved by the soul both in time and in place, while the soul is not moved in place by the body.

To make this very point plain in words, if I possibly can, I need a more attentive reader. Look: so that the hand may be moved to write or to make something, the soul's will is directed to it. The soul beholds incorporeal forms without being in a place. Joined to them inseparably, whether as what is above to what is below or as what is below to what is above, it moves the limb with its whole self, it beholds the truth of the forms with its whole self, and besides this it gives sensation to the whole body everywhere with its whole self. Suppose, then, as has been said, that the soul is intent on those eternal and ever-unchanging forms and is striving to produce, through the body, a bodily square or hexagon or circle on the pattern of those forms. If it turns its mind, that is, its eye, elsewhere, so that, for instance, while wanting to make a square it thinks of a circle, or while wanting to write the name of Paul it thinks of the name of Simon, is not the motion of the limb at once driven to express or draw whatever the mind's attention has turned to think about? So the soul will stand still in contemplating the forms in order to move the body in shaping things that can be formed, and the truth of those forms cannot be seen except by a rational soul. For every rational soul stands still in its desire and in its deliberation. It is not credible that when the writer's hand is moved to write at the soul's bidding, the soul too is moved by the motion of the hand. Unless the soul beheld the shapes of the letters without moving and without being in a place, it could not form them in place by the motion of the fingers.

But perhaps you will say: the part of the soul that is in the writer's fingers is moved, and the rest is not. This is indeed what those maintain who think the soul has parts. And it follows inseparably that if the soul were corporeal, it would have parts, since what is corporeal has parts and everything that has parts is corporeal. Let us inquire, then, whether the mind can be divided into parts, and see whether or not it can be moved in a part of itself corresponding to a part of the body. First and foremost in examining this question, let us hold this: if the mind has parts, it can be cut into parts. Let us observe, then, that no body can be touched as a whole all at once, or touch something as a whole all at once, whereas the soul is whole all at once in each of its motions or acts. For, as we argued above, every body, however large or small, has length, breadth and height. According to the number of its parts it is subject to six motions: every body moves up and down, right and left, forward and backward. It is also moved by a seventh motion, like that of a wheel or a sphere, a perfect motion that, as a sign of eternity, is carried out from itself, through itself and within itself. Every body, then, as we have said, having six parts and being subject to six motions, also certainly has something in the middle, according to its thickness. For there would be no outside to bodies at all if there were not also an inside. So even if any body is enclosed in the hand and touched all over its outside, it is certainly not touched on its inside. Hence it is clear that no body can be touched as a whole all at once, and that no body, however tiny, can be wholly in one place, say a poppy seed or any fraction of that seed. Certainly it does not have its lower parts where it has its upper parts, nor its right side where its left is, nor its front where its back is. But the soul sees through the body as a whole and recalls what it has seen as a whole; it hears as a whole and remembers sounds as a whole; it smells as a whole and remembers scents as a whole; it perceives flavours as a whole through the tongue and, as some would have it, through the palate, and tells them apart; it touches as a whole all things smooth and rough, and approves and disapproves as a whole. Judged by the necessity of place and of times, which I discussed above, it seems wonderful that the soul as a whole gives life to the whole body, and that, while the whole body lives and the whole body senses, the soul as a whole receives forms all at once through a very small part of the body, namely sight; as a whole receives sounds all at once through another part of the same body, namely hearing; as a whole perceives fragrances through the small member of the nostrils; as a whole judges the differences of flavours through the sense of taste; and as a whole distinguishes hot and cold with just the tip of a finger. If, then, it is present as a whole to the eye, in a place, in order to see, how is it that it is not absent as a whole from all the other senses at the same time? How can it sense as a whole everywhere, give life to the individual parts of the body not with parts of itself but with its whole self, and give sensation as a whole through different parts at once? When you have persuaded me that the soul does these things in a local way, then you will persuade me that it is local or has parts. And yet all of these things are still common to man and beast.
19. On the soul: that it is not subject to quantity.

So the soul's freedom from place has become at least somewhat apparent, though I have not yet discussed its principal part, that is, our rational part, in which its incorporeality and freedom from place appear more clearly still. Let us now discuss how the soul is not subject to quantity, even though where there is no place there can be no quantity, since these two are so bound to each other that either both can be in something or neither. The divine essence is subject to none whatever of those Aristotelian categories. The human soul, again, is not subject to all of them, while any body is subject to all. For we do not say of God of what quality he is, because he cannot be compared to something else so as to be called "such". Nor do we say how great he is, because he is not great in bulk; nor what he has, because there is nothing he does not have; nor how he is, because he himself is the measure; nor do we inquire into his state, because he contains all things; nor his place, because only a body is in a place; nor his time, because he is everlastingness; nor his action, since he acts while at rest; nor his being acted upon, because he does not suffer. The tenth category, or rather the first, is substance itself, of which these predicates are woven.
20. That the soul admits of quality.

The human soul, then, just as it does not admit quantity, is subject to quality. For if we ask what someone's body is like, its quality is indicated in this way: he is fair-haired, he is ruddy, he is pale, or he is dark. But if we inquire about the soul, its quality is shown to us in this way: it is proud, it is humble, it is irascible, it is calm, it has a strong memory or it forgets quickly. Likewise, if the quantity of a body is asked about, we are rightly told: his height extends to five feet, he is two feet wide, and he is as much again in thickness. Is the quantity of the soul marked by such indications, or is anything long or wide or thick found in it? If that were so, each person would have a greater soul the greater his body, and we would never truly call a man of very small body great-souled, whereas we often call men of huge bulk small-souled. So we say that Moses was great-souled when, a fearless leader, he entered the paths of the Red Sea, and [?] the people faint-hearted, for they did not believe, though God promised it, that this very thing would be done with the greatest ease. See, then: the soul of one man is beyond doubt greater than the soul of a whole people, greater, that is, in virtue, not in bulk, since if it were in bulk, the bulk even of two souls would be greater than that of one, not to speak of many. There is, therefore, quality in the soul, but there is no quantity, since whatever is subject to the changeableness of affections admits quality, but whatever has no bulk has no quantity. Hence it is that every animate body, when it dies, does not lose its soul but lets it go, because what is not enclosed does not go out, and what is not held is not lost. For if it were held, it would not be lost, and if it were not lost, the body would not die. This is why Papinius says, not as a poet but as a philosopher: "…I hate these limbs and this frail service of the body, deserter of the soul." To make this plainer, let us examine this very matter more carefully and proceed in order and by degrees from the lowest kind of living things up to rational life as well, so that we may see those three things, memory, deliberation and will, of which the unity of the human soul is composed, even though remembering is common to the rational and the irrational soul.
21. THAT MEMORY IS COMMON TO THE RATIONAL AND THE IRRATIONAL SOUL, AND THAT MAN IS EVERY CREATURE.

Hence it is said, not without truth, that memory is the borderland between man and beast. For storks and swallows revisit their nests after a year, horses make their way back to their stables, and dogs recognize their masters. But although the souls of beasts naturally retain images of places, they have no knowledge of their own substance; so they necessarily remain in the recollection of bodily things, which they have taken in through the senses of the body, and, lacking the eye of reasoning, they cannot see, I will not say anything above themselves, but even themselves. Let the whole man, then, give thanks to his Creator, if not as much as he ought, at least as much as he can, since by the bounty of his ineffable kindness he gave him being in common with stones, seminal life in common with plants and trees, sensory and likewise animal life in common with beasts, and rational life in common with the angels. So, to make it plain that the life of plants and shrubs too is incorporeal, and that it is not lost by the body but let go, I ask you whether you deny that plants and bushes live, or whether perhaps you would say that within these living things there are certain souls by which they live. But if they had souls, they would not lack motion of their own, for they are among the things that are moved by a motion not their own. They would also feel a wound inflicted on them. That such things are not present in them we know even from the cutting of bones and the trimming of hair and nails, which we cut off without any sense of pain. There is, therefore, life even where there is no soul.

Look now: to make up this very life of a tree, the seeds of all the elements have come together, each in its part. It has earth in its solidity, water in its sap, air in its growth, fire in its budding. Now if the soul is made of air or is like air, as you declare, then you will not deny that a tree has a soul, since it is evident that a nature like air is present in it. Lower things are, of course, affected by higher ones in a fixed order of things. When the winter cold has passed, through the turning of the heavens and the return of the stars, the heat coming from above first affects the air, which is nearest to it both in place and in nature. And since air yields to fire by as great a degree as it rises above water, it draws water up from the depths of the earth through the roots of trees or of any plants, because the element of fire, which by nature seizes all things, forces the warmed air toward itself; and through the pith of the tree, as fire draws [?] the air, so the air draws the water, and the water the earth. This is why we too, drawing in air through a pipe or a tube of any kind, draw up water without difficulty; and from the depths of wells, by means of a skilfully built device, the water, heavier by nature, is forced upward, and, driven with the help of the air into the narrow passages of the pipes, is pressed out above the top of the well and flows over at the rim. This discord of bodies opposed to one another is thus forced by the Creator's will into a kind of harmony, so that any living body may exist. But if anything among these four elements, which harmonize with one another in measure and in musical fashion in the life of a tree, should happen to exceed or fall short of its measure, the tree itself first sickens and then dies, as if overcome by weakness. You see here that when the parts of the body fall out of the harmony of their unity, life is abandoned by the body rather than the body being let go by life. It is established, therefore, that no life departs from the body locally, nor is in the body as in a place, nor comes to the body locally.

If at this point you search out the secrets of causal reasons, you may observe that rooted living things lack a soul, but do not lack incorporeal life. And to choose one example out of every kind of seed: we certainly know how large a grain of wheat is, and we measure its bulk quite exactly by its capacity. If we wish to see anything corporeal inside it, when we split it we see nothing but as much white meal as the small capacity of its very thin skin encloses. There you have the whole sum of a grain of wheat in corporeal space. Now show me, corporeally, in this same little grain, the swelling of the shoots, the greenness of the blades, the stalks of the straw, the bristles of the ears, the smoothness of the chaff, the richness of the grain, and the seeds of seeds that are to multiply from these without end, all of which are stored in that little grain in causal secrets. Now, therefore, either show corporeally within those seeds all that comes forth from seeds, or confess that the life of plants too is incorporeal; or declare, if you please, that the soul of a man is corporeal and the life of a shrub corporeal. Since no man of sound judgment can tolerate this, let us pass on to animate living things, which not only live but also feel.

In a beast, then, there is a corruptible body and a mortal soul, which neither comes before nor outlasts the life of the body. You see, then, that to the seminal life which we found in plants and shrubs, sensation and motion are added in the body of a beast through the appetite of the soul, but only if the body itself is in good health, its elements harmonizing in due proportion, so that it may answer the commands of the soul with fitting obedience of movement. But how does it come about that the soul, by one and the same command, moves a sound limb and a weak one unequally? Here is a man strong in the vigour of his left hand who has lost the use of his right through a stroke of the humours, as commonly happens. The hand, still attached to the rest of the body, remains the same in form, though not in vigour, and yet it does not serve the soul's commands. What shall we say: that the soul was driven out of it and withdrew locally? And where did it go, where did it depart to from there? Perhaps it betook itself to the remaining part of itself. But the soul was already filling the whole body, and can anything be added to what is full without its overflowing? So perhaps some of the soul has to be breathed out or belched up or somehow digested, because a body that is not whole cannot hold a whole soul. These consequences must certainly follow, beyond doubt, if the soul is a body. Since this can by no means be, consider rather that the soul has not lost its power to command, but the hand has lost its strength to serve. For when, let us say, the harmony of the conjoined elements is upset by a rush of blood, the body is deprived of its ability to serve, the mind meets with difficulty in ruling, and what was a help begins to be a burden. Yet the soul has not lost its power to move; rather, the limb has failed to offer itself properly to the motion required. And in anyone who has lost his sight, so far as the soul is concerned, the power of seeing bodily things through the body remains, but the parts of the organ fail through which it might exercise its powers to perceive bodily things. Just as it is plain, by clear reasoning, that the soul is not driven locally out of a weakened limb, but that the limb, numb with weakness as if close to death, falls away from the living attention of the soul, so too, when the body of any animal falls apart through its own discord, and the particles of the elements return to their own regions, the soul of a beast, having nowhere to direct its attention, perishes, whereas the human soul rests, but only from those motions by which, being itself moved non-locally through time, it moved the body through places.

Let no little bodies, as it were, now set themselves before the eyes of the mind, so that we believe that souls, once they have laid aside their bodies, occupy certain places in the air or in some other element. Understand your understanding, if you can, for to it alone, together with the angel, it is granted to see these things. Do you see anything long, broad or high in your understanding? Does the brightness of any bodily light glow there? Does any measured melody of song, flowing through time, sound there, or the sweetness of a fading fragrance breathe there, or does anything bodily taste there, or anything soft or hard touch there locally? Its sight grows clear with prudence and dark with folly. Its hearing is offended by falsehood and soothed by truth. Non-locally, justice is fragrant to it and iniquity stinks; it wastes away with vanity and grows rich with virtue. It is wretched when it shares a dwelling with foolishness, blessed in the embrace of wisdom. It is all eye, therefore, because it sees with the whole of itself and sees the whole of what it looks at, whereas no body is either seen whole or sees whole. It is all hearing, because it hears with the whole of itself the whole of what it hears, whereas a body hears nothing whole. And it smells, tastes and touches with the whole of itself, whereas such unity and power cannot exist in a body. It has this by its own nature because there to see is the same as to hear, to hear the same as to smell, to smell the same as to taste, and to taste the same as to touch. But images of bodies present themselves to the soul, and, affected by them through the senses of the body, it is bounded not by places but by illusions; and because it remembers only those things whose forms it received through the body, it believes that whatever is not of that kind does not exist, and it cannot sigh for that homeland from which it was deservedly cast down into this exile, since it does not know that it is in exile. Yet it cannot know that it is an exile in the body if it believes itself to be a body. Hence that man, from whom his own substance was not hidden, says: "While we are in the body, we are exiles from the Lord. But we are confident, and we have the good will rather to be exiles from the body and to be present with the Lord." What, I ask, could be said more clearly? All bodies, whether gross and heavy, like water or earth, or thin and light, like fire and air, or those that are formed from these combining seminally, are without doubt included under the name of body. Whatever is a body of any kind can be called a lighter body, a thinner body, a more agile body, a loftier body, a brighter body, but it cannot be called anything but a body. Now the apostle, who says, "While we are in the body, we are exiles from the Lord," would by no means, it seems to me, say that the soul is an exile in the body if he believed it to be a body. For if the soul is a body and is an exile in a body, then it is an exile in its own substance, and it could never cease to be an exile, since it could not exist without itself. But nothing in any way loses itself, because nothing can exist after itself. It is easier for a thing to be utterly abolished so that it is nothing at all than for it both to lose itself and to survive itself. Either, then, the soul is a body and the apostle was mistaken, or, if it is an exile in the body, the soul is not a body.
22. A QUESTION RAISED: HOW THE SOUL IS AN EXILE IN THE BODY.

You may perhaps reply to this and say: How is the soul said to be an exile here only because it is in a body? If we rightly believe in the resurrection, we shall not be without bodies in that eternal homeland either. Here I would like you to answer: is the soul now called an exile because it is in a body, or because it is in such a body? This body, as I mentioned above, does indeed weigh down the soul, but certainly not with a weight that can be weighed; for if it did, each person would be the stronger the more fasting or sickness had wasted his body. This too strongly supports our reasoning, since it is plainly evident that, as regards the life we share with beasts, a man's soul is more burdened by a wasted and dry body than by a well-fed and vigorous one. This happens because a weary body is not so well able to serve the soul's commands with easy movement, and what burdens the soul is not heaviness of weight but difficulty of action. Accordingly, if we consider the life of beasts, which is evidently in us here, this body does not weigh down the soul; but if we look to that life which will be shared with the angels, it does weigh the soul down, by occupying it and enticing it with things necessary or pleasurable, fixing it on beautiful bodies and drawing it away from the contemplation of the supreme beauty. So when what is needed in food or drink for the health of the body is spent beyond what is needed, or the mind is needlessly occupied with the trifles of pleasure, or is afflicted through the body with blows and pains, it is plain that the soul is weighed down and burdened in proportion to the amount and difficulty of its activity. And this is that exile of which the apostle says: "While we are in the body, we are exiles from the Lord." But when one who has deserved it comes to that transformation of the body of which the same apostle says, "We shall all rise again, but we shall not all be changed," then the animal body, which will no longer exist, will not resist the soul's commands, but the spiritual body, which will exist, will serve it in all things. Nor will the body desire anything unworthy, nor will the soul command anything unjust. And since the holy soul is carried up to God by chaste affection, observe that neither its exile nor its homeland is a matter of place. Is God not with the soul in this life, even if the soul is not with God? For it is one thing to be with God and another not to be without God, since one does not come to him locally, nor depart from him locally. Accordingly, that soul is with God which sees, that is, understands God, and that soul is not with God which does not understand God. But God is present non-locally both to the one who understands and to the one who does not. The soul, however, is an exile here to the extent that it is called away from the contemplation of the highest good by the pleasures and pains of the body, through places and times, through images and phantasms; and this will then be wholly at an end, when this corruptible body has put on immortality and this mortal body has put on immortality.

Since this is so, the soul is an exile in the body, by whose corruption, weakness and neediness it is separated from its homeland, that is, from God. Now I think that a substance whose exile is local and bodily, and whose homeland is incorporeal and non-local, cannot truly be called either corporeal or local. And there will be no exile in that body by whose appetite the soul will not be enticed, by whose resistance it will not be occupied, by whose weight it will not be hindered. It is plain, I think, that the soul is in exile not in every body, but only in a fleshly body, because the fleshly body resists, while the spiritual body draws near to incorporeal things. Therefore, to discuss at last only our own substance, as we said before: who can gaze into the abysses of memory alone and penetrate its caverns? In it I hold whatever colours and shapes I have ever seen; in it whatever words or sounds I have received through my ears; in it whatever scents I have drawn in through my nostrils; in it whatever I have come to know through the diversity of tastes; in it whatever I have distinguished by the report of touch. In it are stored up for me, in a certain way, both grammar when I am discussing dialectic, and rhetoric when I am discussing geometry, and astronomy when I am discussing music, and all of these together when I am discussing arithmetic. Knowing, from the forms of the parts of the world that I see, and with the help of reason, those parts that I do not see, I embrace the world in an incorporeal capacity.
23. THAT THE SOUL SEES INCORPOREAL THINGS INCORPOREALLY THROUGH ITSELF, BUT CORPOREAL THINGS THROUGH THE BODY.

But you say to me: You do not embrace the world in your memory, but the image of the world. Understand from this very point that the soul is not corporeal, since you see that it cannot even behold corporeal things corporeally. Set above this memory, then, not in place but in force and power, is a kind of eye, which, whether it is called spirit or mind or intellect, is one and the same, though it goes by different names. So what a stone is to a living thing without a soul, a living thing without a soul is to a living thing with a soul; and what a living thing without a soul is to a living thing with a soul, a living thing with a soul is to one that lives and understands. The irrational soul governs the animal body, for its welfare, and the intellect, capable of reason, governs the rational soul, for the welfare of the rational soul. Meanwhile God works and governs as the principal power, the unmoved source of motion, and the beginningless hinge of substances: first, so that they may exist, and then so that, according to their measure or merit, they may be such as he has determined they ought to be, he who disposes all things only justly. For just as it is fittingly said of bodies that they are here or there, because of the necessity of place, so it is rightly said of souls that they are in this or that state, because they are non-local, that is, because of quality. For just as a bright place or mild air is pleasant to a living body, so tranquillity in thought and security from fear are pleasant to the life-giving mind. Likewise, just as a dark place and a rough touch are painful to the body, so instability of thought and the anxieties of fear are painful to the mind. The soul, therefore, is moved not through places but according to the variety of its affections, both pleasantly and painfully. This much, however, is clear: the soul without the body can properly be soothed or afflicted incorporeally through its affections, but the body without the soul can feel nothing either pleasant or painful. It belongs, then, to the embodied soul to perceive bodily things through the body, and to the same soul to see incorporeal things without the body. So, just as a body without a soul feels nothing, so the mind without the body perceives no bodily things at all. Hence it is that even while the soul governs the body and gives it sensation, whenever it is lifted up toward the highest things, which are always the same, it in some way so deserts the bodily senses, and withdraws from them non-locally, that it does not see what is placed before it, does not hear what sounds close by, and does not understand the page it has read through. The soul is present so as to gather the letters through the eye, join them into syllables and divide them into words, and it is not present so as to know what it has done by these means. I read something aloud clearly; another person, who fixes the eye of his mind on it, understands me as I pronounce it, but I myself do not know what I have read, because my soul, intent on something else, has gone away non-locally. Then, when I come back to myself, or am recalled, I myself am the one who comes back, and I myself am the one to whom I come back; and I was not with myself, because I have come back to myself across an interval not of place but of time; and yet I was not outside myself, because I could not exist without myself. The soul itself is there, so as to see through the eye what is being read, and the same soul is not there, so as to understand what is being read. Or does it not often happen that, when we turn our sight to some reading or our hearing to someone's account, we take in the sounds and the signs with both senses, and yet do not understand what they mean, although it is quite as easy to understand them as to see and hear them? And yet, when we turn the mind's gaze back to what had not been understood, we grasp the very same thing without any difficulty.
24. THAT THE SOUL IS NOT ONE THING AND MEMORY, THOUGHT OR WILL ANOTHER, SINCE THESE ARE ONE AND THE SAME SOUL.

But you go on to say: the state of the soul is one thing, and the affection of thought that is born of the soul is another. For this reason, you say, we should rather suppose that whenever the soul imagines something to itself, it is busy with its own movements within itself, and that if there is anything else it seems to behold, this is rather depicted for it in the mirror of memory. You think this is its nature, not its punishment. That is why your soul is deceived in recognizing itself: it embraces as itself things that are contrary to it, and, affected through the bodily senses by the mockeries of illusion, it is entangled in error to such a degree that it seeks itself as though it were absent from itself, when it is itself the one seeking. For the soul is not what is sought but that by which it is sought. Whatever it seeks is outside itself, and it has no need to seek anything except what is not with it. But it is with itself, because without itself it is nothing. So it ought not to have sought itself, since it could not exist without itself. Therefore, when it seeks itself, and not without itself, it necessarily runs into something else, because it cannot find itself without itself. This is that delusion which grieves whoever understands it, and grieving he groans and laments with the prophet, saying: "All day long I go about in sorrow, for my soul is filled with delusions." But the soul suffers delusions of this kind in memory, and it could stir up and bring forth no phantasms from memory unless it had drawn them from the forms of bodies through the bodily senses. Whether it imagines to itself the very things it took in through the body, or conjectures and fashions things it has not seen from things it has seen, it is nevertheless certain that within a kind of belly of memory it can imagine nothing except what it has received through the body. And these things are not natural to it but penal: since, enticed by bodily allurements, it slipped away from the highest good, which for it is God, down into the body, it has been led on so that it justly suffers within itself what it unjustly loved outside itself. Do not try, then, to persuade me that the soul is the very thing by which you see it disturbed. For if it had remained in the loftiness of its original state, from which it fell away of its own will, the flesh would never have lusted against the spirit, nor the spirit against the flesh. And if the true man, that is, the rational soul, had understood his honor, namely the image of God, he would never have been compared to senseless beasts, that is, so as to live like an animal. Hence that tumult of bodily images that keeps thrusting itself before its eyes, so that whenever it strives by reasoning toward itself or toward its God, it is always called back to bodily things by the phantasms of the body.

For when you say that the soul is one thing and the soul's thought another, you might perhaps have done better to say that the things it thinks about, when it is not thinking about itself, are not the soul, but that thought itself is nothing other than the soul. As for what you said must be added, that the soul is wont to rest to the point of thinking nothing at all, that is simply untrue. The soul can indeed vary the things it thinks, but it cannot not think. For what is that which we call dreaming, except that even when the body is wearied and dissolved in sleep the power of the soul is not free from thoughts? And it is wholly there where it thinks, because it thinks wholly. But the chief reason you are deceived about the state of the soul is that you believe the soul is one thing and the soul's powers another. What it thinks is an accident of it, but that by which it thinks is its substance. You must acknowledge the same about the will. For just as the whole soul is thought, so the whole soul is will, and what wills perfectly wills wholly; and, as was said above, whatever it wills is an accident to it, but willing itself is substance. Hence also in the sacred writings a perfect will, by definition, is judged damnable or praiseworthy according to what it was that it willed in this way or that. So the Lord says in the Gospel: "Whoever looks at a woman to lust after her has already committed adultery with her in his heart." And in a good sense it is said elsewhere by the voices of angels: "Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to men of good will." See: love, as you suppose, is some portion of the mind; as reason teaches, it is the whole mind. If, then, I love something with my whole love, do I not love it with my whole mind? And what becomes of the saying, "You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul," if love is thought to be a part of the soul? For if the soul loves with a part of itself, it certainly does not love wholly. But if it loves wholly, then beyond any doubt it is wholly love. For it is said, and truly said, that God is love; but that love is such that it can neither itself love anything but the good, nor can anything be loved through it except rightly. This love, however, which is the human soul, because of the changeableness of its affections, can either blaze with heavenly charity toward higher things, which for it means God alone, or flow away into lower things with a damnable love. Yet whatever it loves, if it loves with its whole love, it loves wholly; and when it loves wholly, it is wholly love—a unity that, of course, is not found in a body.
25. An example from geometry, arithmetic and dialectic, to instruct the reader in obscure matters: what the soul sees by itself and what it sees through the body.

But you say: when the soul thinks of a dear one who is absent, does it not satisfy its longing as though it had actually seen him? This, as I conjecture and indeed clearly prove, is by far the chief reason that drove you, in your ignorance, to declare the soul corporeal. Rise, I beg you, for a little while above the senses of the body, and, if you can, look closely at what the mind's power of seeing is and how great it is, and, if you are able, distinguish the sight of the mind from the sight of the body. The body certainly sees nothing, since it perceives nothing at all without the soul; and so the mind sees bodily things through the body and incorporeal things through itself. Let us now separate these, as far as the present matter requires, so that it may plainly appear which things the mind sees through the body and which without the body. Anyone with even a little education, I believe, knows in the discipline of geometry what a point is and what a line is; but since among those who will deign to read this there may be someone who does not know, let us look into this very question with a short discussion. A line, as the most learned and eminent men have not only stated but proved by reasoning, is simple length, which cannot be found at all in a body, because every body is long by virtue of length, yet is not itself length, nor can it be long without being at the same time broad and deep. Therefore, as they say, even if you think of a spider's thread, since that is certainly a body, you have not thought of length alone, for it has, in its own measure, a breadth and depth inseparable from its length. So if, as truth compels us to admit, length is something other than breadth, let us set breadth aside and think of length alone. I know, however, that not many can see this clearly. When the philosopher Marcius also denied to the mathematician Adrastus that he could see it, though he saw the carpenters' lines all too well, Adrastus said: "It is certainly no wonder, since you have eyes like the carpenters' and a mind unlike Pythagoras's." But the slower among us need not despair on that account, provided that we who perhaps do not grasp the reasoning yield to authority.

This length, then, of which I had begun to speak, when it begins at a point and ends at a point, is called grammē by the Greeks and linea, "line," by us. Now, if you have been able to grasp what length without breadth is, and have formed a line of bounded length, set two equal lines facing each other (antistatas), opposite one another. When you have done this, understand that you have not made a figure with two equal lines. For we speak of a figure when a space is enclosed by lines, equal or unequal, that touch one another at their ends. So with two equal lines, whether set facing apart or touching at their ends, no figure is closed; but with three equal lines a triangular figure is made. And this is an eternal and unchangeable principle, shining clearly to every human mind even without prompting. Could three equal lines touching one another at their ends ever make anything but a triangle? Is this more true now than it used to be? Did it at some time begin to be true, or will it at some time cease to be? Or is it not easier for the bodily world to perish—whose swelling, spatial forms are certainly an image of these non-spatial and incorporeal forms—than for any of these to vary in kind, or move from its place, or grow old with age, or change in any way whatever? So, lest I drag you through all the minutiae of this discipline or hold your attention on examining the principles of plane figures, cubes or pyramids, let us, on account of the perfection of the circle, talk briefly about just one figure, as we have done so far.

A circle is made from a single line. But here you will rightly be reminded that a line without breadth and depth is more perfect, and yet it has something more perfect than itself. The point, namely, is in the first place the origin of the line: the line begins from it and ends at it, while the point clearly neither arises from anything nor comes to an end. For the point holds in figures the place that one holds in numbers. This line, then, which can be cut crosswise, cannot be split lengthwise, because if it were split it would certainly have breadth; when it is to be cut, it is cut at a point, since, of course, the point itself is not cut. Length is therefore more perfect than breadth, because breadth can be cut both crosswise and lengthwise. Breadth is more perfect than depth, because depth can not only be split and cut but also be cut from the side. So depth cannot exist without breadth and length, and where these three are, there is without doubt a body. Breadth cannot exist without length; length can exist without all of these, but it cannot exist without a point. The point, however, always exists without these and needs nothing in order to be, because there can be no beginning of one. A circle, therefore, is made by one and the same line bent round; but just as in triangles and quadrilaterals there are points at the angles, on which the principle of the figures rests, so in the circle the middle will be occupied by a point, so that the circle may be formed with a fixed measurement. For when you have fixed one leg of the compass and swung the other around the center on the outside, observe as closely as you can how the power of the center, by means of the fixed leg, governs the leg being swung round, and how, there where it is not present locally, it shapes the circle by its power.

Here, if you attend with the purified keenness of your mind, it should already begin to glimmer for you what the soul is. And what of this: if we consult bodily sense, we would believe that two equal lines could be drawn side by side through the middle of a circle, whereas reason plainly proves that two lines can by no means be drawn through the same middle unless one of them is shorter? It seems to me that, as was made clear above concerning the triangle, here too the principle of the circle remains fixed by indissoluble and eternal laws. Now I would like you to tell me: if the soul beholds these things spatially, how is it that when I set about forming something round, triangular or square out of bodies in the West, the same principle of the round or the square, without bulk or motion, is not lacking to me, while at the same moment of time someone else in the East can fashion the same things out of bodies according to the same law of the round and the square? Do you see, even from these things the soul beholds, what the sight of the mind is? Do you understand that the intelligible and the one who understands can by no means be separated? Do you notice, too, what difference there is between the forms we perceive with the body and those we behold with the mind? That the latter are the everlasting world, of which this world is an image, as was divinely said: "For the form of this world is passing away"? Do you see also that, while knowing the lengths, breadths and heights of bodies is of almost no importance, it is quite another matter of which the apostle says that we ought to know what is the breadth and length, the height and depth? For what will it profit me to seek out somewhere the height of the bodily heaven, to search out the distances of the planets, the paths of their circles or the intervals between each, to learn the dimensions of the earth or penetrate the depths of the abyss? It was not about these things, I think, that the apostle wished me to be admonished. They are not only laborious but even harmful if, when we ought to pass through them to things eternal and ever-abiding, we stick fast in them and stay there.

Turn back now and observe that everything long is made long by length, but length itself cannot be called long; just as everything chaste is made chaste by chastity, but chastity itself is in no way called chaste. So when you wish to contemplate pure length, or when you fix the eye of the mind on a triangle or a hexagon, cast off and flee as far as you can not only everything bodily but whatever can resemble the bodily. And when you have seen a triangle formed incorporeally and non-spatially by three points and three lines, or a circle by a point and a line, behold also the power and pre-eminence of numbers, and understand that everything bodily that can be counted is made countable through numbers, but that numbers themselves cannot be counted. For who could, I will not say express, but worthily conceive that number, though it is from one, through one and in one, yet has no beginning and no end? For if we say that one is the beginning of number, what shall we say is the beginning of one itself? There you have the beginning of number in the beginning, so that number comes from it. Now if we wish to count, we add one to one to make two, and one to two to make three, and one to three to make four, and so on: as many times as we multiply one, so many times are single units, as if many, brought into a sum, so that, taken ten times, they are called ten, twenty times twenty, a hundred times a hundred, a thousand times a thousand. Thus you may recognize that every number exists through one just as it proceeds from one. It is plain, too, that one cannot arrive at the end of number, for there is none at all, because beyond every number, which is from one, through one and in one, there is always one more. Yet these three, when we say "from one," "through one" and "in one," are equally eternal, likewise non-spatial, whole everywhere, always equal to the same infinite, because no one is truly greater or smaller than another one. These are what begin, carry on and complete numbers, while they themselves are neither begun nor counted nor ended—because, I believe, of God's wisdom there is no number. For since number is from one, through one and in one, and cannot be counted except in a threefold way, so that by the same number we begin, count and finish, it is itself the whole triad through which all number exists. See what dwells in the human soul; see what it is granted us to see with the eye of the heart! Where are we fleeing, where are we being drawn away to? Why, within ourselves, are we outside ourselves? Why do we seek our homeland spatially, when we left it not by walking but by sinning? Why do we believe that darkness shines, when to see it is surely not to see at all? It is certainly truth we seek: do not suppose that it must be sought across expanses of places, or found through anything bodily. Whoever clings to it will separate himself from the body sufficiently, not only in touch but also in thought. It is certainly the non-spatial we seek; let us not, I beg, seek it through the spatial. Truth itself made for itself a likeness capable of sharing in it. Let us bring this, which is in us, to the one who made it; let us not insult our God by saying to him, "You could not make anything like yourself"—because, if I am a body, I am not like you—for he will convict us out of our own selves.
26. God's secret speech to the soul, on how it ought to inquire into itself.

For truth speaks to me in silence and says to me: You, who surely believe that you are a body, how is it that you use an incorporeal word? Your word, I believe—that is, your meaning—is one thing, and the voice of the word another; what sounds is one thing, what is understood another. For just as a voice can exist without a word, so a word exists without a voice. Yet your word uses a sort of garment of voice in order to sound in the ears, as I used the garment of flesh in order to be seen by men. When you speak, the service of the voice travels as far as the ear, but the word passes non-spatially into the soul, because, just as it reaches the one to whom you speak, so it certainly does not leave you. If one person hears you speaking, your whole word remains with you and the whole is with him; if two hear, they hear the whole; if many, the whole; it is whole for all, whole for each, and whole for you. Do not lose in yourself so great a gift of mine, my likeness, which I most kindly bestowed on you, so that you need not seek outside yourself how to reach toward me. No one comes to the Father except through me, and no one comes to me unless my Father draws him; and no one comes to me or to the Father unless charity is poured into his heart by the Holy Spirit, who will be given only to one who believes rightly, hopes rightly and seeks rightly. After the pattern of this Trinity, in which we are one God, you, man, were made, when it was said: "Let us make man in our image and likeness." Look within yourself, by yourself, O human soul, and remember yourself. See your mind, see your word, see your will. For all that you think is in the mind; what you remember all at once you think all at once; and you wish to think and to remember, that is, you love to have mind and thought. So when you embrace your thought with your mind, that is, when you remember that you think, you surely comprehend your whole thought with your whole mind; and you think your whole love or your mind with your whole thought when you think that you love or remember; and with your whole love you love that same whole mind and that same whole thought when you love remembering and thinking. There is no one, however, who does not love remembering and thinking and loving this very thing. But when your thought and your love are in your mind, if you remember them as great as they are, your mind is as great as they are; and when you think of your love or your mind, if you think of them as great as they are, your thought is as great as they are; and if you love your mind or your thought according to their measure, these and your love are certainly equal. And if each of them loves or thinks or remembers itself wholly and all at once, the three wholes together were not greater than the whole mind recalling equally, or the whole thought knowing, or the whole love loving. That these things are in you—or rather, that you are these things—you will recognize as I shine upon you, if you bring me those eyes by which I deign to be seen. Not even an incorporeal being sees me unless it is purified; how much less should you think that I can be seen by you, if you are a body? I and the Father and our love are one God; you, the rational mind, and your word or your love are one man, made after the likeness of your author, not to his equality: created, that is, not begotten; you yourself are formed, not the one who forms. Withdraw from the things beneath you, which are certainly less formed, that is, less beautiful than you are; draw near to the form that forms, so that you may become more beautiful, and join yourself to it always, because you will receive more beauty from it the more firmly you press yourself into it by the weight of charity. From it, that is, you will obtain the unchangeable state of this image, from which you took your beginning. These and similar things truth speaks to the ear of the heart, admonishing us inwardly that, since we were made in the likeness of the incorporeal God and not in the likeness of the corporeal world, we should recognize that we are incorporeal, not only because we are like the incorporeal God, but also because we are unlike the corporeal world.
27. That the soul, even when absent in body, can be present in spirit to one dear to it.

There, then, is my account of the state, or vision, of the rational soul. Because the question is so great, the reasons bearing on it are beyond counting, and I have touched on the grounds briefly rather than discussed them fully. Still, I think I have given a sufficient answer on the soul's non-locality and incorporeality. You now see clearly that bodily vision is very different from this vision and ranks far below it. So do not be tossed about any longer by the uncertainty of supposing that your dear one, whom you think of as absent (as you say yourself), is absent because he does not appear to you bodily. If he is dear to you in that part of himself by which you are both human beings, and by which you love each other with a mutual love, then he is as present to you as you are to yourself. For whatever you are in substance, that he is too. The vision of the soul is understanding. If you see yourself, you see him, for he is nothing other than you. If he were bodily present, he would of course make himself known to you through the signs of the body. And if through these you happened to learn that he was really your enemy, your soul would be thrown back by the clash of your affections and would in some way recoil from his. Then, though you were bodily in one place and, if one may say so, in the very same footprint, you would be thoroughly divided by the difference of your wills. Since this is so, I do not think that souls are torn apart by distance, when we see that they can be separated even while their bodies are joined. And so it matters little that bodies prevent souls from being present to one another, so long as one does not seek through bodies the image of God within a person, or seek the bodies themselves. For it is a wretched thing, and wholly contrary to the truth, that the image of God, that is, the true human being, should be sought through the body rather than through itself. It is sought and recognized through itself if it is sought through the image of God, and every rational soul is the image of God. So whoever seeks the image of God in himself seeks his neighbour as well as himself, and whoever has come to know that image by seeking it in himself recognizes it again in every human being. You, however, have good reason to complain that your dear one is absent from you, since in him you love the body. Indeed you can love nothing but body in one whom you believe to be nothing but body. Love your God, and in your God love your dear one, the image of your God. Let him likewise, by loving God, love you in God. If you both seek the One and strive toward the One, you will always be with each other, because you abide in the One. I do not see how it could happen that bodies placed in one spot can be present to one another, while souls in the One cannot be present to one another. But this book now calls for an end. I have touched some matters only on the surface and left out a great deal for the sake of brevity, though in view of the excellence of the subject I have not passed over everything. So let us take up what remains to be discussed at the beginning of the second volume.
CLAUDIANUS MAMERTUS, ON THE STATE OF THE SOUL: BOOK TWO
1. THAT ALL THINGS ARE MORE EASILY DISCERNED BY COMPARISON WITH THEIR OPPOSITES

I have often asked myself how the most excellent truth could allow itself to have so many enemies. After long reflection on this very question, an explanation that is not implausible, I think, has occurred to me: all things are better discerned by comparison with their opposites. So light set beside darkness, life beside death, and truth beside falsehood give all the more delight. It was fitting, therefore, that these opposites should each be given advocates suited to their qualities. Then the defender of falsehood would not lie hidden, nor would the champion of truth sit idle, and so the one would not do more harm by working unseen, nor would the other grow sluggish with nothing to do.
2. HOW THE PHILOSOPHERS OF THE WORLD SEARCHED FOR THE TRUTH AND ADVANCED STEP BY STEP UNTIL THEY REACHED GOD

Human beings are so made by nature that they search harder for what is hidden, pursue more eagerly what is denied them, and love more what they obtain only slowly. So truth is loved the more ardently the longer it is desired, the more laboriously it is sought, and the more slowly it is found. This is why there have always been philosophers, from Pythagoras of Italy or Thales of Ionia onward. With outstanding minds, many kinds of learning and conflicting opinions, they sought this same truth over long ages, and some of them, though others disagreed, grasped at least in part something worthy of so great a search. For this reason the teacher of the Gentiles does not so much judge the philosophers to be ignorant of the truth as accuse them of despising what they knew, saying: "The invisible things of God are clearly seen from the creation of the world, being understood through the things that are made, as are his eternal power and divinity, so that they are without excuse; for though they knew God, they did not glorify him as God." So they did know him. The human mind entered the secret place of the hidden Godhead and, having passed beyond everything corporeal, saw in wonder that he is the Creator of the universe. He does not merely surpass all corporeal things, as the irrational soul does, nor merely excel the irrational soul, as the rational soul does, but surpasses all these together by a power far beyond comparison. For the mind saw that body moves through places and times, either passing from place to place or changing its age as time goes by. So it paused a little within itself and, looking up in awe at its own power, hesitated over whether to seek something above itself or to come to rest in itself. But since it was in doubt, it could not doubt that it was not God. For the cause of doubt is ignorance, and only one who is ignorant hesitates. God, however, is ignorant of nothing and therefore cannot doubt.

Moreover, it perceived that it was necessarily ignorant and therefore uncertain. It noted besides that, although it was not subject to movement in place, it was moved in time through its affections. It also saw that nothing which could be moved in place or in time could be the first foundation of things. For nothing can be moved except by something else, whereas that in which the universe stands must stand in itself. Thus, reasoning more deeply about its Author, it recognized what I mentioned in the previous book. It saw that nothing can be moved except by what is unmoved. So the soul must necessarily stand still in order to move the body through time and place, while God stands in himself, moving the soul through time and the body through place and time alike. Now there can be no beginning to the Beginning, and the same must be thought of his immensity and eternity: just as he began from nothing, so he is contained in nothing. So the soul judged that one cannot pass from the lowest, which is all body, to the highest, which is God, without something in between, and it found itself to be that middle between the extremes. It was not like any body, because it was the likeness of God. Nor could it be equal to God, because although it had its beginning from him, it was not made out of him.

It also observed that in the fullness of things there is, in truth, one thing that judges and is not judged, another that judges and is judged, and another that is judged and does not judge. In truth God judges and is not judged, the soul judges and is judged, and bodies are judged and do not judge. The one who judges is least deceived when it clings to the standard by which it judges, and most deceived when it sinks down toward the thing it judges. It understood too that, by the unchangeable force of opposites, body is opposed to the incorporeal as darkness is to light and nothingness to being. It saw that nothing can have its likeness in its opposite, because the fixed order of things does not allow a dead thing to live, a blind thing to see, or something to be a substance and nothing at the same time. Here, then, it understood that there is something in the human soul like God: he is the light that gives light, and the soul is a light that can receive light. So it concluded without hesitation that the soul is incorporeal, and it added this: if the soul were a body and were also the likeness of God, then God would be corporeal. And rightly it preferred to raise up the creature on account of its likeness to the Creator, rather than to lower the Creator on account of that same likeness. For it knew for certain that the bond is unbreakable: two like things are either both incorporeal or both corporeal. It also saw that among real substances there are some things that are not only different in kind but opposed in their natural power, such as water and fire, and yet these are both corporeal. Hence it would be strange if two things that are unlike and even opposed, such as water and fire, could both be corporeal, while two things that are alike and in harmony, namely God and the soul, could not both be incorporeal.
3. HE USES THE GREEK PHILOSOPHERS AS WITNESSES CONCERNING THINGS CORPOREAL AND INCORPOREAL, PROPOSING THE EXAMPLE OF THE CAMEL AND THE ANT

I have searched as far as I could through the books of the philosophers who reason in this way. Rejecting the crowd of lesser figures, I chose the most eminent to bear witness to the truth here. To cite their opinions is really more than is needed. It is not that we lack arguments of our own, but it makes the thing all the more remarkable that our own people fight against us while outsiders fight for us. Nor would I have any wish to borrow anything from them, had not this friend of the body brandished at us certain bogeys of deeper learning merely by mentioning the name of philosophy. Let him, then, hear the voice of truth from the very men he calls up against the truth. Let him listen first to the battle-call of the twofold Greece, the many-voiced trumpet of the Pythagoreans and the clarion of Plato. And let him not puff himself up with the mere vanity of names, but grow rich on the manifold truth of reasoned arguments. As for the Pythagoreans, since Pythagoras himself wrote nothing, their teaching must be sought from his successors. Among them I find that Philolaus of Tarentum was especially distinguished. In many books he discourses, very obscurely, on intelligible things and what each of them signifies. Before he pronounces on the substance of the soul, he gives a remarkable discussion of measures, weights and numbers according to geometry, music and arithmetic, and affirms that the whole universe came into being through these. In this he agrees with the Scripture in which it is said to God: "You have ordered all things in measure, weight and number." I am surprised that our adversary has hurled this sentence from the sacred text at us. For he says, in these words: "God, who made all things from nothing, and who embodied them in matter just as he established them by his work, assigned quantity to all things, among which the soul too is counted, just as he allotted them weight, number and measure."

Observe, good judge of our case, this skilled and eloquent teacher of the present age! He will have nothing created that is incorporeal, and he says that everything corporeal is "embodied". Into what, I ask, is a body embodied? Perhaps you used "in-" to mean "not", so that "incorporated" is to be understood as "not embodied". If so, you freely grant us more than we want. For if the Author of things did not embody any of the things he made, then everything that exists is without a body. And what exists and is without a body must be incorporeal, what the Greeks more elegantly call asōmaton. But if you used the prefix in its plain sense, you have stumbled on the truth without knowing it. Through the same ignorance, however, you slipped on one point only, in saying that all things were embodied. For it is well established that the substance of the twofold creation is arranged by so well-ordered a law that every created incorporeal being is also embodied, but not every corporeal thing is also ensouled. For this reason a body could not be called "embodied", as if it had been put into a body. Embodiment plainly belongs to that nature which was not a body before it was embodied and is not a body after it has been embodied. But perhaps by "all things embodied" you meant that all things were made corporeal, which could certainly be said, though it should not have been. In that case you have strayed both from the proper sense of the word and from the logic of truth. For if every creature is corporeal, nothing is embodied; and if anything incorporeal has been created, then not every creature is corporeal.

But it is one and the same cause that entangles you in so many errors: a great ignorance of things and an astonishing presumption of knowledge. This is why you either believe embodied spirits to be body or, again, define bodies as embodied. In these highly dialectical conclusions of yours, always remember the disgrace of profound error that you think fit to brand on others. Let the divine word also stir you: one must first remove one's own beam before one can take out another's speck. You do not just provoke men who are hesitating over a fight; you strike down peaceable men with the sword-point of abuse. You have also said that measure, weight and number are implanted in every part of creation. Since all agree that these are present together in all bodies, and you declare the soul to be a body, I ask: what is its measure, what its number, what its weight? Suppose the size of the living body determines the size of the soul that gives it life, because the outer body, like a vessel, encloses the soul as a kind of smaller body. Then, as you say, the soul's quantity must be reckoned by the body's quantity.

Oh, if only I could speak with you about these things face to face and in the open! I would deal generously with you. I would give up some points that are mine by right, and would not at once ask about man. Instead I would first ask you, as a favour, to declare in a plain answer, since you are so expert in such matters, whether you judge the souls of the ant and the camel by their foresight or by their bulk. If by foresight, it would be clearer than daylight that the ant's soul surpasses the camel's, so that the camel is almost as much inferior to the ant in mind as it is greater in body. If you preferred bulk for a comparison of this kind, I would of course repeat the same points and ask all the same: if the measure of the soul is the measure of the body, why is the camel dull, below the measure of its body, while the ant is vigorous, beyond the measure of its own? Perhaps then the words would stop that now fly so grandly and so safely from your lips. I would put these very points to you as a choice of two, and let you take whichever you preferred. If you chose bodily bulk, I would set against it the ant's tiny body. If you chose vigour of mind, I would prove that it has nothing to do with bulk, since I would show that there is none of it in the camel's great bodily size. I would also throw at you that line of Virgil, so truly said of the little bees: "Mighty spirits they carry in a narrow breast."

Then, when I had begun to discuss the condition of man, I would ask you, as a new kind of geometer, for a ten-foot measuring rod rather than for judgment, so that I might assess anyone's mind. And if you perhaps wished to take refuge in saying that invisible things cannot be measured by visible ones, I would reply at once that, on your view, the mind that fills the body could be measured by the size of the body that encloses it. If you said that this could not be done, I would press you hard: why can something not be done with one kind of body that can be done with all of them? If you agreed that it could, I would say to you in the words of the prophet: "Go to the ant, O sluggard, and watch her ways and imitate them", that is, her foresight. Or are we perhaps to believe that the heavenly oracle admonished us in order to learn the art of walking from the ant? In this saying, do not let walking be your concern, but skill in acting. Ants, "mindful of winter", plunder "a huge heap of grain" and store it safely away. O man, brought down by the sin of the first-formed man to be compared with the irrational beasts, do likewise: see to it, by the warmth of faith and devotion in your works, that your flight may not be in winter. And understand at the same time that the mighty minds of the little ant and the little bee are not contained in their small bodies. For nothing large [and local] can be contained in a small local thing, and the little bee has a small body and a mighty mind. So its mind is not contained in the body; therefore it is outside itself. But nothing can be outside itself; therefore it is wholly in the body. But a large corporeal thing cannot be contained in a small corporeal one, because every local thing fills a place exactly as large as it is. Either, then, the soul is non-local and therefore incorporeal, or it is not wholly together with itself. But nothing can exist except together with itself; therefore the great thing is present in the small thing non-locally. So the mind is not local, and nothing non-local is corporeal: therefore it is not corporeal. And whatever is not corporeal is not to be measured by bulk; therefore the greatness of the mind does not come from the size of the body.

Now let us see where you might escape to. The little bee denies you greatness of body, and the camel denies you greatness of mind. Take care that such arguments do not topple your favourite opinion, and show that the greatness of the mind is not subject to number, weight and measure according to bodily quantities. Small in a large body, the mind still fills the whole; great in a small body, it does not spill over. But perhaps the mind cannot be measured in bodily terms and yet can be weighed. Let anyone who has grasped how many feet long the mind is dare to claim that he can know how many pounds it weighs. Traces of number are discerned in bodies in three ways. First, every body, whether very large or very small, must be one, and it has this from number.
