Second, it consists of parts, and these parts, as we have said, are right and left, up and down, forward and back. Third, every body can be cut into parts according to this variety of parts. Because of the primal force of number, any one of these parts will in turn be one body, will consist of the same number of parts, and can likewise be cut into parts. Now consider whether, since every living creature has one soul, that soul can be divided in the same way, so that any fraction of a soul is again a soul, just as any fraction of a body is a body. Since I think no one in his right mind can say so, we need not waste time discussing these matters. By their very nature they are so clear that argument would seem rather to obscure them.
4. ON THE MEASURE, NUMBER AND WEIGHT OF THE BODY

Now, unless you scorn it, turn your mind rather to this point, so that the divine power of measure, weight and number may be disclosed to you, so far as it will deign to let itself be seen. We read, of course, that it is said to God: "You have ordered all things by measure, number and weight." You used this testimony above all for one purpose: you wanted it to prove that certain bodily quantities have been placed in our souls too. Let us see, then, where this measure, this weight and this number were located, or when they began to exist, so that God could form all things after them as a kind of pattern. If nothing is uncreated except the Creator, then these things are created. If they are created, then God did not order all things by measures, numbers and weights, since he did not form these things themselves according to them. But it is impious to oppose divine authority; therefore all things were created by numbers, weights and measures. Therefore measure, weight and number are not created, for all things were not created according to them if they themselves were also created. Here we must strive with all the powers of thought, so that it may somehow be recognized that the principal weight is not what is weighed but that by which it is weighed; that number is not what is numbered but that by which it is numbered; and that measure is not what is measured but that by which it is measured. In the same way, magnitude is not the same as what is great, nor equality the same as what is equal, nor beauty the same as what is beautiful. For nothing created is great in itself; something is called great by comparison with what is smaller. That is why we call a mountain small and a grain of millet large, a fly large and an ox small. But when we come to the creative magnitude itself, since it cannot be compared, it is neither greater nor smaller. The same reasoning holds for these principal forms, which Plato calls ideas. For we make both a square table and a square forum by the same law of squaring, and though the forum is a larger square, it is not more square. From this you ought to take an indication of that unweighed weight, that unmeasurable measure and that innumerable number, which three, at once coeternal, always undivided, everywhere and wherever they are wholly present, are one God.

For all the bodies by which we number, weigh or measure anything are themselves numerable, weighable and measurable. Numbers in bodies have a fixed limit, the little weight of a balance has a fixed weight, and the ten-foot rod has a fixed measure. From its size one may go downward to inches and half-inches and on to the smallest thing, below which there is nothing; and one may likewise go upward to the greatest things, even to the spaces of the world itself that are now beyond the reach of the senses. For whatever is bounded has a fixed limit of size. Accordingly the whole mass of the world, since it is compacted of bounded bodies, one body setting a limit to another, is without doubt itself bounded and therefore measurable. If the human mind conceives any spaces beyond it, it does not doubt that the principle of measure could be extended into them through bodily forms; and this could truly be done if there were any place outside the world. But since there can be no place outside every place, local measure does not reach where there is no place; and though what can be measured is lacking, that by which it can be measured remains, because the unmeasurable measure does not fail when the measurable comes to an end. In the same way the principle of weight does not perish when what can be weighed ceases, and number is not ended when the numerable is ended. If, then, the splendor of the immeasurable light glimmers for us with some gleam, you will of course necessarily be prompted at this point to set aside for a little the deception of carnal sights [?] and tell us: to which part of us is the form of a bodily ten-foot rod visible? Since you will not deny, unless perhaps you are too angry, that it can be seen by the body, I go on to ask whether you say that the unmeasurable measure of which we spoke above is visible to the soul or to the body. [?] But may the truth not so abandon anyone that he would contend that divine things will be visible to the body, when he knows that bodies themselves are not seen by it unless it is animated, or, to speak more truly, when he understands that it is rather the soul that perceives through the body than the body that perceives anything by itself. The power of seeing is therefore twofold: the soul sees measure, weight and number by itself; it sees measurable, numerable and weighable things through the body. Through the body, then, it sees the things that are like the body, that is, bodily things; but incorporeal things it sees by itself, since it is like them.

Now, if you please, since all things have been ordered by measures, weights and numbers, let us look for the signs of these in created things. Earth is certainly the lowest of all the elements. In a sphere, plainly, the lowest point is the middle, since there is no lowest point at the outer edges of a sphere. Any part of the earth, then, large or very small, whether a tiny pebble or the finest speck of dust, too small to be touched by a visible point, has both measure according to its size and number according to the arrangement of its parts, by which upper is distinguished from lower, right from left, front from back; this is why even the smallest thing can be divided in two, because it is a body. Its weight is noticed from this: if this very smallest thing is taken from its place of origin and dropped into water, which is of course the element above it, it does not rest from its tireless motion until by its natural weight it has reached the floor of the earth. Keep to this path of reasoning for the other bodies as well. For a drop of water that you pick up on a moistened finger has measure according to the extent of its size and number according to the distance between its parts; and by the law of weight, if you let it go in the air, it does not settle until it has reached its own element. The same reasoning holds for air: none of it can be held under water or carried above fire, and if somehow this happens, the necessity of weight makes it either burst out naturally from the one or sink down of its own accord from the other. That air is measurable and, according to the number of its parts, numerous is clear, I think, from this: it has already been established that the bodily world, of which air is the third part, can be measured. So too the element of fire admits numbers with respect to its parts, because it occupies place, and is subject to measures with respect to its extent, because it is bounded. This earthly fire, as a kind of seed of the highest fires, has its weight directed upward. The more fuel it feeds on and the greater the strength it gains, the more its subtle nature, as though making for its homeland, bursts through great tracts of the dense air; and if the depth of another element did not overcome it, it would reach the place to which it is carried by nature.
5. On the Measure, Number and Weight of the Soul

Here it has become clear that there is nothing bodily that lacks measure, weight and number. Now, since bodies have a unity made of parts, a weight bound to place, and a measurable magnitude, let us ask whether these three are in the soul in the same way as they are in the body. We certainly call a body great in length, breadth and height, and we judge its extent large or small according to its capacity. So any body takes in as much of body as its size allows it to hold. In the same way, then, pass beyond the step of the lower creation, look at the higher creation, and measure the greatness of the soul by its capacity. See, the human soul is capable of wisdom; it is capable of it because it understands it. Therefore, just as before it has obtained wisdom it cannot be called capable of wisdom, so before it becomes a partaker of it, it cannot be called wise. Here I come to ask you: do you judge that what holds wisdom is a spatial extent, or something not in place? My view is this: if the soul of the wise man is capable of wisdom according to spatial extent, then wisdom is great according to bulk. Since the truth does not allow this to be said, what holds it is not in place, so that what is held can be not in place. There you have the greatness of the human mind without bulk; now consider the principle of number.

You have noticed, I think, that these are the signs of numbers in bodies: bodies are well-numbered when their parts correspond to one another with equal balance, according to the most excellent equality of number. Since the highest equality is that of one to one, two to two and three to three, so in the same way we call a body well-numbered when it is formed with fixed proportion: the human body, for example, has the parts that come in pairs set opposite each other, so that they do not differ from each other in size, shape or position, as the ears and eyes do; while the single parts, like the nose and mouth, hold the middle place; and so that they may be beautiful, they imitate the harmony of the highest equality. To find the truth of number in the human soul, then, the soul's principle of action ought first to be in harmony with itself through the balance of the virtues, so that justice corresponds to wisdom and fortitude to temperance; and this balance is certainly numerical, since a thing is closer to numbers the more harmonious it is. But I think that what is more truly numerical in the soul is that it has knowledge of number: it is not numerical in its parts, as the body is, but it discerns number itself and judges according to it. For that three and four make seven, and these and three make ten, nothing but the human soul is able, or ever will be able, to know. As it has become clear concerning measure, then, so it is quite evident concerning numbers that they are in the body visibly and in the soul intellectually.

It remains now to discuss weight. It has become clear that the weight of bodies is that by which they are naturally carried to their own regions, from which they originally come, and do not rest until they have crossed the space of another element and reached their own. The weight of the soul, however, is its will, which is more properly called love, the love by which the soul loves either itself or anything else. For whether it loves incorporeal things for itself, such as true wisdom, or desires bodily things for the body, such as beautiful bodies, it is carried along by the weight of love, which is not in place, until it gains possession of the things it loves. So the weight of a body, wherever it carries the body, inseparably draws its measures and numbers along with it. Likewise the weight, that is, the love of the soul, draws both memory and counsel along with it toward what it loves, since it can neither remember nor think of anything except what it burns with love for. That is why it is said to man by God: "You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul," so that, just as the body is driven by its weight to its own place, the soul may be carried back by its weight to its homeland. By this weight of its own, moreover, the soul is not only joined to other things but is also made firm in itself, because, with love standing between counsel and mind, the mind is loved by counsel and counsel by the mind.
6. On the Measure, Number and Weight of the Divine Trinity: How the Trinity Itself Is These Three

So too the unity of the most exalted Trinity, which incorporeally surpasses all things, is, as they say, measure without measure, weight without weight and number without number. The weight, then, by which these are ineffably one with each other is the love of the Father and the Son. For the apostle, speaking properly of the Holy Spirit, says: "The love of God has been poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit, who has been given to us," clearly showing that by this weight, namely divine love, that ineffable number and that measure are steadfastly borne to the one to whom such weight has come. These three, then, are inseparable in the body, but much more so in the soul; and they are undivided in the soul, but much more so in themselves. And just as nothing came into existence without the one Creator, that is, the Trinity itself, so nothing at all can exist that does not both subsist in threefold form and is one. Every body, plainly, will be one, and measurable, numerable and weighable; and every rational soul subsists by three undivided things, memory, counsel and will, by which it is capable of measure, weight and number, and in accordance with these it judges measurable, weighable and numerable things, that is, bodies. If the soul were a body, it certainly would not grasp incorporeal things; like a body, it could be judged, but it could not judge bodies. So the pattern of the united Trinity flows down from the highest, which is God, through the middle, which is the soul, to the lowest, which is bodies, stamping its signs on bodies and granting knowledge of itself to souls, forming the former visibly and the latter intelligibly. Since, then, nothing receives substance except from being, and nothing becomes one except through three, as we argued above, when is there as much unity in the body, that is, in the trace of the Trinity, as there is in the soul, that is, in the image of the Trinity? And again, when is there as much in the image as there is in the Trinity itself?
7. He Uses Pagan Witnesses to Show That There Are No Bodily Measures [?] or Local Weights in the Soul

But since this is not the time to argue at greater length about how important this question is, I have dwelt on these matters only as long as I judge enough for the wise. I wanted them to recognize fully that the soul has no bodily measures, no weights tied to place and no parts spread out in space, but that it perceives something which no place contains, no weight moves and no division diminishes. Only you, learned judge, who know how to pass a just sentence, must decide whether what receives the placeless can be a place, whether what cannot be cut can have parts, and whether what grasps the infinite can be measured. Now I return to Philolaus, from whom I digressed a long way some time ago. In the third of the volumes he entitled On Rhythms and Meters, he speaks of the human soul as follows: “The soul is placed in the body through number and through an immortal and likewise incorporeal harmony.” And again, after other things: “The body is loved by the soul, because without it the soul cannot use the senses. When death has drawn the soul away from it, the soul leads an incorporeal life in the world.” I will not now go back over the course of reasoning and the very intricate details of argument by which Philolaus makes these points convincing against any opponent you like. If anyone happens to be fired with curiosity or zeal for them, he will draw them from the source itself. For the sake of authority it will be enough for me to have brought in the testimony of so great a philosopher on this matter, just as it will be fitting to set out the testimonies of the others briefly from here on. For it is unfair to demand from anyone argument and testimony alike.

Likewise Archytas of Tarentum, who was also a Pythagorean, wrote a magnificent work on the nature of things. In it, after a long and very subtle discussion of numbers, he says: “The soul is composed after the model of the One, and it rules in the body without occupying a place, just as the One rules among numbers.” What, I ask, could be said that is loftier or truer? It is composed after the model of the One, clearly, because it was made after the image of the One. The One is therefore the chief model of forms, since things capable of receiving form receive their forms from him who had no beginning. Hippon of Metapontum, of the same school of Pythagoras, first sets out unanswerable arguments to support his view and then declares this about the soul: “The soul is something far different from the body. It is vigorous when the body is numb, it sees when the body is blind, and it lives when the body is dead.” But where this comes from, and from what first principle, he says he does not know. I am not now going through the opinions of all the philosophers of the Pythagorean family, as though I meant to build my own work out of other people's volumes by piling them up at length. I consider it enough to have plainly set out the teachings of the foremost members of the Pythagorean school on the present question. I am certain that no learned man will deny that Archippus, Epaminondas, Aristaeus, Gorgiades, Diodorus and all the successors of Pythagoras held this same view and set it down in writing. If I wished to publish them, I would fill a volume with the mere number of their names, not to mention their opinions.

So let Plato step forward into the open. He shows clearly how great a good the human race neglects in itself, especially in our own age. In our age religion has been so fully proclaimed through words and deeds sent from heaven that, with the labour of believing almost taken away, it takes hold of the fruit of knowledge with a lukewarm faith and receives the wages of labour without doing the work. That is why I cannot admire the mind of this Plato as it deserves. So many ages before the Virgin gave birth, before God became incarnate, before man rose again, and before the ineffable unity of the supreme Trinity was preached among the nations, he sought out, found and made known three persons in one Godhead, with praiseworthy daring, wonderful genius and matchless eloquence. These were God the Father; the Father's Mind, which is his Art or Counsel; and the mutual love of these two: one supreme, coeternal, undivided Godhead. He not only taught that it must be believed to be so but proved that it is so. I cannot persuade myself that the soul of this philosopher was corporeal. And if, through some headlong slide into folly, any soul is to be judged a body, I would judge corporeal those souls that believe themselves to be body. In saying this I do not disparage the whole race of souls. I am singling out certain people for the perversity of their own opinion, and they have brought this on themselves. And what is to be done with such men? Ignorance has such a hold on them that they do not know they are unlearned, yet they still claim for themselves the privilege of knowledge. While they spit out the froth of childish words into inexperienced ears, they deceive themselves about knowledge with one and the same lie and mislead others by teaching them. They are like Lysias, whom the same Plato rebukes in the Phaedrus for pouring out words empty of substance. Plato goes so far as to hold that it is worse to be skilled in words while ignorant of causes than to be ignorant of the words because one does not know the things, for he thought ignorant silence better than talkative ignorance. Hence Tully, too, says in the first book On the Orator: “Eloquence is the knowledge of grasping a great many things; without it, fluency of words is empty and laughable.” And a little later: “For speech must blossom and overflow from a knowledge of things. Unless it rests on matter that the orator has perceived and understood, its utterance is empty and almost childish.” But more on this elsewhere.

In the Phaedrus, moreover, Plato declares this about the soul: “The soul is immortal, since it is always moved by itself and is the cause of motion to other things; but the body is not moved by itself.” He does not merely say “it moves other things”, but “it is the cause of motion to other things.” This man of outstanding genius noticed that there are some things whose nature is to be moved by a cause of motion outside themselves. Whatever is moved voluntarily is, as a rule, itself the cause of its own motion. But what is moved either without knowing it or against its will has the causes of its motion in the one who knows or compels. Nor does it conflict with our earlier discussions that we say here that the soul is moved by itself, although we also say that the chief hinge of all motions lies in God. For the soul has from God this very ability to move of its own accord. Just as the cause of the mind's motion is its will, so the cause of the substance that uses the will is God. Although our power to will comes from God, not every motion of our will comes from God. Certainly when we sin by our will, I think, the cause of our motion comes from ourselves; otherwise we would make God the author of sins. Therefore, if a body is not moved by itself, then whatever is the cause of its own motion is not a body, because it has the causes of its motion within itself. Hence the soul is not a body.

The same Plato says in the book he wrote On Nature: “The soul of all living beings is not corporeal. It moves itself, and it also sets in motion the other things that are moved by nature.” In the Phaedo, moreover, the same Plato has Socrates speak with Simmias, Cebes and other philosophers. We see things said there that agree closely with our own views, and they rest not only on the authority of the speaker but on the strength of reason. So we should recognize something beyond the native vigour of the human mind. These souls pursued things so remote, reached things so closed off and saw things so hidden because they were breathed upon by the light of truth. The purpose was this: the teaching that God at length made known to the whole world for the salvation of the human race could use the testimony of pagans among the nations, whose minds had no training in the truth. Paganism, blinded by the cloud of ignorance and hardened into a kind of ice by the chill of unbelief, would yield more readily to the warmth of gospel truth if that same truth had also sounded from the mouths of its opponents. Or why should we not believe that heaven provided these same truths for our use through the philosophers, since we see that they will also be useful for refuting the ignorance of our own people? So in the Phaedo true reason, persuading Socrates, speaks as follows: “As long as we have a body and our mind is mixed with such an evil, we shall never fully attain what we have long desired, and what we desire is knowledge of the truth. First, the body loads us with countless, endless occupations, which wear us down for the sake of the food we need and our daily nourishment. Then, if any diseases attack us, they prevent us from seeking and finding the truth. The body is burdened with desires and lusts and countless fears, with images of all sorts of things and cravings, and with a kind of boundless madness, so that because of it we cannot be wise in anything at all. And if we ever have or make some free time for philosophy, even then the body breaks in on our very thoughts and brings a throng of errors into the mind, so that it blinds us and we cannot see the truth clearly. So in every inquiry this one thing is proved to us, and most plainly: if we ever wish to know anything truly, we must withdraw from the body and consider things with the mind itself. We shall attain what we desire, and what we profess to love, only when we have died, it seems. While we live, there is no hope of it. If it is established that the mind, while mixed with the body, can see nothing pure, one of two things follows. Either true knowledge can come to a human being at no time and in no place, or it comes only when we have departed this life. For the mind of the dead is free and released from the body. During the time we live, we shall come close to knowledge and attach ourselves to it only if we use the body not at all or as little as possible, and do not let the mind into fellowship with it beyond what is necessary. In this way we shall be least filled with the vicious and turbulent nature of the body and shall be pure from its contagion as far as we can. And if we do this, we shall depart uncorrupted and pure and come to all things that are uncorrupted and pure.”

I thought it right to excerpt these words exactly from the dialogue of the very foremost philosopher and insert them into this volume of ours. I believed that anyone in the habit of resisting the deceptive allurements of the body feels in himself this conflict between the unlike natures of body and mind. Taking himself as witness, he would agree on this very point with the carefully examined arguments of by far the greatest man among the philosophers. With reason presiding, he would judge between his mind and his body and ask two questions. If the mind is corporeal, as they say, why is it always hindered in every discovery by an outside body that gets in its way? And why does it blame an outside body for calling it away from contemplating the truth, when it would be its own hindrance if it were itself a body? But I shall not argue about these things. Truth shines clearly by itself and needs no ornament or support from outside. Naked, it is both more beautiful and stronger.

For this reason I have so far thought it best to use the testimonies of my witnesses without arguing in their defence. Only those who are wholly body will doubt these guarantors of the truth. What this same Plato declared about the soul in the Hipparchus, the Laches, the Protagoras, the Symposium, the Alcibiades, the Gorgias and the Crito, and even in the Timaeus, which is a kind of citadel and summit of philosophy, I pass over for the sake of the brevity I have chosen. In recognizing the truth, it matters less how often someone said the same thing than what he thought. Saying things often does not yield a richer knowledge of them; it only makes the words burdensome and long-winded. So in establishing the truth we should consider what many have thought with one mind rather than what one person has often said. Nevertheless, drawn by admiration for Plato, who in my opinion is rightly the foremost of all philosophers, I have often called him as a witness in the present matter. Yet what you read of his here is very little compared with the countless things he wrote about the soul, and [?]. Nor did Porphyry the Platonist, many ages after Plato, ever disagree with his master on this same question. Indeed, with an illustrious voice he reminded the human race of its dignity: “If we wish to be blessed,” he says, “we must flee every body.” There is therefore something incorporeal in us, to which contact with any body at all is hostile. What will this be, if not the image of God? And what is the image of God, if not the human mind? If the mind cannot be blessed in the body and is not incorporeal, it will never be blessed, for it can never be without itself.
8. He calls pagan Roman philosophers as witnesses to the incorporeality of the soul.

We have used many testimonies from many philosophers in the present matter, and we could bring forward many more from Greece itself if the case demanded it or good sense allowed. But we do not want to seem to have sought the truth in one place only, as if one nation alone could see it and the others knew nothing of it. Human nature is capable of truth not because of its region but because of its kind. So let us call Romans too as witnesses, and philosophers at that. Among them, Sextius the father and Sextius the son devoted themselves eagerly to the practice of wisdom and philosophized with great distinction. They gave this verdict about every soul: “Every soul is incorporeal and occupies no place. It is a kind of power that cannot be grasped. Without any extension, it is capacious enough to take in and hold the body.” These men, unless I am mistaken, probed the hidden reasons of things more keenly than some of our own countrymen. These men hold bedroom debates about the search for lofty causes and yawn out something to put one to sleep from their couches. Driven on by a flood of lukewarm ditties and applauded by some dull admirer, they sleep their way through the drowsy notions of old wives' opinions, and they decree that the soul is entwined with the entrails and shut in and contained by the confines of the body. But that invention of an ignorance void of truth we have refuted in the previous book, as the arrangement of topics required. Now, with truth helping us, we refute it again by setting out the great testimonies of the highest authorities on the matter, and by the strength of reason as well. Marcus Varro was the most expert man of his age and, on the testimony of Tully, without doubt the most learned of all. What did he contend for with almost divine argument in his books on music, arithmetic and geometry and in his philosophical books? Surely his aim was to draw the mind, by the wonderful methods of eternal art, away from the visible to the invisible, from what has place to what has none, from the corporeal to the incorporeal. The mind had slipped down into bodies, that is, into things contrary to itself, and he sought to make it master of itself again. If the mind were a body, a body could not be contrary to it. Why should I now bring forward in defence of the truth the opinions of Zoroaster, of the Brahmans of India, of Anacharsis of Scythia, or indeed of the Catos and of Marcus Cicero? Or of Sallust, who almost at the very beginning of his work gives the mind the right to rule and imposes on the body the law of servitude? Why should I prove what judgment the whole world proclaims to us about the condition of the soul, at least in those who have rightly stood out?
9. From here on he calls the teachers of the Church as witnesses to the incorporeality of the soul.

I could certainly do the same thing easily, except that the crowd of witnesses already gathered would not allow any more to be added, and either the time has come or reason now urges me to lay open the divine oracles. And so that we may come to the very springs of the heavenly books, led chiefly by those who have drunk most deeply from them: Gregory of Nazianzus, in his Apology, cries out that there is a great difference between soul and body, and that as the body is fed on bodily things, so the soul is nourished on incorporeal ones. Blessed Ambrose, speaking in church to the people of Milan in most learned and erudite words, says: "Let us separate ourselves from the body, against which we must wage unceasing battle if we wish to be saved." The one and the same opinion of such eminent men must be understood in one and the same sense and treated in the same terms. So I will now say what I remember often saying when we reached this point. Ambrose urges that we ought to be separated from the body. I ask, then, who it is that ought to be separated from the body. For we consist of soul and body, and therefore, since the soul cannot be separated from itself, there is nothing in us that can be separated from the body, if the soul is a body. Why, holy Ambrose, why do you teach so? Why do you smear the bride of Christ with the mud of falsehood? Why do you drive her off the way of truth, by the thrust of perverse preaching, onto pathless precipices? Why do you claim that a body ought to be separated from a body? What good, I ask, will that do a person? Because the nature of the inner man is finer, though it is nothing but body, ought it therefore to be torn apart and separated? Because in the structure of the world's mass some things are finer and lighter and others coarser and heavier, ought the finer therefore to break apart the whole frame of this solid mass? Or will the air be happier if it is no longer together with water and earth? To such lying chatterers he would give an answer of this kind: What is this doctrine that rises up before us, bare in its words, void of power, foreign to reason, empty of truth, hollow with vanity, swollen with pride, the authorless teaching of this new schism, lifted up with arrogance, cast down by falsehood, crammed with abuse, robbing the Creator of his power and the image of its dignity? With an astonishing kind of folly it defames that image by comparing it with bodily substance, asserting, forsooth, that it would profit the soul as little to be separated from the body as it would benefit the air to be separated from the coarser bodies of the world's mass. Further, if there are any of you anywhere in the world to whose minds the secrets of causes have yielded, come quickly, punish yourselves for your ignorance, and marvel at the new dogma: the fourth part of the world's body, within the solid frame of the universe, takes on the dignity of a soul! This, then, is no doubt the greatest soul of all souls, and wiser in proportion to its bulk. So now a person will be all the richer in wisdom the more of this air he has drawn in according to his capacity; and not without reason has the human race accused nature of injustice for producing Lucanian oxen so much larger than men, and so much happier, of course, for being so much more capacious. But enough of Ambrose for now, though he alone would surely be enough; still, I will give others room to testify as well.

Aurelius Augustine, in keenness of mind, in the range of his subjects and in the bulk of his work, is like a Chrysippus in the power of argument, or a Zeno in subtlety of thought, or our own Varro in the size of his volumes. By nature and application he was so outstanding in learning that, as a spiritual sophist, he deservedly dissented from those corporeal Epicureans or Cynics of our age. In his book to Jerome on the origin of the soul he declares: "Although it is hard to persuade slower minds that the soul is incorporeal, I confess that I am persuaded of it." And when he proves by weighty reasons and unanswerable argument that this is so, and asks Jerome's opinion on the matter, all he gets back from Jerome is a letter in his praise, in which Jerome says without hesitation that he could think nothing truer about the soul and argue nothing more perfectly. See: here you have two most illustrious men, far pre-eminent in virtue and learning, who agree with us about the condition of the soul. They lay you low, disarmed, by the weight of their authority and the force of their reasoning, and, separated in body, by the unity of their wisdom they make two souls one. So I am greatly surprised that you cited Jerome as your witness, since the foremost of commentators could hardly argue both for the soul and against it. And yet the passages from him that you set out against us without understanding them serve us so well that you seem to be not a cunning adversary but a planted collusive advocate, who, as if by some secret agreement, has let us win with your own witnesses. For it is a glorious kind of victory to take your weapons from the very person you are fighting, and to have the witness your opponent sought out stand on that side and speak for this one.

Yet lest you think me slow to return the favor, I will point out, as the occasion allows, that Hilary of Poitiers could have been more in agreement with your view. Among his many lofty discussions he held something less correct and argued two things contrary to the truth: first, that nothing created is incorporeal; second, that Christ felt no pain in his passion. But if his passion was not real, our redemption could not be real either. Since blessed Hilary wiped out the fault of this opinion by the virtue of his confession, he bears the pen of censure in such a way that his merits suffer no loss. Therefore it is right to give credence to commentators on the divine Scriptures only so far as they agree with the tenor of the truth. But although I must of necessity refrain from citing a number of writers, since I rightly hasten to the divine oracles on which their authority depends, I would by no means pass over Eucherius. I knew him in his lifetime through his teaching and through discussions face to face, not from reports or reading. Young in years, mature in mind, spurning earth, longing for heaven, humble in spirit, lofty in merit, and likewise most subtle in intellect, full of knowledge, flowing in eloquence, by far the greatest of the great bishops of his age, he published many volumes of various works on matters of faith, and he also preached to the people on the condition of the soul in these words: "Some people," he says, "are in the habit of asking how man and God could be mingled in Christ. They seek the reason for this mystery, which happened once, when they themselves can by no means give the reason for what happens all the time: how the soul is joined to the body so that a man comes to be. So then, just as a corporeal and an incorporeal thing are joined, and the soul is mingled with the body so that a man is produced, so man was joined to God and Christ came to be. And yet, for Christ to come to be, those two incorporeal things, the soul and God, could be joined and mingled more easily than one incorporeal thing is mingled with another that is corporeal, the soul and the body, so that the person of a man may exist." Now bring me those who, though schooled in the same teachings, have degenerated from them, ruining what was wholesome for them and making themselves liable to the harmful errors of others. Through unjust hatred of those who love them they have slid so far that they would rather choose strangers along with falsehood and condemn Eucherius along with the truth.

Here you may see some weighing a matter with sluggish judgment, and others either praising it in ignorance with foolish acclaim or, with their smattering of learning, mocking it while slyly appearing to agree. Among them a certain man is pleased with himself, though no one has praised him except the ignorant or the crafty. Here verdicts on individuals are given according not to their merits but to people's wishes, and to praise some present-day ranters the very greatest authors are condemned. There the man who has been praised, lest he seem to fall short of his admirers' judgment, plucks scraps from his varied reading of different authors and sews them onto his own cheap stuff as if onto sackcloth. Uglier in his ragged clothing than if he were naked, and mute without his thieving study, he struts about cloaked in eloquence. Here you may see another, out of the filth of his stinking haunts and darkness, breathing out the sewer of his belly and the bilge of his mouth, and between belches twittering some petty jibes, while he is praised in parasitic fashion by another who has squandered his money on assorted gluttonies. Amid such rubbish as this, could you safely say anything sober? On the contrary, you will run a great risk from the sluggish crowd. How so? Because nothing is more unjust than an ignorant man. Yet I do not fear these people and their like, and if there is any room now for a warning, I warn and declare beforehand: whoever these are, and whoever the others are who mutter slanders against great men or ravings about the highest matters with their drinking companions, let them either speak openly or keep silent. For truly I will drag them out and pull them forth, even by name, from the hiding places of the little darknesses where they have lurked till now. And let it be known in advance that I shall not have to keep silent about the deeds of those whose names I will not keep silent. Still, let them do as they please and spurn wholesome warnings, though certainly not with impunity; I for my part would rather be rejected by them along with Eucherius than be condemned by the truth along with them. But now is the place and time, as we passed from the philosophers to the commentators, to pass by consistent reasoning from the commentators to the authoritative Scriptures, leaving most of the witnesses unmentioned, as moderation advises.
X. HE CALLS DIVINE WISDOM HERSELF AS WITNESS: TESTIMONIES FROM THE SCRIPTURES.

Let us hear, then, what divine Wisdom declares to the enemies of her image: "The ungodly," she says, "reasoning wrongly, said: Short and wearisome is the time of our life; when it is extinguished our body will be ashes, and our spirit will be dispersed like soft air." The ungodly said this, and of them the same Scripture says a little later: "For their malice blinded them, since God created man indestructible and made him in the image of his own likeness." Here, I believe, you will be stirred more sharply to defend yourself and, as the merits of your case require, will address me in words roughly like these: "Why do you use testimonies scraped together from anywhere at all, which still do not strike at the integrity of our conscience with the truth? What does it matter to me, what concern is it of mine, that the ungodly are punished by God for detracting from the dignity of the divine image, when I know that I am not caught in the snares of this impiety? So I warn you to be off, and not to brand me falsely with the infamy of such an opinion." Now, unless you refuse, I will go back with you to your own words, and from them you can judge whether this oracle of the prophetic word is aimed at the ungodly or at you: whether it does not rather strike you, you yourself, who on the pretext of the privilege of knowledge are devoted to your opinion at the cost of your reputation and anxious for your reputation at the cost of your opinion, and so here reject as someone else's the very things that there you defend as your own.

Yet so that there may be no room either for me to interpret wrongly or perhaps for you to deny, let us now look at both statements on the matter we are discussing. The prophet says that the ungodly say: "When it is extinguished our body will be ashes, and the spirit will be dispersed like soft air." And what do you say? "There are some spiritual natures," you say, "such as angels, archangels and the other powers, and also our soul itself, or certainly this fine air, which nevertheless are by no means to be thought incorporeal." Pay attention, I ask, whoever of us is to judge, and give your verdict whether there is any difference between these statements. The ungodly spoke of the human spirit, that is, of the human soul, saying that the spirit is dispersed like soft air. Our good friend here adds that the human soul and this fine air are alike spiritual but are not on that account incorporeal. Now weigh the same words and their sense. What is called the human spirit there and the soul here agree exactly, just as if both had said "soul" or both had said "spirit"; and as it is said there to be poured out into soft air, so here it is compared to fine air. So to say that the spirit is dispersed like soft air is the same as saying: the spirit is what soft air is. Likewise, to say that our soul is spiritual, and so is this fine air, is as if one said: our soul is what this fine air is. Of these two statements the former is the blasphemy of the ungodly and the latter is your opinion, and they are so united that they cannot be told apart in substance, sense or wording. What, then, follows above all, except that either the opinion of the ungodly is also praiseworthy because it resembles yours, if you think yours worth defending, or, since theirs deserves punishment, yours too is damnable because it is the same?

But why do we go on wandering about in argument any longer, when the prophet has given his verdict on this? "The ungodly," he says, "reasoning wrongly among themselves, said: Short is the time of our life; when it is extinguished our body will be ashes, and our spirit will be dispersed like soft air." And a little later, after some intervening discussion, he adds his judgment: "These things they thought, and they went astray, for their malice blinded them." And as if you were to ask, "What fault, what error is charged in this?" he answers: "They thought the human soul corporeal, and went astray." And as if someone should ask again what truth rules out here, that a person should think the soul a body, the prophet repeats his answer: "They went astray"; that is, they went astray because "God created man indestructible and made him in the image of his own likeness." This amounts to saying: so far is the soul from being a body that it is the divine image. Is there anywhere you can go from here, betrayed by your own testimony, captured by the force of truth, convicted by the prophet's witness? But let each see for himself what he thinks. In my opinion, at any rate, what we have argued so far against the corporealists on behalf of the spiritualists would be quite enough as proof, did I not think it fitting to bring apostolic and even gospel testimonies to bear on the present controversy as well.
XI. HE CALLS THE APOSTLE PAUL AS WITNESS THAT THE SOUL IS NOT IN A PLACE.

So, although in some places, wherever it was useful, I have used testimonies from these Scriptures, it is still right to hack at the scrawny neck of the falsehood-monger with the wholesome cuts of the many-edged sword of truth. Paul, the teacher of the Gentiles, the chosen vessel, says: "Every sin is outside the body, but he who commits fornication sins against his own body." If, apart from the crime of fornication, every sin is outside the body, then it is in the soul. But if it is in the soul and the soul is a body, then not every sin is outside the body. Yet the Apostle says that, apart from fornication, every sin is outside the body. The soul is therefore incorporeal, so that there may be something in which sin can be outside the body. Likewise, writing to the Corinthians, when he was about to pronounce sentence on the man who, defiled by the crime of incest, had violated his stepmother's bed, all but the ravisher of his own mother, he says: "Though absent in body, yet present in spirit, I have already judged the man who did this deed." What is this, Apostle Paul, what is this? How are you absent in body where your spirit is present? If the spirit is a body, why do you not rather say that, being composed of two bodies, you are absent in one and present in the other? Or, if you are one body through and through, why do you not declare that you are absent in one part of your body and present in another? You may well say that you are absent from the Corinthians in body, since you are wholly corporeal in your entirety; but since you are wholly corporeal, and therefore, being absent in body, are wholly absent, I do not know by what part of yourself, where you are not, you claim to be present. Either you convict yourself of lying, or you convince these corporealists that the soul is incorporeal. Is there anything doubtful or obscure here? He who, insofar as he is corporeal, is absent from the Corinthians, is either present by no part of himself or present by something incorporeal. The human spirit, therefore, is incorporeal, and through it the Apostle Paul, though absent with the whole of his corporeal self, could be present to the Corinthians. Such things and countless others like them we could bring forward from almost the whole body of the authoritative books.
XII. ON THE APOSTLE'S STATEMENT THAT HE WAS CAUGHT UP AS FAR AS THE THIRD HEAVEN.

For the sound teaching of the catholic faith climbs, as if by an intermediate step, from the lowest things to the middle and from the middle to the highest. By settled judgment it places bodily creation beneath incorporeal creation, and places this same incorporeal creation, together with what lies beneath it, under the supreme incorporeal Creator. In this way it carries up into the third heaven the followers of Paul: those who with a penetrating mind have passed through the solid mass of the sensible world; who, steadying their straining gaze at the very lowest edge of heaven's outer surface, have with renewed strength crossed all created incorporeal being, with a stronger effort befitting the dignity of a more excellent substance; and who here, their strength restored a little by a pause for breath, have come to rest in the supreme knowledge of the incorporeal Creator. At this point, then, I should like to ask these advocates of the body carefully what their view is of this statement of the Apostle. Since the Apostle says that he was caught up as far as the third heaven, I ask first whether he was caught up in a local or a non-local way; then which these three heavens are, or whether there are more than these; and whether all of them are bodily, or some are incorporeal. Since the course of the argument has brought us this far, let us consult the truth and see what we ought to follow from here.

First, let us examine a little more carefully the question of the number of the heavens, which is by no means easy. We read, of course: “Praise the Lord, you heavens of heavens.” But this may be understood of many heavens or of two. Since no number is stated, it seems possible to take it either as many heavens of many heavens or as two heavens of two heavens. Consider: from the regions touching the earth up to the air lies the element of water. Then comes the depth of the air, as far as the nearest light of the moon. From there stretch the expanses of the ethereal fires, out to the outermost bounds where the world borders on what lies beyond it, where the world is enclosed in the globe of a sphere. Now that we have gone through the whole universe of bodies, where are we to look for a heaven beyond everything in the world? But in this dark cloud, where everything is murky, let us seek counsel again from the inner sanctuary of the teachings that come from above the heavens. “In the beginning,” says the beginning of Genesis, “God created heaven and earth.” If we set opinions aside and seek assurance of the truth, here you have as witness concerning created things the very author of creation. Before all time he created heaven and earth. After that, on one day, he made light, and likewise on the second day he established the firmament and called it “heaven,” using the name loosely. Beneath it he then set the adornment of the stars, which vary in place or manner within fixed limits of their intervals. It is easy to see from this that this visible firmament falls short of the invisible heaven by as great a distance in substance as that by which it rises above the lowest parts of the earth in distance of place. Therefore this firmament can be called “heaven” only by a borrowed and transferred name, since being truly heaven belongs properly to that heaven created before time. Indeed, what we call the starry heaven is called in the book of Genesis “the firmament of heaven,” where it recounts the creation of the lights: “God made,” it says, “two great lights and set them in the firmament of heaven.” On this authority we are allowed to believe that the one heaven that existed before time is the true heaven. Yet we are not forbidden to call the firmament we are discussing “heaven,” since God called the firmament heaven.

But it troubles us again that in the authoritative books the heavens are often named not only in the dual but in the plural. The reply is that the earth, which is a single body, is said in the scriptures to be “the circle of the lands.” Perhaps, then, the heavens are spoken of as many when they are two, just as the earth is spoken of as lands when it is one. To which third heaven, then, was Paul caught up? Come now, please, go out, shake apart the masses of the elements, place the weights of bodies on the scales of judgment and weigh the world: perhaps some heavens will spring out at us from somewhere. Or if the one world does not have more heavens, let the tiny atoms give birth to some worlds for you, as they did for Epicurus, so that Paul may find a third heaven. But what does it contribute to blessedness for anyone to rise from one bodily heaven to another, or from that to a third that is equally bodily, since what is higher in place is not for that reason more blessed in merit? Otherwise human beings would have to give way to little birds, and each of us would reach eternity not by progress but by footsteps.

Local superiority, then, does not make anyone blessed, and a soul that thinks in bodily terms does not find three heavens either, so that at last, failing among bodies, it must give way to incorporeal things. Let us therefore consider the threefold number of the heavens and how they differ, following the reasoning we have already touched on in silent examination. For these people, difference in rank is distance in place. So if the first and second heavens are separated by distance rather than by difference, I ask: what is there between them? Either there is some substance there, or there is nothing. If there is nothing, then no cause will underlie the creation of that heaven, since not even in the lowest parts of the earth has anything come into being except from causes that preceded it in eternity. But if there is some multitude of living beings there, superior to those on earth, then this “supercelestial” substance lies beneath a heaven. From what is above it, it draws the flames of more brilliant stars and the clearer breezes of an air whose element fills the hollow of the empty space between the heavens. That space would in turn be separated from the third heaven by other peoples of living beings and other depths of intervening air.

Now if the Apostle was swept through all this and came as far as the third heaven, what did he find there in particular that could not have been found in the first heaven, if it was something to be sought by place? Yet he himself says that he was caught up as far as the third heaven and heard something divine which a human being is not permitted to speak. Is it really so, Apostle, that God is sought by way of places, or that truth is found only in a place? If that is so, then God too will be local, and you will lose locally the God whom you find locally. If he is only in the third heaven, then he was left behind there, where you found him. But since you are blessed not by a bodily heaven but by the Lord of heaven, and the Lord of heaven is wholly everywhere and is neither sought nor found locally, the true reason for your ascent will surely be that you rise from the heaven of a lower substance to the heaven of a higher substance. For those who seek God there is no ascent from bodily things to bodily things. Where, then, will cornered corporealism flee now? See: it is true that Paul was caught up as far as the third heaven, and again it is not true that there are three bodily heavens. Either, then, you will admit that something created is incorporeal, or you will deny that there are three heavens. But since unquestionable authority teaches, and manifest reason proves, both that there are three heavens and that not all of them are bodily, let us now seek what is true with the help of the one truth, just as we have examined what is false.

We read in the prophet: “He who made heaven and earth. The heaven of heaven is the Lord's, but the earth he has given to the children of men.” Here we must notice that heaven is one thing and the heaven of heaven another. When we say “the heaven of heaven,” it is as if we said “heaven and earth.” This earth is the lowest part of the starry heaven. But God created heaven and earth before anything in time, and made this visible heaven on the second day. This heaven, then, is later in age than the earth, although it is so far superior in quality. The instantaneous creation of the world does not admit successions and spans of time or lengths of days, and this is no time to discuss the six days as a number rather than a span. So understand this: the prophet set as great a difference between heaven and the heaven of heaven as there is, roughly, between this heaven and the earth. Just as this earth is the earth of this heaven, so this heaven is in turn the earth of that heaven. From this we must conclude that the whole body of the world is called “earth” by God, and that what has been given to the Lord is called by its proper name, “heaven.” For Scripture speaks thus: “The heaven of heaven is the Lord's, but the earth he has given to the children of men.”

What, then, shall we say? Has this visible heaven not been given to human beings? Think of the brightness and heat of the sun, the changes of the moon's globe as it waxes and wanes, the wandering yet regular circuits of the stars, the conjunctions of the stars through their great orbits and their fixed progress. They vary the alternation of days and nights. They temper the world with alternating warmth and cold. They mark the divisions of time within measured bounds, and along the same unending track of their lines, by the same circular paths, they bring back things that return endlessly to the same point. They paint the ether with choirs arranged in harmonious order and with musical intervals. Are not all these things either useful to the race of mortals or delightful to look at? For this reason the heaven, insofar as it is bodily, is called “earth,” because it has been given to human beings. In the same way the bodies of water and air, though certainly not as dense as earth, are still called “earth” because they have been given to the children of men. We may add that for all beings that live by the senses, touch comes chiefly from earth. Moreover, just as nothing can be seen without fire, so nothing can be touched without earth. Since fire too can be touched, and the ether is fire, it is not unreasonable that there should be something earthy there as well. The name “earth,” then, includes everything bodily, and by sound judgment everything composite among bodily things. So everything bodily is called earth, because this sensible world, together with the visible heaven, is the earth that has been given to the children of men.

What shall we say of that heaven which has been given to the Lord, not to the children of men? Let us return once more to the divine oracles. The same psalmist says: “Give thanks to the Lord, who made the heavens in understanding.” If, then, the heavens that God inhabits are in understanding, and the heaven given to the Lord, to which everything bodily is earth, can only be incorporeal, it is perfectly clear that everything that understands is not bodily. Now the human mind understands by its very substance. The human mind is therefore incorporeal. There you have the earth: all bodily creation. There you have the heaven: incorporeal, intellectual substance. Now, then, so that you may be caught up through two heavens into the third heaven, with Paul leading the way, pass beyond everything bodily by what is incorporeal in you. Then, with a much keener effort and a swifter flight, rise above what is incorporeal but created, and therefore changeable. And from there, in the third heaven, rest in the most blessed contemplation of the unchangeable Incorporeal itself. Know yourself, human soul, to be incorporeal. By the excellence of your nature, you stand as a mediating substance between the lowest and the highest, so it is both easy and fitting for you either to look down on the body, the lowest thing, below you, or to look up to God, the highest, above you.

Now I ask whether you can offer us any other account of the threefold number and diversity of the heavens. I would gladly have one, but it is clear that no one can give one unless the nature of incorporeal substance stands between body and God. For if apart from God there is nothing but body, then there are not three heavens but two: all body would be one heaven, so to speak, and the Creator of body the other. But Paul was caught up not beyond the third heaven but into it. So all bodily creation and all incorporeal creation must be passed through, like two heavens. To the Creator, however, as into the third heaven, we must come not to pass beyond, which is impossible, nor to return, which we ought not to do, but to stand and remain. This running and this standing are progress and perfection, and these belong to virtues, not to places; for whoever progresses is running, and whoever is perfected has arrived.

We have now crossed the vast fields of a very broad question by quite a short path, and have given, I think, some indications that separate the byways of error from the straight path of truth. Now I ask what the Apostle means when he says that he was caught up “whether in the body or out of the body.” For he says: “I know a man who was caught up—whether in the body or out of the body I do not know,” and the rest, about which we have said what was relevant. First, let us examine what the blessed Apostle here treats as certain and what he admits is uncertain. He knows that a man was caught up; whether in the body or out of the body, he does not know. Notice at once that “man” is spoken of here as one thing and “body” as another. See, then, [?] a distinction has been drawn between what the Apostle says he does not know and what he says he knows. Let us therefore examine whether he is as ignorant of whether he consists of the incorporeal, the bodily, or both, as he is ignorant of whether he was caught up with the body or without it. “I know,” he says, “a man who was caught up, but whether in the body or out of the body I do not know.” Here we may notice that the one who was caught up, and knows that he was caught up, nevertheless perceives that he himself is not his body. So he is unsure whether he was caught up with it or without it, yet he does not doubt that he himself was caught up. With this, all obscurity is cleared away. The one who is uncertain whether he was caught up with the body or without it is nevertheless certain that he is incorporeal and has a body. For if he was not caught up without the body, then the body too was caught up with him, and yet he himself is not the body with which he was caught up. If he was caught up without the body, it is understood all the more that what can exist without the body is not body. “I know,” he says, “a man who was caught up, but whether in the body or out of the body I do not know.” This is as if he said: “I know that I was caught up, but whether with the body or without it I do not know.” So even if you were caught up with the body, you could still have been caught up without the body. You are therefore incorporeal even in the body, if you could have been caught up without the body. For the incorporeal is joined to the body, with its own substance unimpaired, in order to give the body life; but the established law of things does not allow a body to exist without a body.
13. HE CALLS ON GOD FROM THE GOSPEL AS WITNESS TO THE INCORPOREALITY OF THE SOUL.

But now, through my witnesses, the heralds of truth, Truth itself will testify to establish an undoubted faith. The Lord says in the Gospel: “Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul.” Why, I ask you, can someone who can kill the body not kill the soul, unless it is because the soul is not a body? But you say: “It is indeed a body, but a finer one; it is indeed a body, but a lighter one.” My reply is this: granted that it is finer and lighter, yet if it is a body, it can be killed by the one who can kill the body. We are dealing, of course, with these two things, soul and body, which make up the visible human being. The one who said “Do not fear those” did not say “who kill the denser body, the heavier body,” but “who kill the body.” Nor again did he say “the finer and lighter body,” but “cannot kill the soul.” Under this name “body” he certainly included the living body, since only what is alive can be killed. So if the soul is a living body, it can be killed by the one who can kill the body. But the Truth says: “Those who kill the body cannot kill the soul.” The soul, therefore, is not a body, since it cannot be killed by those who can kill the body. But since the reader's attention must be relieved of the burden of continuous reading, let this be the end of this book.
CLAUDIANUS MAMERTUS, ON THE STATE OF THE SOUL: BOOK THREE.
1. ON THE BODY OF LAZARUS: HOW IT LAY LIFELESS IN A PLACE, WHILE THE SOUL DEPARTED FROM THE BODY NON-LOCALLY.

I have now produced guarantors of the truth sufficient, I think, both in authority and in number. It remains to examine what has not yet been discussed in the little work of this advocate of the body. He rashly decides that the soul is contained by the body, and for this purpose he takes an example from the authority of the Gospel and argues as if conclusively. He says that the body of Lazarus, when it was dead, was without life, and that the same body, restored to life, was with life. By this he wants us to believe that the soul is local, since it withdrew from the body and came back to the body again.
2. IN WHAT RESPECT THE SOUL BEARS THE LIKENESS OF GOD.

And to lay down a rule for the whole race of souls in common, he declares that the very soul of our Redeemer is local. He does so by a formidable and, as he supposes, insoluble syllogism: that the soul is where it is and is not where it is not. He argues as though we said that it was either everywhere or nowhere, when in fact, if it were everywhere, it would be God, and if it were nowhere, it would be nothing. The soul is indeed not whole in the whole world. But just as God is wholly everywhere in the universe, so the soul is found wholly everywhere in the body. God by no means fills a smaller part of the world with a smaller part of himself and a larger part with a larger, but is whole in the part and whole in the whole. In the same way, the soul is not in a part of the body by a part of itself. One part of the soul does not give sensation to the eye while another gives life to the finger. Rather, just as it lives wholly in the eye and sees wholly through the eye, so too it lives wholly in the finger and feels wholly through the finger. Or if perhaps it feels wholly in the finger in such a way that it is not wholly in the finger, then it feels wholly where it is not wholly, and it is where it is not. Either, then, the soul is whole in the smallest part of the body while still being whole in the whole, or, since it feels wholly where it is not wholly, it is wholly where it is not wholly. But I have discussed this at length in the first book and set out a good deal on it at the beginning of the second. Anyone who studies those passages carefully will come to this point well prepared. For it is extremely difficult to contemplate incorporeal things. The deceptive sight of the bodily senses so clouds the eye of the mind, weakened by sin, that when the mind wishes to contemplate either itself or God, it sees only the veil of bodily images drawn before it, since it cannot see beyond it. Whoever, then, is put off by the difficulty of this [?], let him apply study and effort, not in order to go off and slander me, but so that he may be able to be cleansed.

Yet I have not so forgotten myself as not to feel that there is more sickness than health in me. Still, I am glad that I left behind with my boyhood years this opinion by which the soul is believed to be a body, because at that time, when I held opinions, I certainly did not know. To hold an opinion belongs to someone who does not know, and ignorance is the contrary of knowledge; so whoever holds an opinion does not know. That is how it came about that I desired knowledge in preference to opinion, knowing that I did not know as long as I was holding opinions. But you, when we inquire into the substance of the soul, say that what is above us cannot be seen by us, since we are not above ourselves. And at the same time you treat as known what you deny can be known, and you assert that the soul of the body is a body. If you say this knowingly, then, since false things cannot be known, you are telling the truth; and if you are telling the truth in this, you are lying when you say that the substance of the soul cannot be known. Either, then, it is false that the soul is a body, or it is false that the substance of the soul cannot be known. Do you see where opinion leads its followers? No one holds opinions except someone who does not know, and ignorance is opposed to knowledge. So you, who want to deliver a certain verdict out of the uncertainty of opinion and to pronounce as one who knows on things you do not know, stand convicted of teaching what you do not know. You are teaching, then, not-knowing; and while you say that something cannot be known, you presume to teach it. Forgive us, we beg you, if we refuse to learn ignorance.
3. THAT THE BODY DOES NOT CONTAIN THE SOUL LOCALLY, BUT THE SOUL CONTAINS THE BODY NON-LOCALLY; AND THAT EVERYTHING THAT EXISTS EITHER IS IN ITSELF, OR IS A SUBJECT, OR IS IN A SUBJECT.

So you say that the soul is contained by the body. Surely that saying of the apostle ought to have come to your mind: "Though our outer man is wasting away, yet the inner is being renewed"? Everything that exists, to put it briefly, is either in itself, or a subject, or in a subject. God is in himself. Among bodily things the body is a subject, and the colour of the body is in a subject. Among incorporeal things it is the mind and learning, which are so bound together that a body is never without colour and a rational mind is never without learning. Now you, who believe that the soul is a body and that it is set upon the body as its subject and contained in it, must consider whether we can prove that what is in a subject remains when the subject itself perishes. For if the soul is contained by the body, it is set upon the body as its subject, and what is contained cannot remain when that which contains it perishes. But the apostle says that as the body grows old the soul is renewed, and as the body is corrupted the soul is made firm. Therefore it is not contained by the body.

I fear that here too you may seem to have formed your opinion as a new Academic: one who knows nothing, as the Academics claim to know nothing, and yet defines without hesitation things he does not know. Consider whether it is not the body that contains the soul but the soul that contains the body. For when the body is corrupted the soul is made firm, just as the body in turn is dissolved when it loses the soul. The soul lives better without the body; the body without the soul does not live, not even a worse life. And so that the question which of these two, of which human substance is made, is in which may not only be settled by argument but also be made plain by authority, let us bring forward a prophetic testimony too. For it says: "The body, which is corrupted, weighs down the soul." We must first consider whether what weighs down is that which is in something, or that in which something is. If it is that in which something is, then a thing is lightened by the very weight with which it is loaded. But if what weighs down is that which is in something, not that in which something is, then the body, which weighs down the soul, is in the soul rather than the soul, which is weighed down by the body, being in the body. The load, of course, is on the bearer, not the bearer in the load. Since this is so, it is the clearest sign that the soul bears a great likeness to its author that, by way of likeness, just as the world is in God non-spatially, so the body is in the soul non-spatially.

Now I ask you to answer my question: if the soul is spatially within the body, how does it contain the body? It is well known that nothing bodily can be contained by a body unless the container is outside and the contained inside. But how can the soul, which you yourself affirm is corporeal, be both inside the body to give it life and outside the body to contain it? Or perhaps it contains the body from outside in such a way that it is not outside? Then we are brought back again to the same difficulty: either the soul is outside the body non-spatially so as to contain the body, or, if it contains where it is not, it is where it is not. But perhaps this reasoning troubles you because it is new. Wake up a little and, if you can, look closely; if you cannot, marvel at the power of the incorporeal: it moves the body while itself standing still, it reaches any places without passing through places, and it acts in those same places non-spatially. If you can discern this, you will not set the soul of Lazarus against us as though it were some kind of body, with a spatial movement of departure and return. Rather, you will recognize that it quickened his body by an incorporeal motion, departed from it non-spatially, and returned to it non-spatially.

Now if the truth of this vision has become clear to you without any cloud, you will not be tossed about by any difficulty over how the soul, once the body has been laid aside, can be in the world non-spatially. It will be non-spatially in any part of the world, just as it was non-spatially in the body. But you, to the prejudice of the whole kind of souls, declare that even the soul of Christ is spatial and corporeal, and you say that the soul of the Redeemer is a body, when not even the soul of a beast is one.
4. That just as the body, though spatial, is in the soul non-spatially, so the world, though spatial, is in God non-spatially.

But perhaps you will object: how can the soul be in a place and yet not be spatial? And I in turn ask you: how can the corporeal world be spatial and yet not be in a place? If you answer that the world is in a place, I ask no less keenly whether the place in which the world is lies outside the world or belongs to the world. If it belongs to the world, the world is not in it; rather, that place is itself, together with the world, in another place. If it is outside the world, I ask again whether the place in which the world is is itself in a place. So either you will admit infinite places, that is, infinite bodies, and thus make a body equal to God, who alone is infinite, or you will grant that the world is not in a place. Turn this reasoning over in your mind, then. Just as you see that so vast an extent of places and spaces is not in a place, so understand that what has no bulk and no extension can be in a place without a place. For if what is spatial is not in a place, much less is what is not spatial in a place.
5. That just as the soul departs from the body non-spatially so that the body dies, so the divinity of Christ departed non-spatially so that Christ, the Son of God, died on the cross.

But whether you understand this point, however clear it is, I might well doubt. What I cannot wonder at enough is that something which follows so simply that recognizing it is, I will not say easy, but hardly avoidable, should have slipped past you like this. You say that Christ's body was alive when it was raised up on the gibbet, but lifeless when it was committed to the tomb. And because of this, which is not to be denied, by the sharpness of your argument the soul will be spatial, because it gave life to Christ's body at one time and not at another. Under the compulsion of this view, then, we shall with profane daring believe that God too is spatial, since he was in Christ when he was crucified and also forsook him in his passion. The Lord himself cried from the cross: "My God, why have you forsaken me?" For if he did not depart, he did not forsake; if he forsook, he certainly departed. Charge God with spatiality now, then! Plainly the next step is that from insulting the likeness of God you are carried on to God himself, and you who defame the image attack its author. So just as non-spatiality is not taken from God because he forsook the man Christ by departing, so the soul does not lose the privilege of non-spatiality when it departs from the dying body.
6. That Mary [?] did not see the angel Gabriel in the substance by which he is spirit, but by means of a visible body which he temporarily took from the air.

Here now, a proud orator, you launch into the condition of the angels and choose Gabriel as a sort of warm-up for your tongue, declaiming thus: "The most blessed Gabriel himself, who testifies that he stands before God, when he announced that the Lord of the heavens was to be poured into Mary's womb, and when he stood before the eyes of the Lord's mother, was without doubt absent from heaven; he did not fly above the seas, he did not fill the empty and widespread reaches of the vast air, but occupied only the place in which he was present." Setting aside the discussion of this view for a little, I confess I am astonished at such a clash of contradictory statements. Now you call the air subtle, now vast; now, with a kind of poetic licence, you call empty the great space of the world, which the element of air fills in its proportion. And you do not understand that there can be no void at all, because where something is, there is not nothing. But air is not nothing; therefore where there is air, there is no void. Nor can that be rightly called a void which is nothing, because what is nothing cannot receive anything. Hence what is capable of holding nothing is not a void. And what is the point of preferring, as the poets do, to call the Lord's mother "genitrix", and of weaving poetic oratory without verse? I, however, ask not how you speak but what you say, and I beg you to answer.

When the most blessed Gabriel stood before the eyes of the Lord's mother, did Mary see in Gabriel that by which Gabriel sees God? For if that was visible to Mary, then the non-spatial can be beheld by the spatial. But if it can, it is not non-spatial. For if anyone is spatial, he sees spatially, and in looking he can take in only a part. So he who sees spatially sees a place, since a part is a place, and a place is certainly a part of places, and places are bodies. And he who sees a part sees with a part of himself, and only a part can be seen by a part. But God has no part, for what is indivisible has no part. Either, then, Gabriel does not see God, or he sees him whole; and what is whole can be seen only by what is whole. But a body can neither be seen whole nor see anything whole. So that by which Gabriel sees God is not a body, because that by which Gabriel saw Mary spatially, and by which Mary saw him spatially, cannot see non-spatially. But to meet you on your own terms: if the whole of Gabriel is nothing but body, then, because of the distinction of parts, the foot is not the whole, nor the mouth, nor the eye. Therefore, when he appeared to Mary, he did not speak with his foot, or see with his mouth, or stand on his eye; each part of his members performed the function proper to its nature. So just as he stood spatially and spoke spatially, so too he saw spatially.

Now, to bring the question to an end, I ask whether the angel Gabriel, being, as you claim, body alone and bodily occupied in looking at Mary, with one and the same sight and at one and the same time saw the non-spatial God non-spatially while he saw the spatial Mary spatially.
