Since this cannot happen, because of the difference between the corporeal and the incorporeal, it remains either that Gabriel never saw Mary or that he ceased to see God. But against this falsehood stands the sentence of the Truth, in which it is said: "For their angels always see the face of my Father." If they always see, there is no time when they do not see. But if, when Gabriel saw Mary, he ceased to see God, then the angels do not always see God. So either Gabriel ceased to see God when he saw Mary, or what the Truth said will not be true. Therefore it is concluded by reasoning that, as is plain, cannot be undone: since the angel could not see God with a spatial sight that was fixed on beholding Mary, and yet we may not deny that God was seen by Gabriel even then (lest the angelic nature, now in unchangeable blessedness, should fall as the devil fell into the misery of ever not seeing God), there must be in him both a corporeal and an incorporeal substance: one by which he may be seen by a body or see bodily, the other by which he incorporeally beholds the incorporeal without end.
7. How far unformed matter differs from nothing, and how far matter already formed differs from the unformed.

Come now, with the sharpness of your excellent intellect and your knowledge of causes and things, investigate, distinguish, and declare: how unformed matter differs from nothing; what is inanimate and yet formed; what is both formed and animate; what place and time are; how spatial motion is also subject to temporal motion, while purely temporal motion is not also subject to spatial motion; what stable motion is, and what eternity is; what it is to be nowhere and to be nowhere absent; what it is never to be and never not to be. And among all these, which between them embrace every substance, seek out the hidden ground of reason and choose something that you would decide the angels are. Certainly they are not nothing, for whatever is something is not nothing. They are not unformed matter, for unformed matter lies between something and nothing. See, we have scarcely moved away from nothing.

Now let us deal with the formed inanimate, which is what you would have the angels consist of. Notice now that just as unformed matter, which can be formed, is superior to nothing, so what is already formed is better than what can be formed but is not formed. Likewise, just as what is formed surpasses what is not formed, so any formed inanimate thing ranks below what is both formed and animate; for as the formed comes near to form, so the animate comes near to life. And just as there are three things, unformed matter, the formed lifeless thing, and the form of things, so likewise there are three: the quickened, the quickening, and life. The life of bodies is one thing, the life of lives another. The body is living, the soul is alive, God is life; so that the soul, which is alive in itself, is life to the body, and thus the body does not live without the soul, just as the soul does not live without God. Understand now that to grant the holy angels only bodies is to deny them life. And so, since every animate thing consists of a twofold substance, and you hold that the angels are only body, a little worm is better than an angel; for although the angel has the form of a body, he does not have even the life a worm has. Moreover, no body is its own life, for the body is one thing and the life of the body another. Either, then, there is a quickening spirit in the angel, or the angel is inferior to every living thing; or else, since he surpasses every created living thing, his life is not just any life but a most blessed one.
8. That angels, good or evil, are spirits, not bodies; that an angel does not see God through a body; and that a corporeal man does not see an angel unless the angel has taken on a visible body.

In Gabriel, therefore, there is both something incorporeal by which he sees God unchangeably, and a body which Mary could see or through which Mary could be seen; and this body, subject to the spirit, carried out spatially what the spirit had known non-spatially, in the Truth itself, was to be carried out. It is clear enough, I think, that the blessed angels are of both substances: incorporeal in that part of themselves to which God is visible, and corporeal in that part by which they themselves are visible to men. For neither can God be seen by an angel through a body, nor can an angel be seen by a man without a body. This being so, it cannot be denied that the devil too, made of the incorporeal and the corporeal, since he was created together with the holy angels, is of a twofold substance. After he swelled with the dropsy of pride and wasted away with the fever of envy, he fell of his own will, non-spatially, from holiness, and was cast down, against his will and spatially, from heaven. Since he ceased to be not an angel but good, he lost his innocence, not his nature. Hence, just as the host of angels that stood firm is blessed in both parts of itself, so the host that fell away will be punished in both. You will by no means be right, then, to deny two substances in the devil; for even if I am set aside, you will certainly be compelled to give way to yourself, to hiss one part of your arguments off the stage with another, and to demolish the false with the true. The devil, then, though himself incorporeal, has his own body, because he will not be able to feel bodily torments without a body. And again, that which feels is one thing, and that through which it feels is another. Indeed, if you pay attention, you will be taught the truth by your own statement. For you said: "If the devil drew his body from this condensed air, then he will carry a borrowed body to his torments", as though I had ever said that anywhere. But I do not deny that I am in your debt, since by this argument you have unwillingly handed us the victory. For when you say that the devil will not carry a borrowed body to his torments, you are clearly admitting that he will carry his own. It does not matter to me whether he has his own body or someone else's; what matters to me is whether he has a body. You, however, not only admit but even argue that the devil not only has a body but has one of his own. For this is your statement: "If the devil drew his body from this condensed air, then he will carry a borrowed body to his torments." Certainly the one who carries is something, and what is carried is something. And when it is said, "he carries his own", the one who carries is meant to be one thing and what he carries another. The devil, therefore, consists of a twofold and diverse substance, because when he carries his body, he is not himself what he carries. For the load is one thing and the bearer another. So you will struggle against us no longer, if you believe yourself, since the body and the one who has the body are two in substance, and these two are different; and for them to be different, one will be incorporeal and the other corporeal. The devil, therefore, consisting of a twofold and diverse substance, is both corporeal and incorporeal.
9. That it must be understood spiritually, not bodily, when Lazarus in Abraham's bosom and the rich man in hell spoke to each other with a chasm set between them.

But if we have given some account of these matters, at least in part, let us now examine, in discussing your own chapter, that chasm which, as you argue, is set between guilty and innocent souls and separates their deserts by places. For this is how you argue: "If souls are not spatial, how does that empty chasm, by its grim interposition, separate sinners from the company and fellowship of the righteous, so that they can neither go from here to there nor cross from there to here?" You have set down this example from the Gospel reading, stripped of the simplicity of the Lord's words, in order, of course, to establish that souls are spatial. But the divine oracle, brought forward unadulterated and in its true form, will make it quite plain what your words have altered, corrupted, and concealed there. The Lord says in the Gospel: "The poor man died and was carried by the angels into Abraham's bosom. The rich man also died and was buried in hell. And being in torment, he saw Abraham far off and Lazarus in his bosom, and said: 'Father Abraham, send Lazarus to dip the tip of his finger in water and cool my tongue, for I am tormented in this flame.' And Abraham answered: 'Remember, son, that you received good things in your life, and Lazarus likewise evil things; and so now he is comforted here, and you are tormented. And besides all this, between us and you a great chasm has been fixed, so that no one can go from here to you, nor cross from there to here.'" Now explain this to me in terms of places and times or bodies. Here, without the to-and-fro of breathed air, without the organ of the chest, the pipe of the throat, the hollow of the mouth and the plectrum of the tongue, produce words with sounds through a soul that is, as you claim, in some way corporeal. Here show me the hand of the soul, the tip of whose finger Lazarus is to dip in water to cool the tongue of the burning rich man. Here teach me something bodily about that supposedly corporeal bosom of Abraham, such that it is narrow in proportion to a human body and yet can hold many; and about that chasm, which is either so small that those it separates can exchange words, or so immense that it cannot be crossed. But this above all I ask: how could that rich man, who burns in the fires of Gehenna among the dead below, have conversed with Abraham if he did not come to the places of blessedness? And how does Abraham converse with the rich man, if he did not go down to hell? For you say, and the view is not at all improbable, that the souls of the saints dwell in the innermost seats of paradise. Hence, since Abraham in paradise and the rich man in hell are separated from each other by some immense and impassable gulf, and yet, as though nothing lay between them, they not only see each other but also converse, then if these things are to be reckoned spatially, you will be forced to admit one of two things: either that Abraham and the rich man neither spoke with each other nor saw each other, or that hell is in paradise or paradise in hell.
10. How this question can be understood spiritually.

But since divine authority cannot be stubbornly resisted, and blessedness cannot be mingled with the wretched, and since we cannot look into the intricacy of this saying with an eye bleared by bodily imaginings, let us set aside places and bodies for a little and consider it. Where an immense space is said to lie between persons separated by judgment, and yet in such a way that they can still exchange speech, let us take note that what is meant is not a distance of places but a difference of merits. For as far as the body is concerned, an unrighteous man can be spatially with a righteous one; but an unrighteous man cannot be in the innocence of the righteous so long as he is unrighteous. Hence, since after death no one can either repent or sin, the unchangeable state between the saved and the lost is called an impassable chasm. Your own speech, then, is turned against you. You see that the testimony which you thought was parting company with us is, as the argument proceeds, uniting with us, and is shutting its door in your face, closing its very narrow paths that lead to the infinite expanses of non-spatial regions. For the narrowness of bodily extent, being unable to hold the immensities of incorporeal subtleties, cannot comprehend distance without place, a word without sound, or a bosom without space. Moreover, whatever things exist in this way are not corporeal. But the souls of Abraham, Lazarus and the rich man exist in this way; therefore they are not corporeal. As for the arguments of a similar kind that follow from here on, those of vigorous judgment ought to find them less laborious to refute. For a sensible judge rightly counts as beaten one who in his weakness is no better than the beaten. So it is not without shame that I am astonished at what you add to prove the corporeality of the soul: "See, if the soul thinks of Alexandria or Jerusalem, and if by thought it was present there with its whole presence, let it tell us the lie of the places, the faces of the people, the movements and doings of the crowds." Is the author of this view not ashamed to take as a sign of the soul's corporeality what ought to have been seen as an argument for its incorporeality?

11. That the sight of the soul is understanding; that just as it sees bodily things through the body, so it sees spiritual things through itself; and that if it saw bodies through itself, it would more easily have seen its own inner organs.

So far I have discussed the mind's incorporeal and non-local sight, and it has been made quite clear that the mind beholds eternal and unchangeable things directly, with no substance in between. The rational soul, then, sees incorporeal and non-local things by itself, and by incorporeal sight it sets the truth, which is God, far apart from falsehood; yet it does not see local and bodily things except through the body. What reason is there, then, to believe it like the things it can see only with the body as its interpreter, and to judge it unlike the things it contemplates by itself? The sight of the soul, as has often been said and I do not mind repeating, is understanding. Bodily things cannot be understood, but the soul can perceive them through the body. And since the soul perceives through the body but understands by itself, the substance of what is perceived and of what is understood is very different. So it follows that the soul, because it is not a body, cannot perceive anything bodily except through the body, but can see by itself the things that are to be understood. Will you, against all reason, have bodily things understood and incorporeal things seen? But in case it should seem to you that the human mind, which you believe to be bodily, can see nothing at all, or only bodily things, or perhaps only incorporeal things by itself, as is proper to its nature, let us air the obscurities of this threefold question as briefly as we can. First, then, let us see whether or not the human mind sees by itself. And since nearly the whole of this business turns on this point, I ask for a reader who is both alert and wakeful. The mind's sight through the body is common to human beings and beasts. It stretches itself out and goes forth through these points, the pupils: the front ventricle of the brain is heated by the invisible flames of the inner organs, and the sight streams out further and further into rays. If it meets any colour or shape, it takes it in, and by the swift passages of its lines it brings it back on the return course as on the outward one. This, then, is what is called sight, as we explained in the first book. Through this sight the human mind, like the beast, tells known things from unknown and white from black [?]. Is this the limit of the human mind's sight? How then does it judge just things from unjust and true from false? Or are we perhaps to believe that fools with bodily eyes surpass the blind wise in judgment? On the question before us let us call as witnesses Appius from the Roman senate, Hermophilus from the Greek school, or Tobit from among the prophets. Appius gave the light of counsel to men whose outward eyes were bright but who were inwardly purblind; Hermophilus taught Theopompus geometry without a measuring rod; and Tobit, while he laid open the way of heaven before his son, gave him an angel as his companion. The mind therefore sees without the body. It does not see anything bulky or coloured or spread out in space, but with incorporeal gaze it contemplates truth itself, which is God, supremely incorporeal. It is plain, I think, that the mind sees incorporeal things by itself and bodily things through the body.

For the sake of little men with sluggish livers, it still remains to discuss whether the human mind can see bodily things by itself, without the body. So now give me your whole attention and be as present as you can. According to you, the human mind is itself bodily and shut up inside the enclosure of the outer body. If it can see anything bodily by itself, surely nothing is easier for it to see than the inside of the body in which it is enclosed. Come, I beg you: turn this bodily sight of the mind that you keep talking about upon your own entrails and upon every part of your body, report back about yourself, and tell yourself and us how the threefold brain is joined together, how the mass of the liver lies, how the strip of the spleen is attached, how the balance of the stomach hangs, how the heart's plectrum strikes; what paths the veins take and how they are woven; where the nerves begin and how they are joined; how the bones meet and fit together; what the hollows of the lungs are like; and how the winding coils of the intestines bend and turn back, laid out with their smooth, knotless bindings. Why, then, do you refuse to give me answers on these matters, with me as judge? Why do you refuse? Clearly because the mind does not see bodily things by itself at all. But why can it not see bodily things, when it has already been shown that it is not without sight? No one who lacks bodily sight sees anything bodily. The mind, however, has sight and sees nothing bodily, so it sees incorporeally. To be able to see incorporeally is incorporeal sight; only something incorporeal has incorporeal sight; and the human mind sees incorporeally. Therefore the human mind is incorporeal. So do not be troubled any longer by these trifles, so as to suppose that the mind is not where it thinks because by nature it cannot gaze on the layout of places, the faces of people, or the movements and doings of nations; for these things are bodily. An incorporeal mind cannot see what is contrary to its nature. Yet it is present where it thinks, though it does not perceive the places it thinks of with bodily sight, just as it is present where it gives life, though it does not see the inner parts of its own body to which it gives life. And if it is plain in every way that the mind cannot see bodily things without the body, nor incorporeal things with the body, let us no longer linger as strangers in Alexandria. Let us return from Egypt, cross the sea of errors and the desert of ignorance, and enter the homeland of truth as the land of promise. Let us not be idle or sluggish, nor yet fearful, so that if anything born of the vice of lying vanity should either clamour at our side or throw itself in our path, it may be struck down with Jesus going before us and helping us.
XII. AGAINST THOSE WHO SAY: THE SOUL IS INCORPOREAL TO ITSELF, BUT CORPOREAL TO GOD.

But look: though the chattering nonsense of certain people who destroy souls does not halt our journey, it does slow us down. Yet spending a little time on it is no loss; indeed it is useful, provided that the truth itself either drives away or crushes whatever opposes or departs from the truth. I hear some people say, people who want souls to be bodily and yet cannot deny that they are incorporeal, that souls are one thing to themselves and another to their Creator. "To God," they say, "souls are bodily, but to themselves they are incorporeal." That is as good as saying that souls are both bodily and incorporeal. I call eternity to witness that answering these empty claims is very hard work for me, precisely because there is nothing here to come to grips with, nothing to dig out from the marrow, nothing worth the exercise of a contest, and certainly nothing that would be a victory to have conquered. If, then, the soul is bodily to its Creator and incorporeal to itself, the method of seeking the truth demands that these two things be examined with the utmost care. Either it is truly the case that the soul is incorporeal, if the soul truly knows this about itself; or else it is true that the soul is bodily, if the soul's maker holds this to be so. If they say that both are true—that it is true that the soul is incorporeal, because it knows this in truth, and also true that the soul is bodily, because the soul's Creator knows it—then they are maintaining that two things wholly contrary to each other are both true, when nothing is contrary to the true except the false. A brilliant and splendid argument indeed, which spurns the one and only truth and finds itself two truths! Still, to hold them by the bonds of their own profession: by their own admission the human mind is incorporeal as far as man is concerned.

Since, then, we agree on this part of the question, it remains for them to show how an incorporeal substance is bodily to the one who created it incorporeal. I do not first ask whether this is so or not; for the present I grant that it is so. But I ask how they know it to be so. If the writings of the divine books contain it, let them read it out; if some line of reasoning suggests it, let them teach it; if they like to practise dialectic, let them prove it. If none of these is available, let them at least yield to their own opinion and not believe that beings which are incorporeal in themselves are bodily outside themselves, since something that can be nothing outside itself cannot be something else outside itself. Accordingly the mind, which is incorporeal in itself, can in no way be bodily outside itself, because its author does not know it to be anything other than what he made, and it cannot know itself to be anything other than what it was made. Hence, if the mind knows the truth when it knows itself to be incorporeal, then God is deceived if he knows as bodily a mind that is truly incorporeal. But God cannot be deceived. Therefore he knows the mind to be incorporeal, so that the truth by which the mind truly knows itself to be incorporeal may not be false. The mind, then, is incorporeal to itself precisely because it is incorporeal to its Creator. Earth is earth to man because it is earth to God; water, air and fire are what they are to man because they are the same to God; and everything that has truly become known to man is, in man's knowledge, what it is. In the same way the human mind cannot possibly be one thing and be known to God as another. For the Creator's knowledge does not come from his acquaintance with things; rather, the existence of things comes from the Creator's knowledge. Therefore the human mind could not be incorporeal unless it were incorporeal to God. For whatever is in any way incorporeal can in no way be bodily. But so as not to dwell here longer than is fitting, come, let us also look into a point that we have not discussed at all.
XIII. THAT MAN CONSISTS OF TWO SUBSTANCES, AN IMMORTAL AND NON-LOCAL SOUL AND A MORTAL AND LOCAL BODY; AND THAT JUST AS THE SOUL SUFFERS IMMORTALLY, SO IT IS GLORIFIED IMMORTALLY AND NON-LOCALLY.

For you say: "When the mind paints for itself, within the secret places of the mind, the likeness of Peter or Paul, say, has it instantly entered the innermost seats of paradise where it knows them to be? Or when, from reading, it has pictured in its heart the flames of that rich man, has it already gone down to the place of his torments and to the depths of the underworld, which are inaccessible to the living?" I have already given you answers, as was fitting, about the incorporeal places of souls, about hell and paradise, and about the soul's incorporeal gaze without the body, when we spoke about the rich man and the poor man and when we treated the soul's twofold sight. But since your statement that the underworld is inaccessible to the living remains undiscussed, I ask in what sense you said it. We consist, of course, of soul and body. And although no one doubts what in us is immortal and what mortal, I will deal with you in such a way that I answer on whichever you prefer. If we die in neither of our substances, then no part of us goes down to the underworld, since you have said the underworld is inaccessible to the living. If we die in both, then the body also goes down to the underworld, and we need not look far for this bodily underworld, since the very tomb of the Lord is the place of the underworld. But sound judgment rejects both of these absurdities. So we neither die in both substances nor fail to die in both. The soul lives on even when the body has been laid aside, though if it is deprived of its God through sin it may rightly be called dead. Yet it will not be at all credible that a sinful soul loses the very fact of being a soul, since even a dead body does not cease to be a body. For the body dies when it loses the soul together with all its life, but the soul does not lose the soul. Therefore the soul is immortal, while the body is mortal. Now if the body does not enter the underworld, since it is committed to the tomb and scattered into the various parts of the world according to the diversity of the elements that had combined in it, and if the mind does not go to the underworld because your opinion closes the underworld to the living, then either there is no underworld or no human being goes down to it. And so the logic of our faith will be in danger, if not even the Redeemer's soul opened up the underworld by going there and returning. A fine thing, that anyone could say that whatever that underworld is, it is inaccessible to the living, when it is clear that it can be entered only by the living!

Remember now that you had staked your treatise on this: if you could prove that the soul is subject to quantity or place, even the opposing side would agree with you about its bodiliness. But if you recall your writings well, you can also notice that you set out what was to be argued rather than arguing what you set out. Nor did you, in the manner of the older Academics, know your own ignorance; rather, like the younger members of that school, you did not know whether you knew anything. Who, having rashly laid down two points on which the whole body of his work necessarily rests, would not strive to make both of them, if he could, or at least one of them, if he could not manage both, if not proven then certainly credible to someone? Two things, of course, combine to win a victory: a good cause must be matched with a good advocate. If one of these is lacking, the force of the case is weakened; if both are lacking, it collapses. So now falsehood, having found in you a defender who is both forgetful and ignorant, has brought about among people of keen understanding not only that it is plain you are not to be believed on these matters, but also that the truth, which is always to be believed, appears clearer and more illustrious through the necessity of conflict and by comparison with falsehood.
XIV. THAT THE SOUL IS NOT HELD ENCLOSED IN THE BODY, NOR IS IT MOVED FROM PLACE TO PLACE, ALTHOUGH IT IS MOVED IN TIME THROUGH AFFECTION.

You freely promised, then, that you would establish quality, quantity and place in the soul, and you immediately added: "How is it not local, since, inserted into the limbs and bound to the inner organs, wandering only in its movements, it is held enclosed by the condition of its substance?" Even if you had perhaps thought something wrongly and argued that it seemed probable, error could hardly make one thing pardonable, ignorance of the error another [?]. But now I am utterly amazed that you said things so conflicting and so different in practically the same moment and almost the same breath: that it is bound to the limbs and yet wanders in its movements, and again that, wandering in its movements, it is held enclosed by the condition of its substance. If the soul moves within the enclosure of the body, as you say, then it moves while standing still, which reason does not allow to be said. But if it is carried by its movements outside the body, then it is not held enclosed by the condition of its substance. And what do you mean by "wandering only in its movements"? As if anything could wander without moving! Or as if it were not easier for something to be moved without wandering—which the mind does through affection, since it is indeed subject to motion, though not according to place—than for something to wander and be moved, which is surely proper to body, since body is subject also to movement through place. Yet you say that the soul both stands still while wandering and wanders while enclosed, when, as was established above, it can both remain still while the body moves and move while the body is still.

So much for your argument about the soul's being in place. On this point, however, I do not charge you with sloth. You simply could not do it, and on this point above all not even the most powerful orator could have done it; for however rich his eloquence, a champion of falsehood can tell lies against plain truth, but he cannot deceive. As for quantity, I cannot say that it was forgetfulness that led you to promise to discuss it and then say nothing about it, since it is quite clear that you could not even have mentioned its name except from memory. We must rather believe that you were neither unwilling nor forgetful, but simply found nothing to say. And again, what sense does it make either to bring up for debate what should be passed over in silence, or to pass over in silence what was put forward? There will be no dispute about quality, for I have not denied that the soul is subject to it. If the soul were without quality as well as without quantity, it would certainly be God; and again, if it were subject to quantity as well as to quality, it would be a body. As it is, the soul has received a kind of intermediate nature, incorporeal but created: it is not God, because it has quality, and it is not a body, because it has no quantity.

As we showed in the arguments we pursued earlier, in questions of this kind the boundless lies open all too widely. Since such a question embraces the origins of the first causes, it cannot be examined far inside unless you use the balance of judgment to distinguish, so far as is permitted to man, the creature of twofold substance. Either one must stop altogether, or one must approach the matter along these lines: first separate body from the incorporeal; then, just as within the whole range of bodies you rank bright things above dark, high above low, precious above cheap, so also among created incorporeal things you should place human souls above those of beasts; among human souls, wise ones above foolish; and further, among those that are strong by nature, learned souls above unlearned.
XV. THAT THE SUN AND MOON AND STARS ARE ONLY BODIES AND HAVE NO SPIRITS; AND THAT JUST AS A BETTER BODY IS RANKED ABOVE A LOWER BODY, SO A SPIRIT THAT REMEMBERS IS RANKED ABOVE A LOWER SPIRIT.

For just as the sun is a body, and any stone, though vastly unlike it, is nonetheless a body all the same, so the nature of every kind of life is entirely incorporeal. But just as one body surpasses another, though both are bodies, so one mind is preferred to another, though both are minds. Here again a rich subject and abundant matter invite me to speak; meeting me almost seductively with their own beauty, they ask, and even compel, to be described. But let those approach these excellences, pre-eminences and summits, above all those, if there are any, "whom burning virtue has raised to the heavens." For my part, my task at present was to answer this question about the state of the soul as it was posed by the man with whom we have engaged, and perhaps somewhat more besides. Whether I have done it rightly or not, a fair and learned judge will decide.
XVI. A BRIEF RECAPITULATION OF THE PRECEDING BOOKS.

Since a reader cannot easily keep in memory the many things we have argued here and there in discussing this question, I have gathered together, briefly and as it were point by point, the things that were set out piecemeal and, as I think, proven, and have brought them under the mind's eye, collected so that they may be reviewed and recognized again together.
1. On the incorporeal.

God is incorporeal, and the human mind is the image of God, since man was made after the likeness and image of God. Now the image of something incorporeal cannot be a body. Therefore, since the human mind is the image of God, the human mind is incorporeal.
2. On life.

Everything non-local is also incorporeal. Now the soul is the life of the body, and in a living body the smallest part of the body lives just as much as the whole body. There is therefore as much life in a part of the body as in the whole body, and this life is the soul. Nothing that is as great in the whole as in any part, and as great in the small as in the large, is local. Therefore the mind is not local; and whatever is non-local is not bodily. Therefore the soul is not a body.
3. On reason.
Again, the rational soul reasons, and reasoning belongs to the soul's very substance, and reason is incorporeal and non-local. Therefore the soul is incorporeal.
4. On the will.
Again, the soul's will is its substance; if the whole soul wills, it is wholly will; and the will is not a body. Therefore the soul is not a body.
5. On memory.

Again, memory is a kind of non-local capacity, which is neither stretched by a multitude of things to be remembered nor thinned by their fewness, and which remembers even bodily things incorporeally. When the mind remembers, it remembers as a whole, and the mind that remembers as a whole is wholly memory; and memory is not a body. Therefore the mind is not a body.
6. On touch.

Again, when a body is touched in one of its parts, it feels the touch where it is touched; but the mind feels as a whole through less than the whole body, that is, through a part of the body. Sensation of this kind is non-local, and everything non-local is incorporeal. Therefore every soul is incorporeal.
7. On approach and withdrawal.
Again, a body neither draws near to God nor withdraws from God, but the mind both draws near and moves away non-locally. Therefore the mind is not a body.
8. On motion.
Again, a body is moved through place, but the mind is not moved through place. Therefore the mind is not a body.
9. On measure.
Again, length, breadth and height are found in a body, and whatever lacks them is not a body. The mind lacks them. Therefore it is not a body.
10. On right and left.
Right and left, up and down, front and back are found in every body, but in no soul. Therefore every soul is incorporeal.

There: we have drawn together from every part of our arguments everything we set out to do in the whole work. What we have recapitulated here as briefly as possible could not have been made convincing without the preceding arguments. And yet, had so great a cause found a fit champion, he would not have dishonoured its dignity, as I have, with speech quite unequal to it. Nor would I myself have been unable to pursue this same question rather more broadly and at greater length. But it was surely fitting to fight only as long as the adversary was able to resist, or, once he gave way and turned his back in flight, to take him captive and strip him of his leaden daggers. To go further, hurling weapons into the air and fighting without an enemy, is empty striving and a waste of strength, as inglorious as it is effortless.
XVII. AGAINST THE FASTIDIOUS CRITIC AND SLANDERER OF THESE BOOKS: HOW HE MAY BE DEFEATED. HE HAS PUT FORWARD A COMPARISON DRAWN FROM THE WORLD.

"Why then," someone will say, "have you ranged over these three volumes against one short page, if a word for a word is enough?" But building a deception and tearing it down are not the same task. Someone may deny that the world is a sphere. He will have denied it in a single word, but not even Timaeus could prove it in a single word. So whatever we have said at some length was required not only by the bare refutation of the false but also by the establishing of the true. Unteaching what is harmful is one thing and teaching what is useful another. Pulling thorns from the soil is not the same as sowing grain, and so rooting out vice is not the same as planting virtue. Much more effort must therefore go into doing both than into doing either one. Since both tasks fell to me, and in so difficult an undertaking, my brevity is more remarkable than my length. The arguments presented themselves from every side, shining out and displaying themselves, and they gave rise to many others. So, although the case could have been argued more broadly, I prescribed a number, set a measure and fixed a limit. I did not want to bring more into the battle than necessary, or fight longer than was reasonable, or go further than was right.
18. At the end of this book he asks his opponent's pardon and chooses that opponent himself as judge of the contest between them.

Now I turn to you, whoever you are. The wrong done by your writings compelled me to speak against them. I beg and beseech you not to be angry with me, for I have returned no abuse and repaid no insult. I have paid you back only truth for falsehood, which is hardly an equal exchange. I am, and will remain, an adversary of those views which harm you all the more the more they are yours, and for your own sake I urge you to oppose them too. I have given these few slight answers as far as the shortness of time allowed. Now weigh both sides for yourself. Take on the role of judge between me and you, and bring out the scales of justice. If our pan sinks lower and is heavier with truth, do not be reluctant or ashamed to turn your desertion into a homecoming and to withdraw from falsehood and take shelter under truth. But if you are obstinate, which I would not wish (and may you not be persuaded to it), then publish something in support of your opinion for the public to read, and do not hide your name. Only let God grant us our faculties and our life. Since each of us has in turn made trial of the ways [?], you will surely find out how great the power of truth is to destroy falsehood.

Venerable sir, if I were not sending you what I write so that you could examine and correct it, it might rightly seem superfluous and proud of me to want to teach someone I know to be learned. It would be like giving a drachma out of my poverty to someone rich in many talents of knowledge. This is why the publication of the books I sent you made me cautious and anxious. I composed them using the most subtle disputation of the philosophical art, and so I did not want to trust my own judgment about their meaning but chose to submit them to the expertise of a better man. I have sent for your judgment and approval not only what I have now gathered from reading them, but also what I committed to memory long ago from various sources. Your worthiness knows well that we have hardly anyone with whom we can confer and so be made firm and steady about the things we are unsure of. Every nature that comes to [?] knowledge is called by its own proper name, and so a name shows the nature of each thing.

So the ancients said that a name is what makes a thing known, because it brings images of the thing itself into the ears, as though through the senses of the body, and memory directs this. Just as we understand one another when we speak, so too we think, whenever we wish, of absent things and of the images held in memory. But the nature of things is twofold, corporeal and spiritual, for every creature is either spirit or body. We perceive corporeal things through the body, and we grasp intellectual things with the intellect. So, as far as this life allows, we have knowledge of everything in two ways. What, then, does it mean to say that there are three kinds of question: whether a thing is, what it is, and what sort it is? Why, I ask, do we ask whether it is, when all knowledge that shows us a thing removes uncertainty and leaves no room for doubt? I think this question was posed because not all things are substances: some things are found which the proofs show [?] are not. For example, if someone asks whether good is a substance or not, we answer that it is not a substance but a privation of evil. The first question rightly asks whether a thing is body or spirit. The next asks what sort it is: whether a body is animal or spiritual, or whether a spirit is rational or irrational. So it was right to define three kinds of question, and I think we have now said enough about them, briefly. Now let us also consider how many kinds of body there are.

Body includes countless species, but there are three kinds: body that lives and has sensation, body that lives but has no sensation, and body that neither lives nor has sensation. I take the kind of body that neither lives nor has sensation to be the four elements: earth, water, air and fire. These are primary and simple, and all bodies are composed of them, namely the bodies of animals, which live and have sensation, and those of trees, shrubs and plants, which live but have no sensation.

Since it is quite clear how these differ from one another, let us now inquire more closely, with God's help, into what they have in common. For with the Lord's inspiration and help we wish not only to examine his creation but also to ascend to the creating substance and behold it with the understanding through the things that have been made. We may not reach the point of understanding his substance and knowing what it is. But at least we can hold with complete clarity what it is not.

Every body, then, is subject to quantity and quality, but body is not found in a subject. For body is a subject and is not in a subject, because body is a substance, not an accident. Accidents exist in a substance; they are not substances. Quantity and quality, then, are accidents of body: quantity lies in measurements and quality in colors. Being a body is not the same as having a certain size, nor the same as having a certain quality. When its color changes the body remains, and when the body is made smaller the quantity it had before is gone. So what is large is not largeness, what is long is not length, what is broad is not breadth, and what is colored is not color itself. Body also has measure, number and weight. That is why holy Scripture says that God arranged all things in measure and number and weight. But I see that this also applies to rational spirit in another way, which I will discuss later. Now let us explain what we began to say about body. We said that what is large is not largeness. In the same way, what is measurable is not measure, what is countable is not number, and what can be weighed is not weight. Body can therefore be diminished [?], since every part of it has an above and a below, a right and a left, a front and a back. It moves through time and place. It does not judge but is judged. It can be divided into parts without end.

Come now, let us see what it is that gives the body life and [?] sensation. For what receives life and what gives it are better matched to life [?]. Life is no less in a part than in the whole. It is not smaller in a smaller part, and it does not give a larger share to a larger part and a smaller share to a smaller one. Life, then, is not body but spirit. The spirit of a beast does not survive after the body, so we must pass over it here and come to rational spirit. Spirit has no quantity. If it were long or broad, it would properly be said to have a certain size. It is wisely distinguished and set apart from body because it is not subject to quantity, although it is subject to quality. Branches of learning belong to the mind as accidents, and so do justice and injustice, chastity and lust. There are four principal virtues: prudence and temperance, fortitude and justice. The prudent mind is not prudence itself, nor is the just mind justice, the temperate mind temperance, or the brave mind fortitude. Being a mind is one thing, and being a just mind is another. When I say "a just mind," I understand two things. I would say the same of prudence, temperance and fortitude, because a mind can exist without being endowed with any virtues at all. But if it does not have them, it follows that it has vice. We conclude that the mind is always the subject of either vices or virtues, and also, as we said, the subject of branches of learning, which cannot exist without it. The science of number is one such branch of learning. It will never happen that four and two make seven, or that seven and three make eleven. Likewise the figure of a circle admits no contrary. It will never happen that a circle is made of two or three lines, a square of three, or a triangle of four. If you add or take away anything, it will no longer be a triangle or a square, for the figure remains eternal and unchangeable. The principles of these branches of learning are in the mind as their subject and cannot exist without it. We conclude that the thing they are in is eternal, just as what is in it is eternal. So the soul is immortal, and it always knows and discerns that it lives. But it does not always think about this. Secure in itself, it knows that it loses itself in many thoughts, and it extends itself as it were through time, not through place. Although the soul is moved through time and not place, it moves the body through time and place. It judges and is judged.

See then, human soul, how great a good you are. You judge bodies, you are joined to reason, and you become a partaker of eternal truth. You must not love the things that are below you. Measure is in you, yet you are not measure. Your thought has number and your pleasure has weight, yet you are neither number nor weight. Turn the will of your love toward that number without number, of which the psalmist says, "and of his wisdom there is no number"; toward that measure without measure and that weight without weight, by which all things are weighed and measured. That is the highest good. By it all kinds of bodies were made good, and by it the great goods of rational beings were made. Leave behind both the good things and the great goods, and love the highest good and the simple good. That good is the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit, and this Trinity is one God. Yet body or spirit should be loved according to the way each ought to be loved. As a most noble expounder of the holy Scriptures said, "You will lay down four rules of love: what is above us, what is beside us, what is ourselves, and what is below us." Let us therefore love that highest good which is above us, not in the order of place but in the order of nature, for the creature cannot be made equal to the Creator. Only the Son is equal to the Father, and likewise the Holy Spirit, because they are not creatures but share one nature among them.
